blockchain.short: A blockchain is a shared digital ledger, copied across many computers, where transactions are grouped into blocks that are linked in order and are extremely hard to change after the fact.
body: Each block holds a batch of transactions plus a cryptographic fingerprint (a hash) of the block before it. Because every block points back to the previous one, changing an old transaction would change its hash and break every block after it. Thousands of independent computers, called nodes, keep their own copy and reject a version that does not follow the rules.

New blocks are added through a consensus mechanism. Bitcoin uses proof of work, where miners spend electricity to compete for the right to add the next block. Ethereum and many newer networks use proof of stake, where validators lock up coins as collateral. Either way, no single company decides which transactions are valid.

For you as a user, the blockchain is the public record of who owns what. When you withdraw coins from an exchange, the transfer is final once it is recorded and confirmed on-chain. There is no customer service desk that can reverse it, which is why sending to the wrong address or the wrong network usually means the funds are lost.
blockchain.example: Suppose you send 0.05 BTC from an exchange to your own wallet. The exchange broadcasts the transaction, and it waits in a queue until a miner includes it in a block, roughly every 10 minutes on Bitcoin. After that block is added, your transfer has 1 confirmation. Many exchanges wait for 2 to 6 confirmations before crediting a Bitcoin deposit, so the money can take 20 to 60 minutes to appear, even though anyone can already see it on a block explorer.
mistakes: Assuming a blockchain transfer can be cancelled or refunded like a card payment once it is confirmed.
Thinking every blockchain is the same network, then sending tokens on one chain to an address on an unsupported chain.
Believing that data on a blockchain is automatically true, when it only proves what was recorded, not whether a project is honest.

faq.q: Is a blockchain the same as Bitcoin?
faq.a: No. Bitcoin is one cryptocurrency that runs on its own blockchain. Ethereum, Solana and many other networks each run their own separate blockchains.

faq.q: Can a blockchain be hacked?
faq.a: Large public blockchains like Bitcoin and Ethereum have never had their core ledger rewritten in a normal way, because that would require controlling a huge share of mining or stake. Most losses come from hacked exchanges, buggy smart contracts or stolen private keys, not from the chain itself.

faq.q: Who controls a public blockchain?
faq.a: No single party. The rules are enforced by the software that thousands of independent nodes run, and changes need broad agreement from developers, node operators and miners or validators.

blockchain.title: What is a blockchain? Meaning and how it works
blockchain.description: Learn what a blockchain is, how blocks and confirmations work, and why on-chain transfers cannot be reversed.

cryptocurrency.short: A cryptocurrency is a digital asset that is issued and transferred on a blockchain, secured by cryptography instead of a bank or central authority.
body: Ownership of a cryptocurrency is recorded on a public blockchain. What you actually hold is a private key, a secret number that lets you sign transactions moving coins from your address. Whoever controls the key controls the coins, which is why exchanges and wallets put so much effort into key security.

The word covers very different assets. Bitcoin is designed as scarce digital money with a fixed 21 million supply. Ether pays for computation on Ethereum. Stablecoins such as USDT and USDC aim to track the US dollar. Thousands of other tokens represent projects, governance rights or simply internet culture, as with memecoins.

Prices are set by trading on exchanges around the clock, every day of the year. That means crypto can move sharply at night or over a weekend, and price swings of 5 to 10 percent in a day are common for many coins. How crypto is taxed and regulated depends on your country, so rules that apply to a friend abroad may not apply to you.
cryptocurrency.example: Suppose you deposit 500 USDT on an exchange and buy ETH at 2,500 USDT per coin. You receive 0.2 ETH, minus a small trading fee. If ETH later trades at 2,750 USDT, your 0.2 ETH is worth 550 USDT, a 10 percent gain before fees. If it falls to 2,250 USDT, the same holding is worth 450 USDT. The number of coins you own stays at 0.2 ETH; only their price in dollars changes.
mistakes: Treating all cryptocurrencies as interchangeable when a stablecoin, Bitcoin and a new memecoin carry completely different risks.
Sharing a seed phrase or private key with someone who claims to be support staff.
Buying a coin because its unit price looks cheap, without checking its total supply and market capitalization.

faq.q: Is cryptocurrency real money?
faq.a: Some countries treat certain cryptocurrencies as legal property or payment methods, while others restrict them. In practice, crypto has value because people are willing to trade it, and it can be exchanged for local currency on exchanges.

faq.q: What was the first cryptocurrency?
faq.a: Bitcoin, launched in January 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first widely used cryptocurrency.

faq.q: Do I need to buy a whole coin?
faq.a: No. Most cryptocurrencies are divisible. You can buy 0.001 BTC or 10 USDT worth of a coin on most exchanges.

cryptocurrency.title: What is cryptocurrency? Meaning explained simply
cryptocurrency.description: Understand what cryptocurrency is, how ownership and private keys work, and why prices move around the clock.

bitcoin.short: Bitcoin (BTC) is the first cryptocurrency, a decentralized digital money with a hard cap of 21 million coins that runs on its own proof-of-work blockchain.
body: Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto. Miners around the world bundle transactions into a new block about every 10 minutes and receive newly created BTC plus fees as a reward. Every four years or so the block reward is cut in half in an event called the halving; the April 2024 halving reduced it to 3.125 BTC per block.

The supply limit of 21 million BTC is written into the protocol, which is why many people see Bitcoin as digital scarcity rather than a payment app. Each bitcoin divides into 100,000,000 units called satoshis, so you can own a tiny fraction.

You can buy BTC on centralized exchanges, hold it in a self-custody wallet, or gain price exposure through products such as the US spot bitcoin ETFs that began trading in January 2024. On exchanges, BTC is the most liquid crypto asset, with BTC/USDT usually the deepest spot pair and the biggest perpetual futures market.
bitcoin.example: Suppose BTC trades at 80,000 USDT and you want to invest 200 USDT. You would receive 0.0025 BTC, which equals 250,000 satoshis. If the price rises 5 percent to 84,000 USDT, your holding is worth 210 USDT. If you instead bought it with 3x leverage on futures, the same 5 percent move would change your margin by about 15 percent, in either direction.
mistakes: Waiting to afford a whole bitcoin, when you can buy any small fraction.
Sending BTC to an address on another network, such as a BEP20 or ERC20 address, without checking the exchange's supported withdrawal network.
Confusing Bitcoin with forks or similarly named tokens such as Bitcoin Cash or wrapped BTC.

faq.q: How many bitcoins are there?
faq.a: The protocol caps supply at 21 million BTC. More than 19 million have already been mined, and the remaining coins are released more slowly after each halving.

faq.q: Who controls Bitcoin?
faq.a: No company or government controls the network. Changes require broad agreement among developers, miners, node operators and users.

faq.q: What is the difference between BTC and XBT?
faq.a: They are the same asset. XBT is an alternative ticker used by some exchanges and data providers to follow currency code conventions.

bitcoin.title: What is Bitcoin (BTC)? Meaning, supply and how it works
bitcoin.description: Learn what Bitcoin is, why its supply is capped at 21 million, how halvings work and how to buy a fraction of a BTC.

ethereum.short: Ethereum is a programmable blockchain that runs smart contracts, and Ether (ETH) is its native coin used to pay gas fees and to stake for network security.
body: Where Bitcoin focuses on being money, Ethereum is designed as a global computer. Developers deploy smart contracts, programs that run exactly as written, and these power stablecoins, decentralized exchanges, lending markets, NFTs and many of the tokens you see on exchanges.

Every action on Ethereum costs gas, paid in ETH. When the network is busy, gas prices rise, which is why many users move to layer 2 networks such as Arbitrum, Optimism or Base that settle back to Ethereum but charge much lower fees. Since 2021, part of every fee is burned, permanently removing that ETH from supply.

In September 2022 Ethereum moved from proof of work to proof of stake in an upgrade called the Merge. Validators now lock up ETH to propose and confirm blocks and earn rewards for doing so. Many exchanges let you stake ETH through their earn products, while liquid staking protocols give you a token that represents staked ETH. Check the lock-up and withdrawal terms before you stake.
ethereum.example: Suppose you want to swap tokens on a decentralized exchange on Ethereum mainnet and the gas cost is 150,000 units at 20 gwei. The fee is 150,000 x 20 = 3,000,000 gwei, or 0.003 ETH. At an ETH price of 3,000 USDT, that is about 9 USDT. The same swap on a layer 2 might cost well under 0.10 USDT, which matters a lot if you are only trading 50 USDT.
mistakes: Withdrawing ETH to a layer 2 or another EVM chain without checking which network the receiving wallet or exchange supports.
Keeping no ETH in a wallet, then being unable to move ERC20 tokens because there is nothing to pay gas with.
Assuming staked ETH can always be withdrawn instantly; unstaking can involve a queue or product-specific lock period.

faq.q: Is Ether the same as Ethereum?
faq.a: Ethereum is the network, and Ether (ETH) is its native coin. In everyday speech many people call the coin Ethereum too.

faq.q: Does Ethereum have a maximum supply?
faq.a: No fixed cap exists. New ETH is issued to validators, while part of every transaction fee is burned, so net supply can rise or fall depending on network activity.

faq.q: What changed with the Merge?
faq.a: In September 2022 Ethereum switched from proof of work to proof of stake. Mining ended, and validators who stake ETH now secure the network.

ethereum.title: What is Ethereum (ETH)? Meaning, gas and staking
ethereum.description: Learn what Ethereum and Ether are, how gas fees are calculated, and what the Merge and proof of stake changed.

altcoin.short: An altcoin is any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin, a broad category that includes Ether, Solana, stablecoins, exchange tokens and memecoins.
body: The name comes from "alternative coin", because early projects were alternatives to Bitcoin. Today the term is used loosely. Some traders exclude stablecoins and only mean volatile coins, while others use "alts" for anything that is not BTC or ETH.

Altcoins range from large networks with years of history and deep liquidity to tiny tokens launched last week. The smaller the market capitalization and trading volume, the more the price can swing on a single large order, and the higher the risk that a project fails or a team sells its tokens.

Many altcoins tend to move in the same direction as Bitcoin, often with bigger percentage swings both up and down. Periods when altcoins outperform BTC are popularly called "altseason", but they are not regular or predictable. Before buying an altcoin, check its circulating supply, unlock schedule, where it is listed and how much it trades each day.
altcoin.example: Suppose BTC falls 8 percent in a day. A mid-sized altcoin that often moves with about 1.5 times Bitcoin's swings might fall around 12 percent, and a small altcoin could drop 20 percent or more. If you held 1,000 USDT in that small coin, a 20 percent drop leaves 800 USDT, and you would need a 25 percent gain just to get back to 1,000 USDT.
mistakes: Buying an altcoin only because its price per coin is low, without comparing market capitalization.
Assuming every altcoin will recover after a crash; many never return to earlier highs.
Ignoring liquidity, then finding that selling a large position moves the price sharply against you.

faq.q: Is Ethereum an altcoin?
faq.a: Technically yes, because it is not Bitcoin. In practice many traders treat ETH as its own category and use "altcoin" for coins beyond BTC and ETH.

faq.q: Are stablecoins altcoins?
faq.a: Under the broad definition they are, but most people do not call USDT or USDC altcoins because they are designed not to fluctuate.

faq.q: What is altseason?
faq.a: Altseason is a slang term for a period when many altcoins rise faster than Bitcoin. It is a description of past market phases, not a scheduled event.

altcoin.title: What is an altcoin? Meaning and risks explained
altcoin.description: Learn what an altcoin is, how altcoins differ from Bitcoin, and why liquidity and market cap matter before you buy.

coin-vs-token.short: A coin is the native asset of its own blockchain, such as BTC or ETH, while a token is an asset created on top of an existing blockchain using a smart contract, such as USDT on Ethereum.
body: A coin is built into the protocol of its blockchain. It usually pays transaction fees and rewards miners or validators: BTC on Bitcoin, ETH on Ethereum, SOL on Solana. A token is created by a smart contract that runs on someone else's chain, following a standard such as ERC20 on Ethereum or SPL on Solana.

This difference matters most when you move funds. A token like USDT exists on several chains at once, and each version lives at a different contract. When you withdraw, the exchange asks you to choose a network. The receiving address must support the same network, or the transfer can fail or be lost.

It also matters for fees. To move a token you pay gas in the chain's coin, not in the token. Holding 100 USDT on Ethereum is not enough to send it; you also need a little ETH in the same wallet. In casual speech people mix the two words, and many exchanges simply call everything a coin.
coin-vs-token.example: Suppose you hold 300 USDT on the Tron network in a wallet with zero TRX. When you try to send the USDT, the wallet warns that you lack resources for the fee. You buy 20 TRX, send it to the wallet, and the transfer goes through. The same 300 USDT on Arbitrum would need a small amount of ETH on Arbitrum instead, because each token pays fees in its host chain's coin.
mistakes: Choosing a different withdrawal network from the one the receiving exchange or wallet supports.
Trying to send a token from a wallet that holds none of the chain's native coin for gas.
Adding a token by name in a wallet without checking the contract address, which is how fake tokens get displayed.

faq.q: Is USDT a coin or a token?
faq.a: USDT is a token. Tether issues it on several blockchains, including Ethereum, Tron and Solana, each as a separate contract.

faq.q: Can a token become a coin?
faq.a: Yes, some projects start as tokens on Ethereum and later launch their own blockchain, then swap holders into the new native coin in a migration.

faq.q: Why does my exchange call everything a coin?
faq.a: It is a simplification for users. On the deposit and withdrawal screens, the network selector shows which chain the asset actually lives on.

coin-vs-token.title: Coin vs token: what is the difference in crypto?
coin-vs-token.description: Learn the difference between a coin and a token, why networks matter for withdrawals, and which coin pays the gas.

satoshi.short: A satoshi (sat) is the smallest unit of Bitcoin, equal to 0.00000001 BTC, so one bitcoin contains 100,000,000 satoshis.
body: The unit is named after Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. Because BTC has eight decimal places, prices and balances can get awkward to read, so many wallets and apps let you display amounts in sats instead.

Counting in sats makes small purchases feel more natural. Instead of saying you bought 0.00025 BTC, you can say you bought 25,000 sats. People who buy a fixed amount every week often talk about "stacking sats", meaning steadily accumulating small amounts.

Sats also appear in fee settings. On the Bitcoin network, transaction fees are commonly quoted in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB). A higher fee rate makes it more likely that miners include your transaction quickly when the network is busy. Exchanges usually charge a fixed BTC withdrawal fee instead and handle the on-chain fee for you.
satoshi.example: Suppose BTC trades at 60,000 USDT. One satoshi is then worth 60,000 divided by 100,000,000, which is 0.0006 USDT. If you buy 30 USDT of BTC each week, you get 0.0005 BTC, or 50,000 sats, each time before fees. After 10 weeks at that same price you would hold 500,000 sats, which is 0.005 BTC.
mistakes: Miscounting decimal places and thinking 0.0001 BTC is 1,000 sats instead of 10,000 sats.
Assuming a satoshi has a fixed dollar value; it changes with the BTC price.
Setting a very low sat/vB fee in a self-custody wallet when the network is busy, leaving the transaction stuck for hours.

faq.q: How many satoshis are in 1 bitcoin?
faq.a: There are exactly 100,000,000 satoshis in 1 BTC.

faq.q: Can I buy satoshis directly?
faq.a: You buy BTC, and any fraction you buy is simply a number of satoshis. Some wallets and apps also let you display your balance in sats instead of BTC.

faq.q: What does stacking sats mean?
faq.a: It is slang for regularly buying small amounts of bitcoin over time, often through a recurring purchase.

satoshi.title: What is a satoshi (sats)? Bitcoin's smallest unit
satoshi.description: Learn what a satoshi is, how to convert sats to BTC and dollars, and why fees are quoted in sat/vB.

market-capitalization.short: Market capitalization is the total value of a cryptocurrency's circulating coins, calculated as the current price multiplied by the circulating supply.
body: Market cap lets you compare the size of projects fairly. A coin priced at 0.01 USDT can be worth far more in total than a coin priced at 500 USDT, depending on how many coins exist. Data sites rank coins by market cap, which is why you see BTC and ETH at the top.

The figure depends on the circulating supply estimate, which data providers calculate differently. Coins held by the team, foundation or investors under lock-up are usually excluded. That is why you should also check fully diluted valuation, which counts all coins that will ever exist.

Market cap is not the amount of money invested, and it is not the amount you could cash out. If a large share of coins were sold at once, the price would fall, so the real liquid value can be far lower. For small coins, look at daily trading volume and order book depth alongside market cap.
market-capitalization.example: Suppose Coin A trades at 2 USDT with 500 million coins in circulation, giving a market cap of 1 billion USDT. Coin B trades at 0.02 USDT with 100 billion coins in circulation, a market cap of 2 billion USDT. Coin B looks cheaper per coin, but the project is valued at twice the size of Coin A. For Coin B to reach 2 USDT, its market cap would need to hit 200 billion USDT.
mistakes: Judging a coin as cheap or expensive by its unit price instead of its market cap.
Treating market cap as money that has flowed in, when it is just price times supply.
Ignoring that circulating supply can grow quickly when locked tokens unlock.

faq.q: How is crypto market cap calculated?
faq.a: Multiply the current price by the circulating supply. A coin at 4 USDT with 250 million coins circulating has a market cap of 1 billion USDT.

faq.q: What is the difference between market cap and FDV?
faq.a: Market cap uses circulating supply, while fully diluted valuation uses the maximum or total supply. A big gap between them means many tokens are still to be released.

faq.q: Why do different sites show different market caps?
faq.a: They use different circulating supply estimates and slightly different price sources.

market-capitalization.title: What is market cap in crypto? Meaning and formula
market-capitalization.description: Learn how crypto market cap is calculated, why unit price is misleading and how market cap differs from FDV.

fully-diluted-valuation.short: Fully diluted valuation (FDV) is a project's value if all of its tokens that will ever exist were already in circulation, calculated as the current price multiplied by the maximum or total supply.
body: Many tokens launch with only a small share of supply circulating. The rest is reserved for the team, early investors, ecosystem funds or future rewards and is released over months or years. Market cap only counts the circulating part, so it can make a project look smaller than it really is.

FDV shows the size the project would have at today's price once every token is out. The ratio between market cap and FDV tells you how much new supply is still coming. If circulating supply is 15 percent of the total, the remaining 85 percent will enter the market over time, and someone has to buy those tokens for the price to hold.

Data sites calculate FDV with either maximum supply or total supply, and some tokens have no maximum at all, so compare like with like. FDV is not a price target; it is a tool for spotting heavy future dilution.
fully-diluted-valuation.example: Suppose a new token trades at 0.50 USDT with 200 million tokens circulating and a maximum supply of 1 billion. Its market cap is 100 million USDT, but its FDV is 500 million USDT. Only 20 percent of the supply is out. If the other 800 million tokens unlock over three years, roughly 22 million tokens enter circulation each month on average, and at today's price that is about 11 million USDT of new supply monthly.
mistakes: Looking only at market cap on a low-float token and missing that FDV is several times larger.
Treating FDV as a forecast of where the price will go.
Comparing one project's FDV based on maximum supply with another's based on total supply.

faq.q: Is a high FDV bad?
faq.a: Not by itself. A high FDV compared with market cap means a lot of supply is still to come, which can create selling pressure if demand does not keep up.

faq.q: What is a low float token?
faq.a: A token where only a small percentage of total supply is circulating. These often have a large gap between market cap and FDV.

faq.q: Does Bitcoin have an FDV?
faq.a: Yes. It is the price multiplied by 21 million BTC. Because most bitcoins are already mined, Bitcoin's FDV is close to its market cap.

fully-diluted-valuation.title: What is FDV (fully diluted valuation) in crypto?
fully-diluted-valuation.description: Learn what fully diluted valuation means, how it differs from market cap and how to spot heavy token dilution.

circulating-supply.short: Circulating supply is the number of coins or tokens that are publicly available and moving in the market right now, excluding locked, reserved or burned tokens.
body: Crypto projects usually report three supply numbers. Circulating supply is what can be traded today. Total supply is everything created so far minus burned tokens. Maximum supply is the hard cap that will ever exist, if there is one. Bitcoin's maximum is 21 million, while some tokens have no cap.

Circulating supply is the input for market capitalization, so it shapes how big a project looks. It changes over time: it grows when locked team and investor tokens unlock, when staking or mining rewards are issued, and it shrinks when tokens are burned or bought back.

Data providers sometimes disagree on which wallets count as circulating, for example treasury or foundation wallets. If a project's numbers differ a lot between sites, read the project's own token documentation and check the unlock schedule.
circulating-supply.example: Suppose a token has a maximum supply of 1 billion and a circulating supply of 300 million at 1 USDT, a market cap of 300 million USDT. Next month, 50 million team tokens unlock. Circulating supply rises to 350 million, an increase of about 17 percent. If the price stayed at 1 USDT, market cap would rise to 350 million USDT, but in practice the extra supply can push the price down if demand does not grow.
mistakes: Confusing circulating supply with maximum supply when calculating value.
Assuming circulating supply is fixed, when unlocks and emissions can raise it every month.
Trusting a single data site without checking the project's published token allocation.

faq.q: What is the difference between circulating supply and total supply?
faq.a: Circulating supply counts tokens that can be traded now. Total supply also includes tokens that exist but are locked or held in reserve.

faq.q: Why does circulating supply increase?
faq.a: Common reasons are scheduled unlocks for teams and investors, staking or mining rewards, and ecosystem incentive programs.

faq.q: Can circulating supply go down?
faq.a: Yes, when tokens are burned or bought back and removed, or when tokens are moved into long-term locks that data providers stop counting.

circulating-supply.title: What is circulating supply in crypto? Meaning
circulating-supply.description: Learn what circulating supply means, how it differs from total and max supply, and why unlocks change it.

bitcoin-halving.short: A Bitcoin halving is a pre-programmed event, roughly every four years, that cuts the number of new bitcoins paid to miners for each block by 50 percent.
body: Bitcoin's rules release new coins through the block reward. The halving happens every 210,000 blocks, which at about 10 minutes per block works out to roughly four years. The reward started at 50 BTC in 2009, dropped to 25, 12.5, 6.25 and, after the April 2024 halving, 3.125 BTC per block.

This schedule is why Bitcoin's supply approaches 21 million but never exceeds it. Each halving slows the growth of new supply, and the last fractions of a bitcoin are expected to be mined around the year 2140. After that, miners will rely on transaction fees alone.

For miners, a halving instantly cuts revenue from new coins in half, so less efficient operations may shut down unless the price or fees make up the difference. For traders, halvings attract a lot of attention and narratives, but past price moves around halvings came with many other factors and do not guarantee any future result.
bitcoin-halving.example: Before the April 2024 halving, the reward was 6.25 BTC per block. With about 144 blocks a day, miners earned roughly 900 new BTC daily. After the halving to 3.125 BTC, that fell to about 450 BTC per day. At an illustrative price of 60,000 USDT, daily new-coin revenue for all miners combined dropped from about 54 million to 27 million USDT, not counting fees.
mistakes: Treating the halving as a guaranteed price catalyst instead of a supply schedule change.
Thinking the halving cuts existing holdings in half; it only affects newly issued coins.
Expecting the halving on an exact calendar date, when it is set by block height and can shift by days or weeks.

faq.q: When is the next Bitcoin halving?
faq.a: It is expected around 2028, after block 1,050,000 is mined. The exact date depends on how fast blocks are produced.

faq.q: What happens when all bitcoins are mined?
faq.a: Miners will no longer receive new BTC and will be paid only through transaction fees.

faq.q: Does the halving affect my BTC balance?
faq.a: No. Your coins stay exactly the same. Only the reward for new blocks changes.

bitcoin-halving.title: What is the Bitcoin halving? Meaning and schedule
bitcoin-halving.description: Learn how the Bitcoin halving works, how the block reward fell to 3.125 BTC and what it means for miners and supply.

proof-of-work.short: Proof of work (PoW) is a consensus mechanism in which miners use computing power to solve a puzzle, and the first to find a valid answer earns the right to add the next block and collect the reward.
body: Miners repeatedly hash a candidate block with a changing number until the result falls below a target set by the network. There is no shortcut; the only way is to try trillions of guesses. Finding a valid hash is hard, but anyone can check it instantly, which is what makes the system work.

Because adding blocks costs real electricity and hardware, attacking a PoW chain is expensive. To rewrite history, an attacker would need more than half of the network's hash rate and would have to keep spending energy to stay ahead. Bitcoin is the best-known PoW network; Litecoin, Dogecoin and Bitcoin Cash also use it.

The network adjusts difficulty automatically. On Bitcoin, difficulty changes every 2,016 blocks so blocks keep coming about every 10 minutes no matter how many miners join. Critics point to PoW's energy use, while supporters argue that the cost is exactly what secures the ledger. Ethereum used PoW until it switched to proof of stake in September 2022.
proof-of-work.example: Suppose the Bitcoin network runs at 600 exahashes per second and a small mining farm contributes 6 exahashes per second, or 1 percent. With about 144 blocks per day, the farm can expect to win around 1.44 blocks daily on average. At 3.125 BTC per block, that is roughly 4.5 BTC per day before fees and electricity costs, though actual daily results vary with luck.
mistakes: Thinking miners solve useful math problems; the puzzle is pure guessing designed to cost energy.
Assuming more miners means faster blocks, when difficulty adjusts to keep timing steady.
Believing a home computer can still mine Bitcoin profitably; specialised ASIC machines dominate.

faq.q: What is the difference between proof of work and proof of stake?
faq.a: Proof of work secures the chain with computing power and electricity. Proof of stake secures it with coins locked up as collateral by validators.

faq.q: Why does Bitcoin use proof of work?
faq.a: It makes attacks costly in real-world resources and lets anyone verify which chain has the most work behind it, without trusting a central party.

faq.q: Is Ethereum still proof of work?
faq.a: No. Ethereum switched to proof of stake in September 2022 with the Merge.

proof-of-work.title: What is proof of work (PoW)? Meaning in crypto
proof-of-work.description: Learn how proof of work secures Bitcoin, why mining uses energy and how it differs from proof of stake.

proof-of-stake.short: Proof of stake (PoS) is a consensus mechanism in which validators lock up the network's coins as collateral to propose and confirm blocks, earning rewards for honest work and losing part of their stake for breaking the rules.
body: Instead of competing with electricity like miners, validators put their own coins at risk. The protocol picks validators to propose blocks, and others vote to confirm them. If a validator signs conflicting blocks or tries to cheat, the protocol can destroy part of its stake, a penalty called slashing.

Ethereum switched to proof of stake in September 2022, cutting its energy use dramatically. Solana, Cardano, Avalanche and many other networks also use variants of PoS. Each sets its own rules for minimum stake, reward rates, lock-up periods and penalties.

Most holders do not run a validator themselves. They delegate coins to a validator, stake through an exchange earn product, or use a liquid staking protocol that issues a receipt token. Each route has trade-offs: exchange staking is simple but custodial, while liquid staking adds smart contract risk. Rewards are paid in the same coin, so their value in dollars still moves with the market.
proof-of-stake.example: Suppose you stake 10 ETH through a provider and the network reward works out to about 3 percent a year, minus a 10 percent commission taken by the provider. Your net rate is 2.7 percent, so after one year you would have about 10.27 ETH. If ETH fell from 3,000 to 2,500 USDT in that year, your position would be worth about 25,675 USDT instead of the 30,000 USDT you started with, so staking rewards do not protect you from price drops.
mistakes: Treating staking rewards as a fixed interest rate when they vary with network activity and the number of stakers.
Ignoring unstaking queues or lock periods and needing the funds urgently.
Forgetting that slashing, provider failures or smart contract bugs can reduce the staked amount.

faq.q: Is proof of stake safer than proof of work?
faq.a: They make different trade-offs. PoW ties security to energy and hardware, while PoS ties it to the value of staked coins that can be slashed. Both have secured large networks for years.

faq.q: Can I lose money staking?
faq.a: Yes. The coin's price can fall, a validator can be slashed, and a staking provider or smart contract can fail. The reward itself does not guarantee a profit in dollar terms.

faq.q: Which cryptocurrencies use proof of stake?
faq.a: Ethereum, Solana, Cardano, Avalanche, Polkadot and many others use some form of proof of stake.

proof-of-stake.title: What is proof of stake (PoS)? Meaning in crypto
proof-of-stake.description: Learn how proof of stake works, how validators and slashing keep it secure and what staking means for holders.

mining.short: Crypto mining is the process of using specialised computers to secure a proof-of-work blockchain by adding new blocks, in exchange for newly issued coins and transaction fees.
body: Miners collect pending transactions, build a candidate block and then race to find a hash that meets the network's difficulty target. The winner broadcasts the block, other nodes verify it, and the miner receives the block reward plus fees. On Bitcoin that reward is 3.125 BTC per block since the April 2024 halving.

Mining today is an industrial business. Bitcoin is mined with ASICs, chips built for a single hashing algorithm. Profitability depends on the coin price, the machine's efficiency, the electricity price and the network's total hash rate. When many new machines join, each miner's share of rewards shrinks.

Because a single miner might go months without finding a block, most join mining pools that combine hash power and share rewards in proportion to the work submitted. Be careful with cloud mining offers that promise fixed daily returns; many are scams, and legitimate ones still carry the same price and difficulty risks.
mining.example: Suppose a miner runs one ASIC that earns about 0.00012 BTC per day at current difficulty. At an illustrative BTC price of 70,000 USDT, that is 8.40 USDT per day. The machine uses 3.2 kWh per hour, or 76.8 kWh a day. At 0.08 USDT per kWh, electricity costs about 6.14 USDT, leaving roughly 2.26 USDT of daily gross profit before hardware costs, pool fees and repairs. If electricity cost 0.12 USDT per kWh, the miner would make a loss of about 0.82 USDT a day.
mistakes: Calculating profit with today's difficulty and price as if they will never change.
Paying for cloud mining contracts that promise guaranteed daily income.
Forgetting cooling, noise, hardware wear and local electricity rules when mining at home.

faq.q: Is crypto mining still profitable?
faq.a: It depends on electricity costs, hardware efficiency, coin price and network difficulty. Large operations with cheap power have a big advantage over home miners.

faq.q: Can you mine Ethereum?
faq.a: No. Ethereum stopped mining when it moved to proof of stake in September 2022. Validators now secure it by staking ETH.

faq.q: What is a mining pool?
faq.a: A mining pool combines the hash power of many miners and splits rewards according to each member's contributed work, giving smaller miners steadier payouts.

mining.title: What is crypto mining? Meaning and how it works
mining.description: Learn how crypto mining works, what drives mining profit, why pools exist and what to watch for with cloud mining.

validator.short: A validator is a participant in a proof-of-stake blockchain that locks up coins as collateral and runs software to propose new blocks and vote on whether other blocks are valid.
body: Validators replace miners in proof-of-stake networks. They must stay online, run up-to-date software and sign blocks correctly. In return they earn rewards from new issuance and transaction fees. If they go offline they may miss rewards, and if they sign conflicting messages they can be slashed, losing part of their stake.

Each network sets its own rules. On Ethereum, running a solo validator requires 32 ETH and a reliable machine. Other chains such as Solana or Cosmos-based networks let holders delegate coins to a validator, which then shares rewards after taking a commission.

When you stake on an exchange or through a liquid staking protocol, a validator is still doing the work in the background. Choosing who runs that validator matters: uptime, commission, slashing history and how concentrated the stake already is all affect your rewards and the health of the network.
validator.example: Suppose you delegate 1,000 SOL to a validator. The network's gross staking reward works out to about 7 percent a year for that validator, and it charges a 5 percent commission on rewards. Gross rewards would be 70 SOL, the validator keeps 3.5 SOL, and you receive about 66.5 SOL over the year. If the validator were offline for part of the year, your actual rewards would be lower.
mistakes: Choosing a validator only by the lowest commission without checking uptime and reliability.
Thinking delegated coins are sent to the validator; on most delegation systems they stay in your account but are locked.
Running a solo validator without backup monitoring and getting penalised for downtime.

faq.q: How much ETH do you need to be a validator?
faq.a: A solo Ethereum validator needs 32 ETH. With less, you can use pooled staking, an exchange product or a liquid staking protocol.

faq.q: What is the difference between a validator and a miner?
faq.a: A miner secures a proof-of-work chain with computing power. A validator secures a proof-of-stake chain with staked coins.

faq.q: What happens if a validator is slashed?
faq.a: Part of the validator's stake is destroyed and it may be removed from the active set. Delegators to that validator can also lose a share, depending on the network's rules.

validator.title: What is a validator in crypto? Meaning explained
validator.description: Learn what a blockchain validator does, how delegation and commission work and what slashing means for stakers.

smart-contract.short: A smart contract is a program stored on a blockchain that runs automatically when its conditions are met, letting people trade, lend or issue tokens without a middleman.
body: A smart contract holds code and often holds funds. When you interact with it, for example by swapping tokens on a decentralized exchange, every node runs the same code and records the result. Nobody can quietly change the outcome, and the contract keeps working as long as the blockchain runs.

Ethereum made smart contracts popular, and today most major chains support them. Stablecoins, ERC20 tokens, lending protocols, NFT collections and liquid staking all run on smart contracts. Each interaction costs a gas fee paid to the network.

"Code is law" cuts both ways. If a contract has a bug, attackers can exploit it and funds may be lost with no bank to reverse it. Some contracts are upgradeable, which means an admin key can change the code. Audits reduce risk but do not remove it. Before you approve a contract to spend your tokens, make sure it is the official address.
smart-contract.example: Suppose a lending contract lets you deposit 1 ETH as collateral and borrow up to 70 percent of its value in USDC. With ETH at 2,000 USDC, you can borrow up to 1,400 USDC. You borrow 1,000 USDC. If ETH falls to 1,500 USDC, your collateral is worth 1,500 and your loan is 1,000, about 67 percent of the collateral. If the protocol's liquidation threshold is 75 percent and ETH drops further to about 1,333 USDC, the contract can automatically sell part of your ETH to repay the loan, with no human approval needed.
mistakes: Approving unlimited token spending for a contract you found through a random link or airdrop.
Assuming an audited contract cannot be hacked.
Interacting with a copycat contract that has the same token name but a different address.

faq.q: Are smart contracts legally binding?
faq.a: Not by themselves. They are code that executes automatically. Whether they create legal obligations depends on the situation and the country.

faq.q: Can a smart contract be changed?
faq.a: Some are immutable once deployed. Others use an upgradeable design that lets an admin or governance vote replace the code, which you can usually check in the project documentation or block explorer.

faq.q: Which blockchains support smart contracts?
faq.a: Ethereum and its layer 2 networks, BNB Chain, Solana, Avalanche, Tron and many others support smart contracts. Bitcoin's scripting is far more limited.

smart-contract.title: What is a smart contract? Meaning with an example
smart-contract.description: Learn what a smart contract is, how it runs on a blockchain and the risks of bugs, upgrades and token approvals.

layer-1.short: A layer 1 (L1) is a base blockchain that processes and finalises transactions on its own network with its own consensus and native coin, such as Bitcoin, Ethereum or Solana.
body: An L1 is responsible for everything: ordering transactions, reaching consensus, storing data and securing the chain. It has its own native coin used for fees and, on proof-of-stake chains, for staking. Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Tron are all layer 1 networks.

L1 designs trade off three goals: security, decentralization and scalability. Ethereum keeps its base layer conservative and pushes most activity to layer 2 networks. Solana aims for high throughput on the L1 itself, with more demanding hardware for validators. Neither choice is free; each shapes fees, speed and how many people can run a node.

For you, the L1 decides which wallet format you use, which coin pays gas and how long withdrawals take. When an exchange lists withdrawal networks for a token, many of those options are different L1s, each with its own fee and confirmation time.
layer-1.example: Suppose you want to send 100 USDT to a friend. On an exchange you might see options such as Ethereum, Tron and Solana, all of which are layer 1 networks. The exchange might charge a few USDT for the Ethereum route because base-layer gas is expensive, and well under 1 USDT for Solana. If your friend's wallet only supports Tron, you must pick Tron, even if another network is cheaper, or the funds may not arrive.
mistakes: Assuming the same address works on every L1; formats and supported tokens differ.
Choosing the cheapest withdrawal network without checking that the receiver supports it.
Judging an L1 only by transaction speed while ignoring decentralization and security.

faq.q: What is the difference between layer 1 and layer 2?
faq.a: A layer 1 settles transactions on its own chain. A layer 2 processes transactions separately and posts proofs or data back to a layer 1, inheriting much of its security.

faq.q: Is Bitcoin a layer 1?
faq.a: Yes. Bitcoin is the original layer 1. Systems such as the Lightning Network are built on top of it.

faq.q: Why are there so many layer 1 blockchains?
faq.a: Teams make different design choices for speed, cost, programming languages and decentralization, and each L1 competes for users and developers.

layer-1.title: What is a layer 1 (L1) blockchain? Meaning
layer-1.description: Learn what a layer 1 blockchain is, how L1s differ from layer 2s and why the network matters for your transfers.

layer-2.short: A layer 2 (L2) is a network built on top of a layer 1 blockchain that processes transactions off the main chain and posts the results back to it, giving lower fees while borrowing much of the L1's security.
body: The most common Ethereum L2s are rollups. They bundle hundreds of transactions together and post a compressed summary to Ethereum. Optimistic rollups, such as Arbitrum, Optimism and Base, assume transactions are valid unless someone proves fraud during a challenge window. Zero-knowledge rollups, such as zkSync and Starknet, post cryptographic proofs that the batch is correct.

Because the cost of using Ethereum is shared across the whole batch, an L2 transaction often costs a small fraction of the same action on mainnet. L2s typically use ETH for gas, and the same 0x address format works across Ethereum and its EVM-compatible L2s.

L2s add their own risks. Some still rely on a single sequencer to order transactions or have admin keys that can upgrade the system. Moving funds back to Ethereum through an optimistic rollup's official bridge can take around a week, although many exchanges support direct deposits and withdrawals on popular L2s.
layer-2.example: Suppose you make 20 small token swaps a month. On Ethereum mainnet each swap costs about 6 USDT in gas when the network is moderately busy, so 120 USDT a month. On an L2 the same swap might cost about 0.05 USDT, or 1 USDT a month in total. If your average swap is only 100 USDT, mainnet fees would eat 6 percent per trade, while L2 fees would be 0.05 percent.
mistakes: Withdrawing to an L2 address from an exchange that does not support that L2, assuming the 0x address makes it the same network.
Having USDC on Arbitrum but no ETH on Arbitrum to pay gas.
Expecting an optimistic rollup's native bridge withdrawal to arrive in minutes.

faq.q: Are layer 2 networks safe?
faq.a: Major rollups inherit much of Ethereum's security, but they also have their own risks, such as centralized sequencers, upgrade keys and bridge bugs. Maturity varies between projects.

faq.q: Do I need ETH on a layer 2?
faq.a: On most Ethereum L2s, yes. Gas is paid in ETH on that L2, so you need a small ETH balance on the same network.

faq.q: Is Polygon a layer 2?
faq.a: Polygon's original PoS chain is usually described as a sidechain with its own validators, while Polygon also builds zero-knowledge rollup technology. Check which Polygon network you are actually using.

layer-2.title: What is a layer 2 (L2)? Rollups explained simply
layer-2.description: Learn what a layer 2 is, how rollups cut gas fees, and what to check before moving funds to Arbitrum, Base or zkSync.

gas-fee.short: A gas fee is the payment you make to a blockchain network to process a transaction or run a smart contract, paid in the chain's native coin such as ETH on Ethereum.
body: On Ethereum and similar chains, every operation consumes a set amount of gas units. A simple ETH transfer uses 21,000 units, while a token swap might use 100,000 to 200,000. You pay the number of units multiplied by the gas price, quoted in gwei, where 1 gwei equals 0.000000001 ETH.

Since 2021, Ethereum's fee has two parts: a base fee that the protocol burns and a priority fee, or tip, that goes to the validator. When the network is busy, the base fee rises automatically. If you set a gas limit too low, the transaction can fail and you still pay for the work done.

Gas fees differ widely between networks. Layer 2s and chains like Solana or Tron are usually much cheaper than Ethereum mainnet. When you withdraw from an exchange, you usually pay the exchange's fixed withdrawal fee instead, which it uses to cover gas, so it can differ from the live network cost.
gas-fee.example: Suppose you send USDT on Ethereum, which uses about 65,000 gas units, when the gas price is 30 gwei. The fee is 65,000 x 30 = 1,950,000 gwei, or 0.00195 ETH. With ETH at 3,200 USDT, that costs about 6.24 USDT. If you waited until the gas price dropped to 10 gwei, the same transfer would cost 0.00065 ETH, about 2.08 USDT.
mistakes: Leaving a wallet with tokens but no native coin to pay gas.
Lowering the gas limit to save money and having the transaction fail, still paying for the attempt.
Sending a small amount over Ethereum mainnet when the fee is a big share of the transfer.

faq.q: Why are gas fees so high sometimes?
faq.a: Block space is limited. When many people want to transact at once, such as during a popular token launch or a market crash, the base fee rises until demand cools.

faq.q: Do I get my gas back if a transaction fails?
faq.a: Usually not. The network still used resources to process the failed transaction, so the gas spent is lost.

faq.q: Is a withdrawal fee the same as a gas fee?
faq.a: Not exactly. An exchange withdrawal fee is set by the exchange to cover on-chain costs and may be higher or lower than the live gas fee.

gas-fee.title: What is a gas fee in crypto? Meaning and how to calculate
gas-fee.description: Learn what gas fees are, how gwei and gas limits work and why fees differ between Ethereum, layer 2s and other chains.

airdrop.short: An airdrop is a distribution of free tokens to wallet addresses or exchange users, usually to reward early users, decentralize ownership or promote a new project.
body: Projects run airdrops in different ways. Some take a snapshot of wallets that used their protocol before a certain date and let those wallets claim tokens. Others reward holders of an existing coin, or distribute tokens to exchange users who complete tasks or join a program such as a launchpool.

Real airdrops have been valuable, which is exactly why fake ones are everywhere. Scammers send worthless tokens to your wallet or post claim links on social media. Visiting the link and connecting your wallet can trigger a token approval or signature that lets them drain your assets.

Before claiming, find the claim page through the project's official channels, check that the contract address matches, and never enter your seed phrase. Many airdropped tokens face heavy selling at launch because recipients paid nothing, and in many countries airdropped tokens may be treated as taxable income.
airdrop.example: Suppose a protocol announces that every wallet that made at least 5 transactions before a snapshot can claim 400 tokens. You qualify. On the claim day the token trades at 1.20 USDT, so your allocation is worth 480 USDT. Claiming costs about 2 USDT in gas on the network used. If many recipients sell and the price drops to 0.70 USDT a week later, the same 400 tokens are worth 280 USDT.
mistakes: Clicking an airdrop link from a direct message or a random token in your wallet.
Signing a wallet request you do not understand while claiming.
Spending more on gas and farming activity than the eventual airdrop is worth.

faq.q: Are crypto airdrops free money?
faq.a: The tokens are free to receive, but claiming can cost gas, farming can take time and money, and the value often drops after launch. Many airdrop offers are scams.

faq.q: How do I know if an airdrop is real?
faq.a: Check the project's official website and verified social accounts, confirm the contract address, and never connect your wallet to a site you reached from an unsolicited message.

faq.q: Should I sell an unknown token that appeared in my wallet?
faq.a: Be careful. Interacting with an unknown token's website or contract can be a trap. It is often safest to ignore or hide it.

airdrop.title: What is a crypto airdrop? Meaning and how to stay safe
airdrop.description: Learn what a crypto airdrop is, how projects distribute tokens and how to spot fake airdrop claim links.

memecoin.short: A memecoin is a cryptocurrency inspired by an internet joke, animal or cultural trend, whose price is driven mainly by community attention rather than a product or cash flow.
body: Dogecoin, launched in 2013 as a joke about a Shiba Inu dog meme, is the original memecoin. Since then thousands have followed, especially on Solana, Ethereum and BNB Chain, where anyone can create a token in minutes through launch platforms.

Memecoins can rise many times over in days when social media attention spikes, and they can lose most of their value just as quickly. Many have huge supplies, little liquidity and concentrated holders. Early buyers or the creators often hold a large share and can sell into new demand.

If you trade memecoins, size positions so that losing the whole amount would not hurt you. Check whether liquidity is locked, how much supply the top wallets hold, whether the contract can mint more tokens, and whether the token is listed on established exchanges. A large exchange listing increases access, but it does not make the token less volatile.
memecoin.example: Suppose you put 100 USDT into a new memecoin at 0.0002 USDT per token, buying 500,000 tokens. Two days later it trades at 0.0006, and your holding is worth 300 USDT. A week after that, the creator wallet sells and the price drops to 0.00005. Your tokens are now worth 25 USDT, a 75 percent loss from your entry and over 90 percent from the peak.
mistakes: Buying after a token has already risen several hundred percent because of FOMO.
Ignoring holder concentration and liquidity, then being unable to sell without crashing the price.
Confusing a copycat token with the real one because it uses the same name and ticker.

faq.q: What was the first memecoin?
faq.a: Dogecoin (DOGE), created in 2013, is widely considered the first memecoin.

faq.q: Are memecoins a scam?
faq.a: Not all of them, but the category has many rug pulls and pump-and-dump schemes. Even legitimate memecoins are highly speculative because their value depends on attention.

faq.q: Why do memecoins have such huge supplies?
faq.a: A huge supply makes the price per token tiny, which feels cheap to buyers. What matters is market cap, not the unit price.

memecoin.title: What is a memecoin? Meaning, examples and risks
memecoin.description: Learn what a memecoin is, why meme tokens swing so hard and what to check before buying one.

tokenomics.short: Tokenomics is the economic design of a cryptocurrency, covering how many tokens exist, who received them, how new tokens are released and what the token is actually used for.
body: Good tokenomics analysis starts with supply: maximum supply, circulating supply and how fast new tokens are issued through rewards or unlocks. Next comes allocation, meaning what share went to the team, investors, community, treasury and airdrops, and when each group can sell.

Then look at demand. Does the token pay fees, give governance rights, earn staking rewards or get burned when the product is used? A token with heavy future supply and little real use relies on new buyers to absorb the selling.

Most projects publish tokenomics in a whitepaper or documentation page, often with a vesting chart. Compare that with what you see on-chain and on data sites. Large unlocks, big insider allocations and unlimited minting rights are common warning signs, while clear schedules and genuine usage are healthier signals.
tokenomics.example: Suppose a token has 1 billion maximum supply: 20 percent to the team, 18 percent to investors, 40 percent to community rewards, 12 percent to the treasury and 10 percent to an airdrop. Team and investor tokens unlock monthly over 36 months after a 12-month cliff. That is 380 million tokens, or about 10.6 million released each month once the cliff ends. If only 150 million tokens circulate today, the first monthly unlock alone adds about 7 percent to circulating supply.
mistakes: Only reading the total supply and skipping the vesting and unlock schedule.
Assuming a token has value because it has a use, without checking whether that use creates real demand.
Trusting the project's tokenomics chart without checking on-chain wallets and data sites.

faq.q: What makes good tokenomics?
faq.a: Transparent supply, fair allocation, long vesting for insiders and real uses that create demand. There is no single formula, but heavy insider allocations and unclear minting rights are red flags.

faq.q: What is a vesting cliff?
faq.a: A cliff is a period at the start when no tokens unlock. After it ends, a lump sum or regular monthly unlocks begin.

faq.q: Where can I find a token's tokenomics?
faq.a: Check the project's whitepaper or documentation, then compare it with data sites and token unlock trackers.

tokenomics.title: What is tokenomics? Meaning and what to check
tokenomics.description: Learn what tokenomics means, how supply, allocation and vesting work and the red flags to look for in a token.

token-unlock.short: A token unlock is a scheduled event when previously locked tokens, usually held by the team, investors or a treasury, become free to transfer and sell, increasing circulating supply.
body: Most new projects do not release all tokens at launch. Insiders' tokens follow a vesting schedule, often with a cliff, a waiting period, followed by monthly or daily releases. Some unlocks are linear and small; others are one large cliff unlock that releases a big share at once.

Unlocks matter because they add supply. If the people receiving tokens bought them at much lower prices, some may sell. Traders often watch large unlocks, especially those over a few percent of circulating supply, because they can weigh on the price. The market sometimes prices this in before the date.

An unlock does not mean recipients will sell. Some stake or hold, and some unlocks go to ecosystem funds that release tokens slowly. Check who receives the tokens, how large the unlock is relative to daily trading volume, and whether similar past unlocks led to selling.
token-unlock.example: Suppose a token has 400 million in circulation at 0.80 USDT, a market cap of 320 million USDT, and averages 25 million USDT of daily trading volume. Next Tuesday, 60 million tokens unlock for early investors who paid 0.10 USDT. That unlock is 15 percent of circulating supply and worth about 48 million USDT at today's price, almost two days of normal trading volume.
mistakes: Ignoring the unlock calendar before buying a recently launched token.
Assuming every unlock causes a price drop; size, recipients and timing all matter.
Comparing an unlock to total supply instead of to circulating supply and daily volume.

faq.q: Do token unlocks make the price go down?
faq.a: Not always. Large unlocks to insiders with low cost bases can add selling pressure, but the effect depends on demand, how much was already priced in and whether recipients sell.

faq.q: Where can I see token unlock schedules?
faq.a: Project documentation usually lists vesting terms, and token unlock tracking sites show upcoming events in a calendar.

faq.q: What is linear vesting?
faq.a: Linear vesting releases tokens in small equal amounts over time, such as every day or month, rather than in one lump sum.

token-unlock.title: What is a token unlock? Meaning and why it matters
token-unlock.description: Learn what a token unlock is, how vesting schedules work and how to judge whether an unlock is large.

token-burn.short: A token burn is the permanent removal of tokens from circulation by sending them to an address that nobody can access or by destroying them through a smart contract.
body: Burned tokens still exist on the blockchain in a technical sense, but no one holds a key to spend them. Common burn addresses are made of zeros or follow a known pattern, so anyone can verify the balance on a block explorer.

Projects burn tokens for different reasons. Some burn part of every transaction fee, as Ethereum has done with its base fee since 2021. Others use revenue to buy tokens on the market and burn them, as BNB does with its periodic burn program. Some burn unsold tokens after a sale.

A burn reduces supply, but it does not by itself create demand. If a project burns 1 percent of supply while unlocking 5 percent, net supply still grows. Check how burns are funded, whether they are automatic or discretionary, and how they compare with new issuance.
token-burn.example: Suppose a token has 500 million in circulation. In a quarter, the project spends 2 million USDT of revenue buying tokens at an average of 0.40 USDT, receiving 5 million tokens, and burns them. Circulating supply drops to 495 million, a 1 percent reduction. In the same quarter, 12.5 million new tokens unlock for the team. Net supply therefore still rises by 7.5 million tokens, or 1.5 percent.
mistakes: Assuming any burn announcement means the price will rise.
Not checking whether burns are larger or smaller than new token issuance and unlocks.
Believing a project's burn claim without verifying the burn address on a block explorer.

faq.q: Why do crypto projects burn tokens?
faq.a: To reduce supply, offset issuance, share revenue with holders indirectly or remove unsold tokens. The effect depends on how much is burned relative to new supply and demand.

faq.q: Can burned tokens be recovered?
faq.a: No, if they were sent to a true burn address or destroyed by a contract, no one can access them again.

faq.q: Is ETH burned?
faq.a: Yes. Since 2021, the base fee portion of every Ethereum transaction fee is burned.

token-burn.title: What is a token burn? Meaning in crypto
token-burn.description: Learn what a token burn is, why projects burn coins, and how to compare burns with new issuance.

bull-market.short: A bull market is a sustained period when prices rise broadly and investor confidence is high, commonly described as a gain of 20 percent or more from a recent low.
body: The term comes from the way a bull attacks, thrusting its horns upward. In crypto, bull markets tend to be faster and more extreme than in stocks. Bitcoin often leads, and altcoins and memecoins frequently follow with bigger moves later in the cycle.

Typical signs include rising prices on higher trading volume, new all-time highs, positive funding rates on perpetual futures, record exchange sign-ups and heavy social media attention. Sentiment gauges such as the Fear and Greed Index often sit in the greed zone for long stretches.

Bull markets are not straight lines. Pullbacks of 20 to 30 percent inside a crypto bull market have been common, and leverage that looks safe while prices rise can be wiped out in one sharp correction. Nobody can reliably tell in real time whether a bull market is starting or ending, so a written plan for entries, exits and position size is more useful than predictions.
bull-market.example: Suppose a coin rises from 20 to 50 USDT over six months, a 150 percent gain. Along the way it drops from 40 to 30 USDT in a week, a 25 percent pullback, before recovering. A trader who bought at 40 with 5x leverage and isolated margin would likely have been liquidated during that dip, even though the coin later reached 50. A spot holder who sized the position modestly could simply wait it out.
mistakes: Increasing leverage as prices rise because recent trades worked.
Assuming every dip in a bull market will recover quickly.
Buying coins only because they are trending on social media, late in a big move.

faq.q: How long does a crypto bull market last?
faq.a: There is no fixed length. Past crypto bull markets have lasted from several months to more than a year, and every cycle has had different drivers.

faq.q: What does bullish mean?
faq.a: Bullish means expecting prices to rise. A trader who is bullish on BTC thinks its price will go up.

faq.q: What is the opposite of a bull market?
faq.a: A bear market, a sustained period of falling prices and weak sentiment.

bull-market.title: What is a bull market in crypto? Meaning and signs
bull-market.description: Learn what a crypto bull market is, the common signs traders watch and why pullbacks still hit leveraged positions.

bear-market.short: A bear market is a sustained period of falling prices and pessimistic sentiment, commonly described as a decline of 20 percent or more from a recent high.
body: The name comes from a bear swiping its paws downward. In crypto, bear markets can be deep: past cycles have seen Bitcoin fall more than 70 percent from its peak and many altcoins lose over 90 percent. Long bear markets are often called crypto winter.

Common signs include lower highs and lower lows, falling trading volume, negative funding rates, project shutdowns, layoffs at crypto firms and fading media attention. Sharp relief rallies of 20 to 40 percent still happen and can trap traders who think the bottom is in.

Bear markets reward patience and risk control. Some people use dollar-cost averaging to build long-term positions slowly, while traders may short or stay in stablecoins. Whatever you do, check the counterparty: several lenders and exchanges failed during the 2022 downturn, so where you hold assets matters as much as what you hold.
bear-market.example: Suppose a coin falls from 100 to 30 USDT over a year, a 70 percent decline. To return to 100 it needs to rise about 233 percent. A person who invested 50 USDT every month during the fall would have bought more coins at lower prices: for example, 0.5 coins at 100, 1 coin at 50 and about 1.67 coins at 30, so 150 USDT buys about 3.17 coins at an average cost of roughly 47 USDT.
mistakes: Catching a falling price with large lump sums instead of planned, smaller entries.
Mistaking a sharp relief rally for the end of the bear market and adding leverage.
Keeping funds on a platform without checking its solvency and withdrawal history.

faq.q: What does bearish mean?
faq.a: Bearish means expecting prices to fall. A trader who is bearish might sell, hold stablecoins or open a short position.

faq.q: How long do crypto bear markets last?
faq.a: Past crypto bear markets have lasted roughly one to two years, but there is no rule, and future ones may differ.

faq.q: What is crypto winter?
faq.a: Crypto winter is slang for a long, deep bear market when prices, activity and funding all stay low.

bear-market.title: What is a bear market in crypto? Meaning and signs
bear-market.description: Learn what a crypto bear market is, how deep declines can be and how traders manage risk when prices keep falling.

fomo.short: FOMO, or fear of missing out, is the anxious urge to buy an asset after its price has already risen sharply, driven by the worry that others are profiting without you.
body: FOMO usually shows up when a coin is trending everywhere: big green candles, screenshots of gains and friends asking whether you bought yet. The emotional pull is strongest at exactly the point where the move is already large and the risk of a pullback is highest.

In trading, FOMO leads to chasing: buying with market orders at the top of a spike, skipping your usual analysis, using more leverage than usual or putting in more money than you planned. Late buyers often provide the liquidity that early buyers sell into.

The fix is a process you decide before the excitement. Set a maximum position size per trade, decide entry levels in advance and place a stop-loss when you open. If you missed a move, it is fine to wait. There will always be another opportunity, but recovering from a large loss takes time.
fomo.example: Suppose a coin rises from 1.00 to 1.60 USDT in two days and you buy 1,000 USDT worth at 1.60 because everyone is talking about it. The next day it drops back to 1.20, a 25 percent fall from your entry, and your position is worth 750 USDT. Had you set a rule to risk no more than 2 percent of a 5,000 USDT account, your stop-loss plan would have capped the loss at about 100 USDT.
mistakes: Buying with a market order into a vertical price spike.
Abandoning your planned position size because a coin is trending.
Treating screenshots of other people's gains as evidence that a trade is still early.

faq.q: What does FOMO mean in crypto?
faq.a: It means fear of missing out, the urge to buy because prices are rising fast and you do not want to miss gains.

faq.q: How do I avoid FOMO trading?
faq.a: Write down your entry rules, position size and stop-loss before you trade, and only act when a setup meets those rules.

faq.q: Is FOMO the opposite of FUD?
faq.a: Roughly. FOMO pushes people to buy out of greed and anxiety, while FUD pushes people to sell out of fear and doubt.

fomo.title: What does FOMO mean in crypto? Fear of missing out
fomo.description: Learn what FOMO means in crypto trading, how it leads to chasing tops and simple rules to keep it under control.

fud.short: FUD, short for fear, uncertainty and doubt, describes negative news, rumours or opinions that make people worried about an asset, whether the concerns are valid or not.
body: In crypto, FUD can be a genuine warning, such as reports that an exchange has delayed withdrawals, or a misleading rumour spread to push prices down. People also label any criticism of their favourite coin as FUD, which can make them ignore real problems.

The skill is separating noise from signal. Ask where the claim comes from, whether it is backed by data you can check, and whether primary sources confirm it. Exchange announcements, on-chain wallet flows, regulatory filings and official project statements are stronger than anonymous posts.

FUD often triggers quick, emotional selling. If a claim turns out to be false, prices can recover just as fast. If it is true, waiting too long can be costly. Having a plan for what would make you exit, decided before the news, helps you react calmly either way.
fud.example: Suppose a rumour spreads that a token's team wallet is dumping, and the price falls from 2.00 to 1.70 USDT in an hour, down 15 percent. You check a block explorer and see that the team wallet moved 5 million tokens to a staking contract, not to an exchange. Within a day the price recovers to 1.95. In another case, if you had seen those 5 million tokens arrive at an exchange deposit address, the concern would have had real evidence behind it.
mistakes: Panic-selling on an unverified post without checking primary sources.
Dismissing every critical report as FUD, including real warnings about a platform's solvency.
Trusting screenshots of supposed exchange messages that could be edited.

faq.q: What does FUD mean in crypto?
faq.a: FUD stands for fear, uncertainty and doubt. It refers to negative information or rumours that can push people to sell.

faq.q: Is all FUD false?
faq.a: No. Some FUD is misleading, but some is a real warning. Check the evidence before deciding.

faq.q: How can I verify crypto FUD?
faq.a: Look for official announcements, regulatory documents and on-chain data such as wallet movements on a block explorer.

fud.title: What does FUD mean in crypto? Meaning explained
fud.description: Learn what FUD means in crypto, how to tell real warnings from rumours and what evidence to check before reacting.

hodl.short: HODL is crypto slang for holding an asset for the long term instead of selling during price drops, originating from a misspelling of "hold" in a 2013 Bitcoin forum post.
body: During a sharp price drop in December 2013, a user on the Bitcointalk forum posted that they were "hodling", a typo of holding. The word stuck, and many later turned it into the backronym "hold on for dear life". Today a hodler is someone who buys and plans to keep their coins through ups and downs.

HODLing is a strategy, not a guarantee. It has worked for some assets over long periods, but many coins that people held for years never recovered. A thoughtful approach involves holding only assets you understand, keeping position size within what you can afford to see fall a long way, and storing coins safely.

Long-term holders often move coins to a self-custody wallet, such as a hardware wallet, so they do not depend on a single exchange. If you do that, back up your seed phrase offline and check the receiving address and network carefully when withdrawing.
hodl.example: Suppose you buy 0.1 BTC at 40,000 USDT, spending 4,000 USDT. Six months later BTC drops to 24,000 and your holding is worth 2,400 USDT, down 40 percent. A hodler does not sell. If BTC later trades at 60,000 USDT, the same 0.1 BTC is worth 6,000 USDT, a 50 percent gain on the original 4,000. But if you had held a small altcoin that never recovered, the same patience would have locked in the loss.
mistakes: Holding any coin forever without checking whether the project is still active.
Putting money you need soon into a long-term hold.
Leaving long-term holdings on an exchange without considering custody risk.

faq.q: What does HODL stand for?
faq.a: It started as a typo of hold in 2013. Many people now say it stands for hold on for dear life, but that meaning came later.

faq.q: Is HODLing a good strategy?
faq.a: It depends on what you hold, how much and for how long. It avoids overtrading and emotional selling, but it also means sitting through big drawdowns.

faq.q: What is a hodler?
faq.a: A hodler is someone who buys crypto and keeps it for the long term instead of trading in and out.

hodl.title: What does HODL mean? Origin and meaning in crypto
hodl.description: Learn what HODL means, where the term came from and what to consider before holding crypto long term.

all-time-high.short: An all-time high (ATH) is the highest price an asset has ever reached in its trading history, and the opposite, the lowest price ever, is called an all-time low (ATL).
body: Data sites and exchanges show how far a coin is from its ATH, for example "down 65 percent from ATH". This gives context: a coin that has fallen far from its peak may still be in recovery, while a coin breaking a new ATH has no historic sellers waiting at higher prices.

ATH figures can differ between sources. One exchange may record a brief spike to a price that others never traded, and some sites use closing prices while others use intraday highs. Check which data you are looking at.

New all-time highs often attract attention and FOMO. Breaking an ATH can lead to further gains, but it can also mark a local top if buyers become exhausted. Distance from ATH is a description of the past, not a target, and a coin below its old high is not guaranteed to return there.
all-time-high.example: Suppose a coin's ATH is 12 USDT and it now trades at 3 USDT, down 75 percent. Many beginners think it only needs to rise 75 percent to get back, but it actually needs to quadruple, a 300 percent gain, to reach 12 again. If it rose 75 percent from 3, it would only be at 5.25 USDT, still 56 percent below the ATH.
mistakes: Buying a coin only because it is far below its ATH and assuming it must return.
Miscalculating the recovery needed after a large percentage drop.
Chasing a breakout to a new ATH with high leverage.

faq.q: What does ATH mean in crypto?
faq.a: ATH means all-time high, the highest price an asset has ever traded at.

faq.q: What is ATL?
faq.a: ATL means all-time low, the lowest price an asset has ever traded at.

faq.q: Why do different sites show different ATHs?
faq.a: They use different exchanges, price feeds and methods, such as intraday highs versus daily closes.

all-time-high.title: What is an all-time high (ATH) in crypto? Meaning
all-time-high.description: Learn what ATH and ATL mean, how to read distance from all-time high and why recovery needs larger gains than drops.

volatility.short: Volatility is a measure of how much and how quickly an asset's price moves up and down over a given period, and higher volatility means larger, faster swings.
body: Crypto is known for high volatility. Daily moves of 3 to 5 percent are common for Bitcoin, and small altcoins can move 20 percent or more in a day. Stablecoins are designed to have very low volatility because they track a currency such as the US dollar.

Traders measure volatility in different ways: the standard deviation of returns, the average true range (ATR) on a chart, or implied volatility from options prices. You do not need the formulas to use the idea. Look at how big a typical daily candle is compared with the price.

Volatility matters most when you use leverage. A 10 percent move against a 10x position wipes out roughly all of your margin, and liquidation can happen before that because of maintenance margin and fees. Matching your position size and stop-loss distance to a coin's normal volatility is one of the simplest ways to avoid being stopped out by ordinary noise.
volatility.example: Suppose Coin A usually moves about 2 percent a day and Coin B about 8 percent. You want to risk 50 USDT on a trade. If you place your stop just outside a normal day's range, about 3 percent away for Coin A and 12 percent for Coin B, you could open a position of about 1,667 USDT in Coin A but only about 417 USDT in Coin B for the same 50 USDT risk.
mistakes: Using the same position size and leverage for a calm coin and a wildly volatile one.
Placing stop-losses inside a coin's normal daily range and getting stopped out by noise.
Assuming low volatility will last; quiet periods are often followed by sharp moves.

faq.q: Why is crypto so volatile?
faq.a: Crypto markets trade 24/7, many coins have low liquidity, leverage is widely available and news spreads fast, so prices react quickly and sharply.

faq.q: Is high volatility good or bad?
faq.a: It cuts both ways. It creates bigger opportunities for traders but also bigger losses, especially with leverage.

faq.q: Which crypto has the lowest volatility?
faq.a: Stablecoins such as USDT and USDC aim to stay close to 1 US dollar. Among volatile assets, large coins like BTC usually swing less than small altcoins.

volatility.title: What is volatility in crypto? Meaning and why it matters
volatility.description: Learn what volatility means, how traders measure it and how to size positions and stop-losses around it.

centralized-exchange.short: A centralized exchange (CEX) is a company-run trading platform where you deposit funds into an account and trade crypto through the exchange's order book, with the company holding custody of your assets.
body: Binance, OKX, Bybit, Bitget, Coinbase and Kraken are examples of centralized exchanges. They match buyers and sellers in an order book, offer spot trading and often futures, earn products, copy trading and fiat on-ramps. Most require identity verification (KYC) before you can trade or withdraw.

The convenience comes with custody risk. When your coins sit on an exchange, the exchange controls the private keys and you hold a claim on its books. If the company is hacked, freezes withdrawals or fails, you depend on its reserves and on the law where it operates. Proof of reserves reports, licensing and a long track record help you judge an exchange.

Exchanges differ in fees, available coins, liquidity, supported networks, futures rules and which countries they serve. Compare maker and taker fees, withdrawal fees and order book depth for the pairs you actually trade, and check whether the exchange is permitted to serve users in your country.
centralized-exchange.example: Suppose you trade 20,000 USDT of volume a month in spot. Exchange A charges 0.10 percent taker fees and Exchange B 0.08 percent. On A you pay 20 USDT a month in fees, on B 16 USDT, a difference of 48 USDT a year. If Exchange B's order book is thinner and you lose 0.05 percent more to slippage on each market order, that adds 10 USDT a month and wipes out the saving.
mistakes: Leaving all your crypto on one exchange without considering custody risk.
Comparing exchanges only on headline fees and ignoring spreads, slippage and withdrawal fees.
Using an exchange that does not serve your country, then getting stuck at withdrawal or verification.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CEX and a DEX?
faq.a: A CEX is run by a company that holds your funds and matches orders. A DEX runs on smart contracts, and you trade directly from your own wallet.

faq.q: Are centralized exchanges safe?
