faq.a: Large, regulated exchanges with proof of reserves and strong security are safer than unknown ones, but any custodial platform carries some risk. Many people keep long-term holdings in self-custody.

faq.q: Why do exchanges require KYC?
faq.a: Anti-money-laundering rules in most countries require exchanges to verify customer identity before allowing trading or withdrawals.

centralized-exchange.title: What is a centralized exchange (CEX)? Meaning
centralized-exchange.description: Learn what a centralized crypto exchange is, how custody and KYC work and what to compare between exchanges.

spot-trading.short: Spot trading is buying or selling a cryptocurrency for immediate delivery at the current market price, so you actually own the coins once the trade is filled.
body: When you buy BTC with USDT on the spot market, the BTC lands in your exchange account right away. You can hold it, withdraw it to your own wallet or sell it later. The most you can lose is the money you spent, because there is no borrowing involved on a standard spot account.

This differs from derivatives such as perpetual futures, where you trade a contract that tracks the price, can use leverage, and can be liquidated. Spot is generally the first step for beginners because it is simpler and has no funding rates or liquidation.

Your costs in spot trading are the trading fee, the bid-ask spread and any slippage when you use market orders. Limit orders that rest on the order book are usually charged the lower maker fee. Exchanges also offer spot margin, which adds borrowing, but that is no longer plain spot risk.
spot-trading.example: Suppose ETH trades at 2,400 USDT and you buy 0.5 ETH on spot with a market order. You pay 1,200 USDT plus a 0.1 percent taker fee of 1.20 USDT. If ETH rises to 2,640 USDT, a 10 percent move, your 0.5 ETH is worth 1,320 USDT. Selling with another 0.1 percent fee costs about 1.32 USDT, leaving about 117.48 USDT profit. If ETH fell 50 percent instead, you would still own 0.5 ETH and could not be liquidated.
mistakes: Confusing the spot market with futures in the app and opening a leveraged position by accident.
Using market orders on thinly traded pairs and losing a lot to slippage.
Forgetting to include both buy and sell fees when calculating profit.

faq.q: What is the difference between spot and futures trading?
faq.a: In spot you own the coin. In futures you trade a contract on the coin's price, often with leverage, and your position can be liquidated.

faq.q: Can you lose money in spot trading?
faq.a: Yes, if the price falls below what you paid. But on a standard spot account you cannot lose more than you invested.

faq.q: Can I withdraw coins bought on spot?
faq.a: Yes. Coins bought on the spot market are yours to hold or withdraw, subject to the exchange's withdrawal rules and network fees.

spot-trading.title: What is spot trading in crypto? Meaning and example
spot-trading.description: Learn what spot trading is, how it differs from futures and how fees, spreads and slippage affect your result.

trading-pair.short: A trading pair is two assets that can be exchanged for each other on a market, such as BTC/USDT, where the first is the base asset you buy or sell and the second is the quote asset used to price it.
body: In BTC/USDT, BTC is the base and USDT is the quote. A price of 65,000 means one BTC costs 65,000 USDT. Buying the pair means buying BTC and paying USDT; selling it means selling BTC and receiving USDT.

Most crypto volume is quoted in stablecoins such as USDT and USDC. Exchanges also list pairs against BTC, ETH, their own tokens and fiat currencies like EUR. The same coin can have very different liquidity on different pairs, so a coin that trades well against USDT may have a wide spread against BTC.

If the pair you want does not exist, you may need two trades, for example selling coin A for USDT and then buying coin B with USDT. That means paying fees twice. Some exchanges offer a convert feature that does the routing for you, but the price may include a spread, so compare it with the order book.
trading-pair.example: Suppose you hold 0.02 BTC and want SOL, but the exchange has no SOL/BTC pair. You sell 0.02 BTC on BTC/USDT at 70,000, receiving 1,400 USDT minus a 0.1 percent fee, so 1,398.60 USDT. Then you buy SOL on SOL/USDT at 140 USDT, getting 9.99 SOL before the second fee and about 9.98 SOL after it. In total you paid roughly 2.8 USDT in fees across both trades.
mistakes: Mixing up base and quote and entering an order for the wrong amount.
Trading a coin on a thin pair when a more liquid pair is available.
Forgetting that a two-step route through USDT costs two fees and two spreads.

faq.q: What does BTC/USDT mean?
faq.a: It is the market where BTC is bought and sold using USDT. The price shows how many USDT one BTC costs.

faq.q: What is the base and quote currency?
faq.a: The base is the first asset in the pair, the one being bought or sold. The quote is the second asset, used to express the price.

faq.q: Why do most pairs use USDT?
faq.a: USDT is the most widely used stablecoin on exchanges, so USDT pairs tend to have the most liquidity and the tightest spreads.

trading-pair.title: What is a trading pair in crypto? Base and quote
trading-pair.description: Learn how crypto trading pairs work, what base and quote mean and why the pair you choose affects liquidity and fees.

order-book.short: An order book is the live list of all open buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) for a trading pair, sorted by price, showing how much people are willing to trade at each level.
body: Bids appear on one side, usually green, with the highest bid at the top. Asks appear on the other, usually red, with the lowest ask nearest the middle. The gap between the best bid and the best ask is the spread. When a market order arrives, it fills against these resting orders, starting from the best price.

Depth is the amount available at each level. A deep book has large size close to the current price, so big orders barely move it. A thin book has little size, so a moderate market order can push through several levels and cause slippage. Depth charts show the same data as two curves.

Order books change constantly as traders add, cancel and fill orders, and many orders come from market makers and bots. Large visible orders, sometimes called walls, can be cancelled at any time, so do not treat them as guaranteed support or resistance. For your own trades, the book helps you decide whether to use a limit or market order.
order-book.example: Suppose the ask side of a pair shows 2 coins at 10.00, 3 coins at 10.05 and 5 coins at 10.20 USDT. You place a market buy for 8 coins. You fill 2 at 10.00, 3 at 10.05 and 3 at 10.20, paying 20.00 + 30.15 + 30.60 = 80.75 USDT. Your average price is about 10.09, roughly 0.9 percent above the best ask you saw on screen.
mistakes: Placing a large market order without checking how much size sits near the best price.
Treating a big visible wall as a guaranteed floor or ceiling.
Reading the last traded price instead of the bid and ask when deciding what you will actually pay.

faq.q: How do you read a crypto order book?
faq.a: Bids show what buyers are willing to pay and asks show what sellers want. The best bid and best ask meet in the middle, and the quantities show how much you can trade at each price.

faq.q: What does a thin order book mean?
faq.a: It means there are few orders near the current price, so trades can move the price a lot and cause slippage.

faq.q: Do DEXs have order books?
faq.a: Some do, such as on-chain order book exchanges, but many DEXs use automated market makers with liquidity pools instead.

order-book.title: What is an order book in crypto? How to read it
order-book.description: Learn how to read a crypto order book, what bids, asks and depth mean and how the book causes slippage.

bid-ask-spread.short: The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest price a buyer is willing to pay (the bid) and the lowest price a seller is willing to accept (the ask) for an asset at a given moment.
body: If the best bid for a coin is 99.90 USDT and the best ask is 100.10, the spread is 0.20 USDT, or about 0.2 percent of the price. When you buy with a market order you pay the ask; when you sell you receive the bid. A round trip with market orders therefore costs you the spread on top of trading fees.

Spreads are tight on liquid pairs such as BTC/USDT on major exchanges, often just one tick wide. They widen on small coins, during fast-moving news, in quiet hours and on platforms with little liquidity. Market makers earn part of their income by quoting both sides and capturing the spread.

Instant buy or convert screens often hide the spread inside the quoted price instead of showing a separate fee. Compare that price with the order book mid price to see what you are really paying. Using limit orders lets you avoid crossing the spread, at the risk that your order is not filled.
bid-ask-spread.example: Suppose a small altcoin shows a best bid of 0.4950 and a best ask of 0.5050 USDT. The spread is 0.0100, which is 2 percent of the 0.50 mid price. If you buy 1,000 USDT worth at the ask and immediately sell at the bid, you would get back about 980 USDT before fees, a 20 USDT loss from the spread alone. On BTC/USDT the same round trip might cost a few cents.
mistakes: Ignoring the spread and counting only the trading fee as your cost.
Using an instant buy screen without comparing its price with the order book.
Trading illiquid coins with market orders during volatile news when spreads widen.

faq.q: What is a good bid-ask spread?
faq.a: On highly liquid pairs it can be a tiny fraction of a percent. On small coins, spreads of 0.5 to 2 percent or more are common, which makes frequent trading expensive.

faq.q: Why does the spread widen?
faq.a: Spreads widen when liquidity is thin, volatility is high or market makers pull their quotes, for example around major news.

faq.q: How can I avoid paying the spread?
faq.a: Use limit orders at your chosen price instead of market orders, accepting that your order may not fill.

bid-ask-spread.title: What is the bid-ask spread in crypto? Meaning
bid-ask-spread.description: Learn what the bid-ask spread is, how it adds to your trading costs and why it widens on small coins and during news.

slippage.short: Slippage is the difference between the price you expect when you place a trade and the average price at which the trade actually fills, usually caused by thin liquidity or fast-moving markets.
body: On a centralized exchange, slippage happens when your market order is larger than the size available at the best price, so it fills across several price levels in the order book. It also happens when the price moves between the moment you click and the moment your order arrives.

On decentralized exchanges using liquidity pools, every trade moves the price along a curve. The bigger your trade relative to the pool, the worse your average price, which is called price impact. DEX interfaces let you set a slippage tolerance; if the final price is worse than that limit, the transaction fails instead of filling.

Slippage can work in your favour, but in practice it usually costs money on market orders. To reduce it, trade liquid pairs, split large orders, use limit orders and avoid trading in the seconds after major news. On DEXs, a very high slippage tolerance can make you an easy target for front-running bots.
slippage.example: Suppose you want to buy 5,000 USDT of a token showing a price of 2.00 USDT. On a thin pool, your trade pushes the price up, and you receive 2,450 tokens instead of the expected 2,500. Your average price is about 2.041, so slippage was roughly 2 percent, costing about 100 USDT. Splitting the order into five 1,000 USDT trades spaced out over time could reduce the impact if liquidity refills between them.
mistakes: Setting slippage tolerance to 10 percent or more on a DEX without understanding why a trade failed.
Placing one large market order in a thin order book instead of splitting it or using limit orders.
Blaming the exchange for slippage that came from your own order size.

faq.q: What is a good slippage tolerance?
faq.a: For liquid pairs, many traders use around 0.5 percent or less. Volatile or low-liquidity tokens may need more, but a high setting increases the risk of a bad fill.

faq.q: Is slippage a fee?
faq.a: No. Slippage is not charged by the exchange; it is the difference in price caused by liquidity and market movement.

faq.q: Can slippage be positive?
faq.a: Yes. If the price moves in your favour before your order fills, you can get a better price than expected.

slippage.title: What is slippage in crypto? Meaning and how to reduce it
slippage.description: Learn what slippage is, why it happens on exchanges and DEXs and practical ways to reduce it on large trades.

market-order.short: A market order is an instruction to buy or sell immediately at the best price currently available in the order book, prioritising speed of execution over a specific price.
body: When you place a market buy, the exchange matches it against the lowest asks until your size is filled. A market sell fills against the highest bids. You know the order will execute right away on a liquid pair, but you do not know the exact average price until it is done.

Market orders remove liquidity from the book, so they are charged the taker fee, which is usually higher than the maker fee. They also cross the bid-ask spread and can suffer slippage if your order is large compared with the depth available.

Use market orders when getting filled matters more than the exact price, such as closing a losing position quickly. For entries where you have time, a limit order often gives a better price and a lower fee. Some exchanges add price protection that cancels the part of a market order that would fill too far from the reference price.
market-order.example: Suppose SOL shows a best ask of 150.00 USDT and you market-buy 40 SOL. The book has 25 SOL at 150.00 and 30 SOL at 150.10, so you fill 25 at 150.00 and 15 at 150.10. You pay 3,750.00 + 2,251.50 = 6,001.50 USDT, an average of about 150.04. With a 0.1 percent taker fee you pay another 6.00 USDT. A limit order at 150.00 might have saved the extra 1.50 and part of the fee, but might not have filled fully.
mistakes: Using a market order on a low-liquidity coin and receiving a much worse average price.
Placing a market order during a fast spike and buying the very top.
Forgetting that market orders pay taker fees, which add up for frequent traders.

faq.q: Is a market order or limit order better?
faq.a: A market order is better when you need to execute immediately. A limit order is better when price matters more and you can wait.

faq.q: Why did my market order fill at a different price?
faq.a: Because it filled against the available orders, which may be spread over several price levels, and the price can move between clicking and execution.

faq.q: Do market orders pay maker or taker fees?
faq.a: Taker fees, because they take liquidity from the order book.

market-order.title: What is a market order in crypto? Meaning and example
market-order.description: Learn how a crypto market order works, why it pays taker fees and when slippage makes it more expensive than expected.

limit-order.short: A limit order is an instruction to buy or sell only at a specific price or better, so a buy limit fills at your price or lower and a sell limit fills at your price or higher.
body: If BTC trades at 62,000 USDT and you place a buy limit at 61,000, your order rests in the order book until a seller is willing to trade at 61,000 or lower. If the price never drops there, your order never fills. You control the price, but you give up certainty of execution.

A limit order placed away from the current price adds liquidity to the book, so it is usually charged the lower maker fee. If you set a buy limit above the current ask, it fills immediately like a market order and pays the taker fee, unless you choose a post-only option.

Limit orders can be partially filled. If you want 1 BTC at 61,000 and only 0.3 BTC is offered there, you get 0.3 and the rest waits. You can choose how long the order stays active with time-in-force settings such as GTC, IOC or FOK.
limit-order.example: Suppose ETH trades at 2,600 USDT and you place a buy limit for 2 ETH at 2,500. Two days later the price dips to 2,480 and your order fills at 2,500, costing 5,000 USDT. With a maker fee of 0.08 percent you pay 4 USDT in fees. If you had used a market order at 2,600, you would have paid 5,200 USDT plus a 0.1 percent taker fee of 5.20 USDT. But if ETH had bounced at 2,520, your limit order would never have filled.
mistakes: Setting a buy limit above the market price and paying taker fees by accident.
Forgetting about open limit orders that fill days later when market conditions have changed.
Assuming a limit order guarantees a fill when the price touches your level; there may be orders ahead of you in the queue.

faq.q: What happens if my limit order does not fill?
faq.a: It stays open until it fills, you cancel it, or it expires according to its time-in-force setting. No funds are spent until it executes.

faq.q: Why did the price touch my limit but my order did not fill?
faq.a: Other orders at the same price were placed earlier and were filled first, and the price moved away before reaching yours.

faq.q: Are limit orders cheaper?
faq.a: Often yes. Limit orders that rest on the book are usually charged maker fees, which are lower than taker fees on most exchanges.

limit-order.title: What is a limit order in crypto? Meaning and example
limit-order.description: Learn how a limit order works, why it usually pays maker fees and why it may not fill even when price comes close.

stop-loss.short: A stop-loss order is an order that automatically closes your position when the price reaches a level you set, limiting how much you can lose on a trade.
body: You choose a trigger price below your entry for a long position, or above it for a short. When the market reaches that trigger, the exchange sends a market order or a limit order to close the position. Exchanges may let you choose whether the trigger uses the last traded price or the mark price.

A stop-loss turns an open-ended risk into a planned one. If you know where your stop is, you can size the position so that being stopped out costs a fixed share of your account, such as 1 or 2 percent. On leveraged positions, a stop placed well before your liquidation price protects you from losing the whole margin.

Stops are not perfect. In a fast crash or a price gap, a market stop can fill noticeably below the trigger because of slippage, and a stop-limit may not fill at all. Placing a stop too close to the entry can get you stopped out by normal volatility, so set it where your trade idea is proven wrong.
stop-loss.example: Suppose you have a 10,000 USDT account and you want to risk at most 1 percent, or 100 USDT. You plan to buy a coin at 50 USDT with a stop-loss at 46, a risk of 4 USDT per coin. That means you can buy 25 coins, a position of 1,250 USDT. If the price falls to 46, the stop sells and you lose about 100 USDT plus fees and any slippage, instead of watching the loss grow.
mistakes: Moving the stop-loss further away when the price approaches it.
Setting stops at obvious round numbers where many other stops cluster.
Relying on a stop placed beyond the liquidation price on a leveraged position.

faq.q: Where should I put my stop-loss?
faq.a: Place it at a price that would show your trade idea is wrong, such as below a key support level, then size the position so the loss at that level fits your risk limit.

faq.q: Can a stop-loss fail?
faq.a: A stop-market order will almost always execute, but it can fill at a worse price during gaps or crashes. A stop-limit can fail to fill if the price moves past your limit.

faq.q: Does a stop-loss protect me from liquidation?
faq.a: It can, if it triggers before the liquidation price. Check both levels on your futures position.

stop-loss.title: What is a stop-loss order in crypto? Meaning
stop-loss.description: Learn how a stop-loss order works, how to size a trade around it and why stops can still fill at a worse price.

take-profit.short: A take-profit order is an order that automatically closes all or part of your position when the price reaches a target level, locking in gains without you having to watch the market.
body: For a long position, the take-profit sits above your entry; for a short, below it. When the trigger is hit, the exchange closes the position with a market or limit order. On futures, take-profit and stop-loss can often be attached to the position directly when you open it.

Take-profit targets help you follow a plan instead of reacting to emotion. Many traders set targets at previous highs, resistance levels or a multiple of their risk, such as two or three times the distance to their stop-loss. Some scale out, closing half at a first target and the rest at a second.

The trade-off is that a take-profit caps your upside on that portion if the price keeps running. In fast markets, a market-triggered take-profit can fill slightly differently from the trigger, and a limit take-profit might be skipped if the price spikes through and reverses.
take-profit.example: Suppose you buy 1 ETH at 2,000 USDT with a stop-loss at 1,900, risking 100 USDT. You set two take-profits: half at 2,200 and half at 2,300. If ETH reaches 2,200, you lock in 100 USDT on the first 0.5 ETH. If it then reaches 2,300, the second half adds 150 USDT, for a total of 250 USDT before fees, a reward of 2.5 times the 100 USDT you risked.
mistakes: Setting take-profit targets so close that fees and spread eat most of the gain.
Removing a take-profit during a rally out of greed, then watching the price fall back.
Forgetting that a full take-profit closes the whole position, leaving no exposure if the trend continues.

faq.q: How do I set a take-profit?
faq.a: Choose a target based on your analysis, such as a resistance level or a risk multiple, and attach the order when you open the position or add it afterwards.

faq.q: Should I use take-profit and stop-loss together?
faq.a: Many traders do, so both outcomes are planned. Some exchanges let you link them as an OCO order, where one cancels the other.

faq.q: What is TP in crypto trading?
faq.a: TP is short for take-profit, the price where you plan to close a position with a gain.

take-profit.title: What is a take-profit order? Meaning in crypto trading
take-profit.description: Learn how take-profit orders lock in gains, how to set targets and how scaling out with partial take-profits works.

stop-limit-order.short: A stop-limit order combines a stop price and a limit price: when the market reaches the stop price, a limit order is placed at your limit price, so it only fills at that price or better.
body: You set two prices. The stop price is the trigger. The limit price is the worst price you will accept once triggered. For a sell stop-limit protecting a long position, you might set a stop at 95 and a limit at 94. When the price trades at 95, a sell limit at 94 is placed in the book.

The advantage over a stop-market order is price control: you will not sell far below your chosen level during a sudden crash. The risk is that the order may not fill at all. If the price gaps from 95 straight to 90, your limit at 94 sits unfilled and your position stays open while losses grow.

Leave enough room between the stop and limit prices for the coin's normal volatility. Liquid pairs can use a small gap; volatile small coins need more. Exchanges sometimes call these conditional or trigger orders, and their settings can differ, so check how your exchange labels them.
stop-limit-order.example: Suppose you hold 100 coins bought at 12 USDT and set a stop-limit with a stop at 10.00 and a limit at 9.90. The price falls to 10.00 and a sell limit for 100 coins at 9.90 is placed. If buyers exist down to 9.90, you sell for about 990 USDT, a loss of roughly 210 USDT. But if bad news drops the price straight to 9.00, your order does not fill, and the position is worth only 900 USDT, a 300 USDT loss, until you act.
mistakes: Setting the limit price equal to the stop price, so the order often fails to fill in a fast move.
Using a stop-limit to protect a highly leveraged position where a missed fill can lead to liquidation.
Assuming a triggered stop-limit means the position is closed without checking the open orders.

faq.q: What is the difference between a stop-loss and a stop-limit?
faq.a: A stop-market order sends a market order when triggered and almost always fills. A stop-limit sends a limit order and only fills at your limit price or better.

faq.q: Why did my stop-limit order not execute?
faq.a: The price likely moved through your limit price too quickly, leaving your limit order unfilled in the book.

faq.q: How far should the limit be from the stop?
faq.a: It depends on the coin's volatility and liquidity. A wider gap raises the chance of a fill but allows a worse price.

stop-limit-order.title: What is a stop-limit order? Meaning and example
stop-limit-order.description: Learn how a stop-limit order works, how it differs from a stop-market order and why it may not fill in a crash.

trailing-stop.short: A trailing stop is a stop order that automatically follows the price at a set distance as it moves in your favour, then triggers if the price reverses by that distance.
body: You set a callback rate, such as 5 percent, or a fixed price distance. For a long position, the stop rises as the price makes new highs but never moves down. If the price then falls 5 percent from its highest point since activation, the order triggers and closes the position, usually with a market order.

Trailing stops let you protect profits in a trend without guessing the top. They work best in strong directional moves. In choppy markets, a tight trailing distance can stop you out on normal swings before the trend continues.

Many exchanges let you set an activation price, so the trailing only starts once the trade is already in profit. Settings vary between platforms, for example whether the callback uses last price or mark price, so read the order details on your exchange before relying on it.
trailing-stop.example: Suppose you buy a coin at 40 USDT and set a trailing stop with a 10 percent callback. The price climbs to 50, so the stop moves up to 45. It then rises to 56, moving the stop to 50.40. The price then drops, and when it reaches 50.40 the order triggers. You exit with a gain of about 10.40 USDT per coin, roughly 26 percent, even though you did not sell at the 56 top.
mistakes: Setting a callback rate smaller than the coin's normal daily swings.
Expecting the trailing stop to move down again if the price falls; it only ratchets in your favour.
Not checking whether the order triggers on last price or mark price on futures.

faq.q: What is a good trailing stop percentage?
faq.a: It should be wider than the coin's normal pullbacks. Large coins may suit a few percent, while volatile altcoins may need 10 percent or more.

faq.q: Does a trailing stop guarantee my exit price?
faq.a: No. It usually triggers a market order, so the fill can be slightly worse than the trigger in fast markets.

faq.q: What is an activation price in a trailing stop?
faq.a: It is the price at which the trailing begins. Before that price is reached, the order is inactive.

trailing-stop.title: What is a trailing stop? Meaning and example
trailing-stop.description: Learn how a trailing stop follows the price, how the callback rate works and how to avoid being stopped out by noise.

oco-order.short: An OCO (one-cancels-the-other) order pairs two orders, typically a take-profit and a stop-loss, so that when one of them executes, the other is automatically cancelled.
body: OCO solves a simple problem. If you place a take-profit limit and a separate stop-loss on the same coins, and one fills, the other might later fill too and open an unwanted position, or the exchange might reject it for lack of balance. With OCO, the exchange links them and cancels the leftover one for you.

A typical spot OCO for a long position is a sell limit above the price as the take-profit and a sell stop-limit or stop-market below as the stop-loss. On futures, the same idea is often built into the take-profit and stop-loss fields attached to a position.

OCO is useful when you cannot watch the market, because both exits are planned in advance. Check how your exchange implements it: some reserve the full balance for both legs, and the stop leg may be a stop-limit that can fail to fill in a sharp move.
oco-order.example: Suppose you hold 0.5 BTC bought at 60,000 USDT. You place an OCO sell for 0.5 BTC with a limit at 66,000 and a stop at 57,000. If BTC rises to 66,000, the limit fills for a gain of 3,000 USDT and the stop is cancelled. If BTC falls to 57,000 first, the stop triggers for a loss of about 1,500 USDT and the take-profit is cancelled. Your reward-to-risk on the trade is 2 to 1.
mistakes: Placing two separate exit orders instead of an OCO, then accidentally leaving one open after the other fills.
Not knowing whether the stop leg is a stop-limit, which can fail to fill in a crash.
Setting the take-profit and stop so close together that normal volatility hits one at random.

faq.q: What does OCO mean in crypto?
faq.a: OCO stands for one-cancels-the-other, two linked orders where filling one cancels the other.

faq.q: Can I use OCO for buying?
faq.a: Yes. A buy OCO can combine a buy limit below the price with a buy stop above it, so you enter on either a dip or a breakout.

faq.q: Do all exchanges support OCO orders?
faq.a: Many major exchanges do on spot, but naming and options vary, and some only offer linked take-profit and stop-loss on futures positions.

oco-order.title: What is an OCO order? One-cancels-the-other explained
oco-order.description: Learn how an OCO order links a take-profit and a stop-loss so that one cancels the other, with a worked example.

post-only-order.short: A post-only order is a limit order that is only allowed to add liquidity to the order book; if it would fill immediately against an existing order, the exchange cancels or adjusts it instead.
body: A normal limit order placed at or across the best price fills straight away and pays the taker fee. Post-only prevents that. It guarantees that if your order executes, it does so as a maker, paying the lower maker fee or, at some fee tiers, earning a rebate.

This matters for active traders and market makers whose costs add up over many trades. It also protects you from accidentally crossing the spread when the price moves between setting your order and submitting it.

The trade-off is that your order may be rejected or never filled when the market is moving. Some exchanges simply cancel a post-only order that would take liquidity, while others reprice it to the best available maker price. Check your exchange's rules and fee schedule, as maker and taker fees differ by platform and VIP level.
post-only-order.example: Suppose you trade 200,000 USDT of volume a month. If your exchange charges 0.02 percent maker and 0.05 percent taker on futures, all-taker trading costs 100 USDT a month while all-maker trading costs 40 USDT. Using post-only orders for most entries could save around 60 USDT a month, or 720 USDT a year, as long as you still get filled at the prices you want.
mistakes: Being surprised when a post-only order is cancelled because it would have filled immediately.
Using post-only when you urgently need to exit a position.
Assuming maker fees are the same on every exchange or account tier.

faq.q: Why was my post-only order cancelled?
faq.a: Because at the moment it arrived, it would have matched an existing order and paid taker fees. The exchange cancelled it to keep it maker-only.

faq.q: Does post-only guarantee maker fees?
faq.a: Yes, if it fills, it fills as a maker. It does not guarantee that it will fill.

faq.q: Is post-only the same as a limit order?
faq.a: It is a type of limit order with an extra rule that it must not take liquidity.

post-only-order.title: What is a post-only order? Meaning in crypto trading
post-only-order.description: Learn what a post-only order is, how it guarantees maker fees and why exchanges cancel it when it would fill instantly.

time-in-force.short: Time in force is an order setting that controls how long an order stays active and how it handles partial fills, with common options GTC (good till cancelled), IOC (immediate or cancel) and FOK (fill or kill).
body: GTC is the default on most exchanges. The order stays in the book until it fills completely or you cancel it, though some platforms auto-expire very old orders. It is the right choice for patient limit orders.

IOC fills whatever it can immediately at your price or better and cancels the rest. If you want 10 coins and only 6 are available at your limit, you get 6 and the remaining 4 disappear instead of waiting. FOK is stricter: the entire order must fill immediately, or nothing fills at all.

IOC and FOK are useful when you want an immediate result with price control, such as entering only if enough size is available, or arbitrage trades that only make sense at full size. Some exchanges also offer GTD (good till date) or post-only as a time-in-force option. Labels and choices vary, so check your order panel.
time-in-force.example: Suppose the ask side shows 3 BTC at 64,000 and 2 BTC at 64,050 USDT, and you send a buy limit for 4 BTC at 64,000. As GTC, you get 3 BTC now and 1 BTC waits in the book. As IOC, you get 3 BTC and the last 1 BTC is cancelled. As FOK, nothing fills, because only 3 BTC is available at 64,000 or better and the order needs all 4.
mistakes: Leaving old GTC orders open and forgetting about them until they fill unexpectedly.
Using FOK on a thin market and wondering why nothing ever fills.
Assuming IOC keeps the unfilled remainder in the book.

faq.q: What does GTC mean in crypto trading?
faq.a: GTC means good till cancelled. The order stays open until it fills or you cancel it.

faq.q: What is the difference between IOC and FOK?
faq.a: IOC fills any available part immediately and cancels the rest. FOK fills the whole order immediately or cancels it entirely.

faq.q: Which time in force should beginners use?
faq.a: GTC for normal limit orders is usually fine. Just review your open orders regularly.

time-in-force.title: Time in force: GTC, IOC and FOK meaning explained
time-in-force.description: Learn what time in force means in crypto trading and how GTC, IOC and FOK orders handle partial fills.

maker-taker-fees.short: Maker and taker fees are the two trading fee rates an exchange charges: a maker fee when your order adds liquidity to the order book, and a usually higher taker fee when your order removes it.
body: A maker order is one that does not fill immediately. It rests in the order book and waits for someone else to trade against it, so it makes the market deeper. A typical maker order is a limit buy below the current price or a limit sell above it.

A taker order fills right away against orders that are already in the book. Market orders are always takers, and a limit order priced across the spread also fills as a taker. Because takers consume liquidity, most exchanges charge them more.

Fees are a percentage of the trade value, not of your profit. They differ by exchange, by product (spot versus futures) and by your fee tier, which usually depends on 30-day trading volume or token holdings. Some venues pay a small rebate to makers on certain markets. Check the fee schedule of your own exchange before comparing costs.
maker-taker-fees.example: Suppose your exchange charges 0.02% for makers and 0.05% for takers on futures. You open a 20,000 USDT position with a market order, paying 20,000 × 0.05% = 10 USDT. If you had used a limit order that rested in the book, the fee would be 20,000 × 0.02% = 4 USDT. Closing the same size again as a taker adds another 10 USDT, so a round trip costs 20 USDT as a taker versus 8 USDT as a maker. Over a hundred trades, that gap becomes 1,200 USDT.
mistakes: Assuming every limit order is a maker order, when a limit priced through the spread fills instantly and pays the taker fee.
Calculating fees on margin instead of on the full leveraged position size.
Ignoring the closing fee and only counting the cost of opening a trade.

faq.q: Why are taker fees higher than maker fees?
faq.a: Makers add orders that others can trade against, which keeps spreads tight. Exchanges reward that with a lower rate and charge takers more for using the existing liquidity.

faq.q: How do I make sure I pay the maker fee?
faq.a: Use a post-only limit order. If it would fill immediately as a taker, the exchange cancels or adjusts it instead of executing it.

faq.q: Are maker and taker fees the same on every exchange?
faq.a: No. Rates depend on the exchange, the product and your fee tier, and they change over time, so always check the current fee page.

maker-taker-fees.title: What are maker and taker fees? Crypto fees explained
maker-taker-fees.description: Learn the difference between maker and taker fees, how they are calculated on crypto exchanges and how to pay less per trade.

liquidity.short: Liquidity is how easily you can buy or sell an asset quickly, in size, without moving its price much.
body: On an exchange, liquidity shows up in the order book. A liquid market has many buy and sell orders close to the current price, so the bid-ask spread is narrow and a large order fills at nearly the price you see. An illiquid market has few orders, wide gaps between price levels and a wide spread.

Liquidity matters because it sets your real trading cost. In a thin market, a market order walks through several price levels and fills at a worse average price, which is called slippage. Thin markets also move more sharply on small orders, which can trigger stop-losses and liquidations.

Liquidity is not fixed. Major pairs like BTC/USDT are usually deep on large exchanges, while small tokens can be thin even on big venues. It also drops at weekends, during holidays and in sudden sell-offs. In DeFi, liquidity comes from liquidity pools rather than an order book, but the idea is the same: more depth means less price impact.
liquidity.example: Imagine you want to sell 50,000 coins of a small token. The best bid is 1.000 USDT, but only 10,000 coins are wanted there. The next 20,000 coins are bid at 0.990, and the remaining 20,000 at 0.970. Your market sell brings in 10,000 + 19,800 + 19,400 = 49,200 USDT, an average of 0.984, about 1.6% below the price on screen. On a liquid pair, the same order might fill within 0.05% of the displayed price.
mistakes: Judging liquidity by the last price or the 24-hour volume figure instead of looking at order book depth near the price.
Placing large market orders in thin pairs and being surprised by the fill price.
Assuming a token that is liquid on one exchange is equally liquid on every exchange.

faq.q: How can I check the liquidity of a crypto pair?
faq.a: Look at the bid-ask spread and at how much volume sits within 1% or 2% of the current price in the order book. Many exchanges show this as a depth chart.

faq.q: Why is low liquidity risky?
faq.a: Low liquidity means larger slippage, wider spreads and sharper price moves. Getting out of a position quickly can cost much more than expected.

liquidity.title: What is liquidity in crypto? Meaning and why it matters
liquidity.description: Understand crypto liquidity, how order book depth affects your fill price, and how to check whether a market is liquid enough.

trading-volume.short: Trading volume is the total amount of an asset traded over a set period, usually shown as the 24-hour volume in coins or in USD value.
body: Every time a buyer and a seller match, the trade adds to volume. Exchanges and data sites usually display 24-hour volume, and charts show volume per candle as bars under the price. Volume can be counted in the base coin (for example 5,000 BTC) or in quote value (for example 300 million USDT).

Traders read volume as a measure of participation. A price breakout on rising volume suggests many traders agree with the move. A move on very low volume is easier to reverse. Volume also hints at liquidity, although depth in the order book is a more direct measure.

Volume figures need care. Spot and derivatives volume are often reported separately, and derivatives volume is usually far larger because it counts leveraged notional value. Some venues and tokens have inflated numbers due to wash trading, so compare volume across several sources and check it against order book depth.
trading-volume.example: Suppose a token shows 40 million USDT of 24-hour volume on an exchange, but the order book only holds 30,000 USDT of orders within 2% of the price. Real traders would need over 1,000 full turnovers of that depth in a day to produce such volume. That mismatch is a warning sign. By contrast, a pair with 40 million USDT of volume and 2 million USDT of depth within 2% looks far more consistent.
mistakes: Treating high 24-hour volume as proof that a market is liquid or trustworthy.
Comparing spot volume on one site with derivatives volume on another.
Reading a single volume spike as a buy or sell signal without looking at price direction.

faq.q: Is high trading volume good?
faq.a: It usually means more participation and easier execution, but not always. Volume can be inflated, and high volume during a sell-off reflects heavy selling, not strength.

faq.q: What is the difference between volume and market cap?
faq.a: Market cap is the value of all coins in circulation at the current price. Volume is how much of the coin changed hands over a period.

trading-volume.title: What is trading volume in crypto? Meaning explained
trading-volume.description: Learn what crypto trading volume measures, how to read volume bars on a chart and why some volume numbers can be misleading.

wash-trading.short: Wash trading is when the same person or group buys and sells an asset to themselves to create fake trading volume and a false impression of demand.
body: In a wash trade there is no real change of ownership. One account sells to another account controlled by the same party, or a bot trades back and forth with itself. The goal is to make a token, an NFT collection or an exchange look more active than it really is.

Inflated volume can push a token up rankings, attract traders who look for busy markets, help meet listing requirements or make an exchange seem bigger. It can also be used to fake NFT sale prices. In many traditional markets wash trading is illegal, and regulators increasingly apply similar rules to crypto, though the details vary by country.

For you as a trader, the risk is false confidence. A market with fake volume may have very little real depth, so your order can move the price sharply. Signs to check include volume that is huge relative to order book depth, trades of identical size repeating at regular intervals, and volume that is much higher on one small venue than on major exchanges.
wash-trading.example: Suppose an NFT is bought for 1 ETH, then sold between two linked wallets for 5 ETH, 12 ETH and 20 ETH within a day. The records now show 37 ETH of volume and a last sale of 20 ETH, yet the owner only ever paid 1 ETH and no outside buyer took part. A newcomer who pays 15 ETH because the last sale was 20 ETH may find no real buyers above a few ETH.
mistakes: Trusting volume rankings without checking order book depth or the spread.
Using the last NFT sale price as a fair value when sales went between linked wallets.
Assuming a token is popular because it shows large volume on a single small exchange.

faq.q: How can you spot wash trading?
faq.a: Compare volume with order book depth, look for repeated identical trade sizes, and check whether the same wallets trade back and forth. Volume concentrated on one obscure venue is another warning sign.

faq.q: Is wash trading illegal in crypto?
faq.a: It depends on the country and the asset. Many jurisdictions treat it as market manipulation, and enforcement in crypto has been increasing.

wash-trading.title: What is wash trading? Fake crypto volume explained
wash-trading.description: Learn what wash trading is, why it inflates crypto and NFT volume, and the practical signs that a market's volume may be fake.

market-maker.short: A market maker is a trader or firm that continuously places both buy and sell orders on a market, providing liquidity and earning from the spread between them.
body: A market maker quotes a bid slightly below the fair price and an ask slightly above it. When other traders hit those orders, the market maker buys low and sells high in small amounts, many times a day. The profit per trade is small, so the business depends on volume, speed and careful risk control.

Market makers keep order books deep and spreads tight, which lowers costs for everyone else. Exchanges often attract them with lower maker fees, rebates or special programs, and token projects sometimes hire market makers to support liquidity after a listing.

The main risk for a market maker is inventory: if the price moves strongly in one direction, they end up holding the losing side. In DeFi, automated market makers (AMMs) replace human quoting with a formula and a liquidity pool. Not every market maker is benign; some arrangements between projects and market makers have been criticised, so trading activity alone does not prove healthy demand.
market-maker.example: Suppose ETH trades around 3,000 USDT. A market maker posts a bid at 2,999.50 and an ask at 3,000.50 for 2 ETH each. If one trader sells 2 ETH into the bid and another buys 2 ETH from the ask, the market maker earns 2 × 1.00 = 2 USDT before fees. Repeating that thousands of times a day adds up, but a sudden 5% drop while holding 50 ETH would cost about 7,500 USDT.
mistakes: Thinking market makers always push prices in one direction, when their core job is quoting both sides.
Assuming a tight spread on a new token means deep liquidity, when a single market maker can pull its orders at any time.
Confusing a market maker with a maker order; any trader can place maker orders.

faq.q: How do crypto market makers make money?
faq.a: Mainly by capturing the bid-ask spread on many small trades, plus maker rebates or fee discounts where exchanges offer them.

faq.q: What is the difference between a market maker and an AMM?
faq.a: A market maker actively places and updates orders in an order book. An AMM is a smart contract that prices trades from a pool of tokens using a formula.

market-maker.title: What is a market maker in crypto? Meaning explained
market-maker.description: Learn what crypto market makers do, how they earn the spread, why exchanges need them and how they differ from AMMs.

candlestick-chart.short: A candlestick chart is a price chart where each candle shows the open, high, low and close price of an asset over one time period.
body: Each candle covers a fixed timeframe, such as 1 minute, 1 hour or 1 day. The thick part, called the body, runs from the opening price to the closing price. The thin lines above and below, called wicks or shadows, show the highest and lowest prices reached during that period.

Colour tells you direction. On most platforms a green candle closed higher than it opened, and a red candle closed lower. Some apps let you swap colours, and in some regional settings red means up, so check your chart settings.

Candles help you see how buyers and sellers fought during each period. A long lower wick means price fell but buyers pushed it back up. A small body with long wicks on both sides shows indecision. Traders combine candles with volume and support and resistance levels, but a single candle pattern is not a reliable prediction on its own.
candlestick-chart.example: Take a 1-hour BTC candle that opens at 64,000 USDT, drops to 63,200, rises to 64,600 and closes at 64,400. The body runs from 64,000 to 64,400 and is green because the close is higher. The upper wick stretches from 64,400 to 64,600 (200 USDT), and the lower wick from 64,000 down to 63,200 (800 USDT). That long lower wick shows sellers pushed price down 800 USDT before buyers took it back.
mistakes: Reading a pattern on a 1-minute chart as if it carried the weight of a daily candle.
Acting on a candle before it has closed, when its shape can still change completely.
Assuming green always means up without checking the platform colour settings.

faq.q: What do the wicks on a candlestick mean?
faq.a: Wicks show the highest and lowest prices traded during the candle's timeframe. Long wicks mean price moved far but was pushed back before the close.

faq.q: Which timeframe should I use for candlestick charts?
faq.a: It depends on how long you plan to hold. Short-term traders use minutes or hours, while longer-term holders usually focus on daily or weekly candles.

candlestick-chart.title: What is a candlestick chart? How to read crypto candles
candlestick-chart.description: Learn how to read a candlestick chart: open, high, low, close, wicks and colours, with a worked crypto example.

support-and-resistance.short: Support and resistance are price zones where an asset has repeatedly stopped falling (support) or stopped rising (resistance), because buying or selling interest tends to cluster there.
body: Support forms where buyers have stepped in before, so price tends to bounce. Resistance forms where sellers have taken profit or opened shorts before, so price tends to stall. These levels often line up with previous highs and lows, round numbers like 50,000 or 100,000, and areas where a lot of volume traded.

Think of them as zones, not exact lines. Price often pokes slightly through a level before reversing. When a level finally breaks with strong volume, it can flip roles: old resistance becomes new support, and old support becomes new resistance.

Traders use these zones to plan entries, stop-losses and take-profit targets. A common approach is to place a stop-loss a little beyond a support zone rather than exactly on it, because many traders place stops at the same obvious level and those orders can be swept in a quick move.
support-and-resistance.example: Suppose SOL has bounced from around 140 USDT three times in two months and failed to break 175 USDT twice. You buy near 142 with a stop-loss at 134, just under the support zone, and a target at 172, just under resistance. Your risk is 8 USDT per coin and your potential gain is 30 USDT. If SOL later closes several days above 175, that old ceiling may start to act as support.
mistakes: Treating a support level as a guarantee that price cannot fall further.
Placing a stop-loss exactly on an obvious round number where many other stops sit.
Drawing dozens of lines on a chart until every price looks like a level.

faq.q: What happens when support breaks?
faq.a: Price often moves quickly lower as stop-losses trigger, and the broken support can later act as resistance if price comes back up to it.

faq.q: Is support and resistance reliable in crypto?
faq.a: It is a useful planning tool, not a prediction. Levels fail often, especially in fast markets, so always combine them with a stop-loss and sensible position size.

support-and-resistance.title: What is support and resistance? Crypto trading basics
support-and-resistance.description: Learn what support and resistance are, how to find them on a crypto chart and how traders use them for entries and stops.

dollar-cost-averaging.short: Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) is a strategy of buying a fixed amount of an asset at regular intervals, regardless of price, to spread your entry over time.
body: Instead of trying to pick the perfect moment, you invest the same amount on a schedule, for example 100 USDT every week. When the price is low, that amount buys more coins. When the price is high, it buys fewer. Over time your average cost per coin is smoothed out.

DCA reduces the risk of putting everything in right before a big drop, and it removes much of the stress of timing the market. Many exchanges offer recurring buy or auto-invest features that do this automatically, usually on the spot market.

DCA does not guarantee a profit. If the asset keeps falling for years, you still lose money. In a steadily rising market, a single lump-sum purchase at the start would usually have done better. Fees also matter: very small, frequent purchases can lose a noticeable share to trading fees or spreads, so check the cost of the recurring buy feature you use.
dollar-cost-averaging.example: Suppose you invest 200 USDT in BTC on the first day of four months. Prices are 50,000, 40,000, 50,000 and 62,500 USDT. You buy 0.004, 0.005, 0.004 and 0.0032 BTC, for a total of 0.0162 BTC for 800 USDT. Your average cost is 800 ÷ 0.0162 ≈ 49,383 USDT, lower than the simple average of the four prices (50,625) because the fixed amount bought more when the price was low.
mistakes: Believing DCA removes risk entirely, when a long decline still produces losses.
Stopping the plan during a downturn, which is exactly when DCA buys the most coins.
Using tiny daily buys where fees take a large share of each purchase.

faq.q: Is DCA better than investing a lump sum?
faq.a: Not always. A lump sum often does better in a rising market, while DCA reduces the damage from bad timing. Many people choose DCA because it is easier to stick with.

faq.q: How often should I DCA into crypto?
faq.a: Weekly or monthly schedules are common. Pick an interval and amount you can keep up comfortably, and check that fees stay small relative to each purchase.

dollar-cost-averaging.title: What is dollar-cost averaging (DCA) in crypto?
dollar-cost-averaging.description: Learn how dollar-cost averaging works in crypto, how it lowers your average entry and where it can still lose money.

position-sizing.short: Position sizing is deciding how much to put into a single trade so that, if your stop-loss is hit, you lose only a planned share of your account.
body: Good position sizing starts with risk, not with how confident you feel. Many traders limit each trade to losing 1% or 2% of their account. You then work backwards: the distance between your entry and stop-loss tells you how large the position can be.

The basic formula is position size = amount you are willing to lose ÷ distance to stop-loss. A wide stop means a smaller position, and a tight stop allows a larger one. Leverage changes how much margin you need to open the position, but it does not change how much you lose when the stop is hit.

Sizing also protects you from a losing streak. If you risk 20% per trade, five losses in a row can wipe out most of your account. At 1% per trade, the same streak costs about 5% and you can keep trading. With leveraged products, also check that your liquidation price sits well beyond your stop-loss.
position-sizing.example: Suppose your account holds 5,000 USDT and you risk 1%, which is 50 USDT. You want to buy ETH at 2,500 USDT with a stop-loss at 2,400, a 100 USDT distance. Position size = 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 ETH, worth 1,250 USDT. If the stop triggers, you lose 0.5 × 100 = 50 USDT plus fees. Using 5x leverage, you would post only 250 USDT of margin, but the loss at the stop would still be 50 USDT.
mistakes: Choosing position size by leverage or by feel instead of by the stop-loss distance.
Forgetting to include fees and slippage in the planned loss.
Increasing size after a few wins or losses, which turns a plan into a gamble.

faq.q: How much should I risk per trade?
faq.a: Many traders use 1% to 2% of their account per trade. The right number depends on your strategy and tolerance, but small fixed risk makes losing streaks survivable.

faq.q: Does leverage increase my position size?
faq.a: Leverage lets you open a bigger position with less margin. Your profit and loss still depend on the full position size, so size first and pick leverage second.

position-sizing.title: What is position sizing? How much to risk per trade
position-sizing.description: Learn how to calculate position size from your account risk and stop-loss distance, with a clear crypto trading example.

risk-reward-ratio.short: The risk-reward ratio compares how much you could lose on a trade, up to your stop-loss, with how much you could gain, up to your take-profit target.
body: You measure risk as the distance from entry to stop-loss and reward as the distance from entry to take-profit. A trade risking 100 to make 300 has a risk-reward ratio of 1:3. Some platforms and traders write it the other way round as reward-to-risk, so check which convention is being used.

The ratio matters because it works together with your win rate. With a 1:3 ratio, you can be wrong on most trades and still come out ahead. With a 1:0.5 ratio, you need to win far more often than you lose just to break even, before fees.

A good ratio on paper is only useful if the target is realistic. Setting a take-profit far beyond a strong resistance zone makes the ratio look attractive but lowers the chance of reaching it. Fees and slippage also reduce the real reward, especially on short-term trades with small targets.
risk-reward-ratio.example: Suppose you buy at 1.00 USDT with a stop-loss at 0.95 and a target at 1.15. Risk is 0.05 and reward is 0.15, so the ratio is 1:3. Over ten such trades with equal size, if you win 3 and lose 7, you gain 3 × 0.15 = 0.45 and lose 7 × 0.05 = 0.35 per coin, netting 0.10 per coin before fees. Break-even win rate for 1:3 is 1 ÷ (1 + 3) = 25%.
mistakes: Moving the stop-loss further away during the trade, which quietly destroys the planned ratio.
Picking unrealistic targets just to make the ratio look good.
Ignoring win rate and assuming a high ratio alone makes a strategy profitable.

faq.q: What is a good risk-reward ratio?
faq.a: Many traders look for at least 1:2, but the right ratio depends on your win rate. A strategy that wins often can work with a lower ratio.

faq.q: How do I calculate the break-even win rate?
faq.a: Divide risk by the sum of risk and reward. For a 1:2 ratio that is 1 ÷ 3, about 33% before fees.

risk-reward-ratio.title: What is the risk-reward ratio in trading? Explained
risk-reward-ratio.description: Learn how to calculate the risk-reward ratio, how it links to your win rate and why realistic targets matter in crypto.

arbitrage.short: Arbitrage is buying an asset where it is cheaper and selling it where it is more expensive at the same time, to profit from a price difference between markets.
body: Crypto trades on many exchanges at once, and prices are not always identical. If BTC is slightly cheaper on one venue than another, an arbitrageur buys on the cheaper one and sells on the more expensive one. Their trades push the prices back together, which helps keep markets consistent.

There are several types. Spatial arbitrage uses price gaps between exchanges. Triangular arbitrage cycles through three pairs on one exchange, such as USDT to BTC to ETH and back. Funding rate and basis arbitrage pair a spot position with a futures position to collect a funding payment or a price gap while staying market-neutral.

Real-world arbitrage is harder than it looks. Trading fees, withdrawal fees, network confirmation times, deposit and withdrawal suspensions and slippage can wipe out a small gap. Professional firms keep funds on several exchanges in advance so they do not have to transfer during the trade. Regional price premiums can also persist for long periods because of capital controls.
arbitrage.example: Suppose ETH trades at 3,000 USDT on exchange A and 3,018 on exchange B, a 0.6% gap. You hold funds on both and buy 2 ETH on A for 6,000 USDT while selling 2 ETH on B for 6,036 USDT. Gross profit is 36 USDT. With taker fees of 0.1% on each side, you pay about 6 + 6.04 = 12.04 USDT, leaving roughly 24 USDT. If you also had to withdraw ETH between venues, a network fee would cut that further.
mistakes: Forgetting withdrawal fees and transfer time when the gap is only a fraction of a percent.
Assuming a price gap is free money when deposits or withdrawals are suspended on one side.
Leaving one leg of the trade open, which turns arbitrage into an ordinary directional bet.

faq.q: Is crypto arbitrage still profitable?
faq.a: Large, easy gaps are rare on major pairs because many bots compete for them. Smaller opportunities exist, but costs and execution speed decide whether they are worth it.

faq.q: Is arbitrage risk-free?
faq.a: No. Execution delays, fee changes, frozen withdrawals and exchange risk can all turn an expected profit into a loss.

arbitrage.title: What is arbitrage in crypto? How price gaps are traded
arbitrage.description: Learn how crypto arbitrage works across exchanges, the main types, and the fees and risks that shrink real profits.

whale.short: A whale is an individual or entity that holds or trades such a large amount of a cryptocurrency that their moves can noticeably affect its price or liquidity.
body: There is no official threshold. For bitcoin, people often call addresses holding 1,000 BTC or more whales, but for a small token a holder of a few percent of supply can be a whale. Whales include early adopters, funds, companies, exchanges and token project treasuries.

Whales matter because large orders can move thin markets, trigger stop-losses and liquidations, and change sentiment. Because blockchains are public, analysts track large transfers, especially big deposits to exchanges, which may signal an intention to sell, and big withdrawals, which may signal long-term holding.

Interpreting whale activity is tricky. Many large addresses belong to exchanges holding funds for millions of users, and a transfer between two wallets of the same owner looks like a big move but changes nothing. Treat whale alerts as one data point, not a trading signal on their own. Also check how concentrated a token's supply is before you buy it.
whale.example: Suppose a token has 100 million coins in circulation and one address holds 8 million, or 8% of supply. The order book only has 400,000 USDT of bids within 5% of the 0.50 USDT price, which is about 800,000 coins. If that whale tried to sell even 2 million coins at market, the order would exhaust those bids and push the price far more than 5% lower.
mistakes: Treating every large on-chain transfer as a whale selling, when it is often an exchange moving funds internally.
Copying whale trades blindly without knowing their reasons or time horizon.
Ignoring how concentrated a token's supply is before buying.

faq.q: How much crypto do you need to be a whale?
faq.a: There is no fixed number. It depends on the asset: what counts as a whale for a small token would be a modest holding in bitcoin.

faq.q: Can whales manipulate crypto prices?
faq.a: Large holders can move prices, especially in thin markets, and some manipulation does happen. In deep markets a single trader has less impact.

whale.title: What is a crypto whale? Meaning and why it matters
whale.description: Learn what a crypto whale is, how large holders can move prices and how to read whale transfers on-chain with care.

futures-contract.short: A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price in the future, which lets you trade price moves with margin and leverage without holding the asset itself.
body: With crypto futures you do not buy the coin. You open a position that gains when the price moves in your favour and loses when it moves against you. You can go long if you expect a rise or short if you expect a fall, which is the main difference from buying on the spot market.

Futures are traded on margin. You post a fraction of the position value as collateral, and the exchange lets you control a larger position. That is leverage: it multiplies both gains and losses, and if your losses eat too far into your margin, the position is liquidated.

Crypto exchanges offer two main kinds. Delivery futures have an expiry date and settle on that date. Perpetual futures never expire and use a funding rate to stay close to the spot price. Contracts can also be margined in stablecoins such as USDT or in the coin itself. Contract size, tick size, fees and margin rules differ by exchange, so read the contract specification before trading.
futures-contract.example: Suppose BTC trades at 50,000 USDT and you open a long futures position of 0.2 BTC, worth 10,000 USDT, using 5x leverage. You post 2,000 USDT of margin. If BTC rises to 52,500 (+5%), your profit is 0.2 × 2,500 = 500 USDT, a 25% return on margin. If BTC falls 5% to 47,500, you lose 500 USDT, also 25% of your margin, before fees.
mistakes: Thinking futures losses are limited to the price change on the margin, when they are based on the full position size.
Opening futures without knowing whether the contract is perpetual or has an expiry date.
Using maximum leverage because the exchange allows it.

faq.q: What is the difference between futures and spot trading?
faq.a: In spot trading you buy and own the coin. With futures you trade a contract on its price, can go long or short, and usually use margin and leverage.

faq.q: Can you lose more than you invest in crypto futures?
faq.a: On most retail crypto exchanges, liquidation closes your position before your balance goes negative, and an insurance fund covers gaps. Your margin can still be lost entirely, and with cross margin more of your account is at risk.

futures-contract.title: What is a futures contract in crypto? Explained
futures-contract.description: Learn how crypto futures contracts work, how margin and leverage change your profit and loss, and perpetual versus delivery futures.

perpetual-futures.short: Perpetual futures (perps) are futures contracts with no expiry date that use a periodic funding rate to keep their price close to the underlying spot price.
body: A normal futures contract expires, so its price naturally converges with spot at the end. A perpetual has no end date, so it needs another anchor. That anchor is the funding rate: at set intervals, traders on one side pay traders on the other side.

When the perp trades above the index price, funding is usually positive and longs pay shorts, which encourages shorting and pulls the price down. When it trades below, funding turns negative and shorts pay longs. Funding is commonly settled every 8 hours, but some exchanges and pairs use 1, 2 or 4 hours.

Perps are the most traded crypto derivative. Centralized exchanges such as Binance, OKX, Bybit and Bitget list hundreds of them, and on-chain venues such as Hyperliquid offer perps too. You can hold a position as long as your margin covers losses and funding, but liquidation is based on the mark price, not only the last traded price.
perpetual-futures.example: Suppose you hold a 10,000 USDT long on a BTC perp and the funding rate is +0.01% per 8-hour interval. Each interval you pay 10,000 × 0.01% = 1 USDT to shorts, so 3 USDT a day and about 90 USDT over 30 days if the rate stayed unchanged. If funding flips to -0.02%, you would instead receive 2 USDT per interval while staying long.
mistakes: Ignoring funding costs on a long-held leveraged position, where they can add up to a significant amount.
Assuming funding is always settled every 8 hours on every pair.
Watching only the last traded price when liquidation depends on the mark price.

faq.q: Why are they called perpetual futures?
faq.a: Because they never expire. You can keep the position open indefinitely as long as you meet the margin requirements.

faq.q: Who pays the funding fee on perpetual futures?
faq.a: It depends on the sign of the rate. Positive funding means longs pay shorts, and negative funding means shorts pay longs. The exchange does not keep it.

perpetual-futures.title: What are perpetual futures (perps)? Crypto explained
perpetual-futures.description: Learn how perpetual futures work, why they never expire, how funding keeps them near spot and what that costs you.

delivery-futures.short: Delivery futures are crypto futures contracts with a fixed expiry date, such as a weekly or quarterly contract, that settle at a set price when they expire.
body: Unlike perpetual futures, a delivery contract has an end date written in its name, for example a BTC contract expiring at the end of a quarter. On that date the position closes automatically and settles. On most crypto exchanges settlement is in cash, using an average index price over a short window, rather than physical delivery of coins.

Because there is a set expiry, there is no funding rate. Instead, the contract usually trades at a premium or discount to spot, called the basis. In normal conditions longer-dated contracts trade at a premium, reflecting borrowing costs and demand for leveraged longs. As expiry approaches, that gap shrinks toward zero.

Traders use delivery futures to lock in a price for a known date, to hedge, or to earn the basis by buying spot and selling the future. If you want to keep exposure after expiry, you must roll the position into the next contract, which can cost fees and a different basis. Expiry times and settlement rules differ by exchange.
delivery-futures.example: Suppose BTC spot is 60,000 USDT and the quarterly contract expiring in 90 days trades at 61,200, a 2% premium. You buy 1 BTC spot and short 1 BTC of the quarterly contract. At expiry the future settles at the spot price. Whether BTC ends at 50,000 or 70,000, your combined position earns about the 1,200 USDT premium, roughly 2% over the quarter, before fees.
mistakes: Forgetting the expiry date and being surprised when the position settles automatically.
Assuming the futures price must equal spot before expiry.
Rolling into the next contract without checking how wide its premium is.

faq.q: What happens when a crypto futures contract expires?
faq.a: The exchange closes all open positions at the settlement price, which is usually based on an index average shortly before expiry, and credits or debits your profit and loss.

faq.q: Do delivery futures have funding fees?
faq.a: No. They converge with spot through the expiry itself, so their price difference from spot shows up as a premium or discount instead.

delivery-futures.title: What are delivery (quarterly) futures in crypto?
delivery-futures.description: Learn how quarterly delivery futures work, how they settle at expiry and how they differ from perpetual futures.

coin-margined-futures.short: Coin-margined (inverse) futures are futures contracts where margin and profit or loss are in the underlying coin, such as BTC, instead of a stablecoin.
body: In a coin-margined BTC contract you deposit BTC as margin, and gains and losses are paid in BTC. Contracts are often quoted in USD value, for example 100 USD per contract, which is why they are called inverse: your profit in BTC follows the formula position value × (1 ÷ entry price − 1 ÷ exit price).

This structure suits holders who already have the coin and want to measure results in it. Miners and long-term holders use coin-margined shorts to hedge, because the BTC they post as margin rises in value as the short loses, and falls as the short gains.

The catch is double exposure on longs. If you go long with BTC as margin, both your position and your collateral lose value when the price falls, so liquidation can come faster than you expect. Profit and loss are also not linear in USD terms. Contract sizes and available coins differ by exchange.
coin-margined-futures.example: Suppose you open a 10,000 USD long on a BTC inverse contract at 50,000 USD. If BTC rises to 60,000, your profit is 10,000 × (1 ÷ 50,000 − 1 ÷ 60,000) ≈ 0.0333 BTC, worth about 2,000 USD at the new price. If BTC instead falls to 40,000, your loss is 10,000 × (1 ÷ 40,000 − 1 ÷ 50,000) = 0.05 BTC, and the BTC you posted as margin has also lost 20% of its USD value.
mistakes: Opening a leveraged long with coin margin without realising the collateral falls along with the position.
Expecting profit and loss to be linear in USD as it is with USDT contracts.
Confusing contract count with coin amount when sizing the position.

faq.q: Why are coin-margined futures called inverse?
faq.a: Because profit and loss in the coin are calculated from the inverse of the price. That makes payoffs non-linear when measured in the coin.

faq.q: Who should use coin-margined futures?
faq.a: They suit people who hold the coin and think in coin terms, such as miners hedging output. Many beginners find USDT-margined contracts easier to understand.

coin-margined-futures.title: What are coin-margined (inverse) futures? Explained
coin-margined-futures.description: Learn how coin-margined inverse futures work, how profit is calculated in BTC and why longs carry double exposure.

usdt-margined-futures.short: USDT-margined (linear) futures are futures contracts where margin, profit and loss are all in the stablecoin USDT, so results move in a straight line with the price.
body: In a USDT-margined contract you post USDT as margin and every price move translates directly into USDT. A 1 USDT move on a 1 BTC position is a 1 USDT gain or loss. That simple, linear relationship is why these contracts are called linear and why most beginners start with them.

Because one margin currency covers many markets, you can trade BTC, ETH and hundreds of smaller coins from a single USDT balance. With cross margin, profits on one position can support another. Some exchanges also offer USDC-margined contracts that work the same way.

Your collateral does not fall with the coin, unlike inverse contracts, so a long position has only one source of risk. You still carry stablecoin risk: if USDT lost its peg, your margin would be worth less. Contract sizes, maximum leverage and fees differ by exchange and pair, so check the contract details.
usdt-margined-futures.example: Suppose you short 2 ETH on a USDT-margined perpetual at 3,200 USDT with 1,280 USDT of margin, which is 5x leverage on a 6,400 USDT position. If ETH drops to 3,000, you earn 2 × 200 = 400 USDT. If ETH rises to 3,400, you lose 2 × 200 = 400 USDT, about 31% of your margin. The same 200 USDT move always means the same 400 USDT result, whatever the price level.
mistakes: Assuming a stablecoin margin means the position itself is low risk.
Letting one bad position drain the whole USDT balance in cross margin mode.
Mixing up USDT-margined and coin-margined versions of the same contract.

faq.q: What is the difference between USDT-M and COIN-M futures?
faq.a: USDT-M contracts use USDT for margin and profit, with linear payoffs. COIN-M contracts use the coin itself, so payoffs are non-linear and the collateral moves with the price.

faq.q: Are USDT-margined futures better for beginners?
faq.a: They are usually easier to understand because profit and loss are simple to calculate in a stable unit. The leverage risks are the same.

usdt-margined-futures.title: What are USDT-margined (linear) futures? Explained
usdt-margined-futures.description: Learn how USDT-margined linear futures work, why profit and loss are simple to calculate and how they differ from inverse contracts.

funding-rate.short: A funding rate is a periodic payment between long and short traders that keeps a perpetual futures price close to the spot price.
body: Perpetual futures never expire, so the exchange needs a mechanism that pulls their price toward the index price of the spot market. At each funding time, if the rate is positive, traders holding longs pay those holding shorts. If it is negative, shorts pay longs. The payment goes between traders, not to the exchange.

The rate is usually built from two parts: a premium component that measures how far the perp trades from the index, and an interest component. Exchanges publish the predicted rate and a countdown to the next settlement. Funding is commonly settled every 8 hours, but some exchanges and pairs use 1, 2 or 4 hours, and rates may be capped.

Funding is calculated on your position value, not on your margin, so leverage makes it matter more. You only pay or receive funding if you hold a position at the settlement moment. Persistently high positive funding shows that many traders are leveraged long, which can make the market vulnerable to sharp drops when they unwind.
funding-rate.example: Suppose you hold a 30,000 USDT short on a SOL perpetual with 3,000 USDT of margin. The funding rate is +0.03% every 8 hours, so as a short you receive 30,000 × 0.03% = 9 USDT per interval, or 27 USDT a day. A trader holding the opposite 30,000 USDT long pays that same 27 USDT a day, which is almost 1% of a 3,000 USDT margin every day.
mistakes: Calculating funding on margin instead of the full position value.
Assuming funding is always settled every 8 hours on every exchange and pair.
Reading high positive funding as a guaranteed signal that price will fall.

faq.q: Is a negative funding rate bullish?
faq.a: It shows that shorts are dominant and paying longs, which can fuel a short squeeze. It is a sentiment indicator, not a reliable price signal on its own.

faq.q: Do I pay funding if I close before the funding time?
faq.a: No. Funding applies only to positions open at the exact settlement time on your exchange.

funding-rate.title: What is a funding rate? Meaning in crypto futures
funding-rate.description: Learn what a funding rate is, who pays whom, how often it settles and how to calculate its cost on a perpetual position.

leverage.short: Leverage is using borrowed funds or margin to open a position larger than your own capital, which multiplies both profits and losses.
body: Leverage is shown as a multiplier such as 3x, 10x or 50x. At 10x, 1,000 USDT of margin controls a 10,000 USDT position. A 1% price move then changes your margin by about 10%, in either direction.

The main risk is liquidation. The higher the leverage, the smaller the price move needed to wipe out your margin. At 10x, a move of roughly 10% against you, minus a buffer for maintenance margin and fees, ends the position. At 50x, about 2% is enough. Leverage also increases fees and funding in relation to your margin, because both are charged on the full position.

Leverage is a tool for capital efficiency, not a way to make a bad trade good. Many experienced traders choose their position size first, based on how much they can afford to lose at the stop-loss, and only then select leverage to free up margin. Maximum leverage differs by exchange, pair and position size, and some countries cap retail leverage on crypto derivatives.
leverage.example: Suppose you have 500 USDT and open a long on ETH at 2,000 USDT with 20x leverage, a position of 10,000 USDT or 5 ETH. If ETH rises 3% to 2,060, you gain 5 × 60 = 300 USDT, a 60% return on margin. If ETH falls 3% to 1,940, you lose 300 USDT, 60% of your margin, and a fall of under 5% would likely trigger liquidation.
mistakes: Choosing leverage before deciding how much you are willing to lose on the trade.
Forgetting that fees and funding are charged on the full leveraged size.
Assuming low leverage cannot be liquidated; it can, just after a larger move.

faq.q: What does 10x leverage mean?
faq.a: It means your position is ten times your margin. A 1% price move changes your margin by about 10%.

faq.q: What leverage should a beginner use?
faq.a: Lower leverage gives you more room before liquidation. More important than the number is sizing the position so a stop-loss costs only a small part of your account.

leverage.title: What is leverage in crypto trading? Explained simply
