leverage.description: Learn how leverage works in crypto, how it multiplies gains and losses, and why higher leverage brings liquidation closer.

margin-trading.short: Margin trading is trading with funds borrowed from an exchange, using your own assets as collateral, so you can open larger positions or short-sell.
body: In spot margin trading you borrow coins or stablecoins from the exchange and pay interest, usually charged hourly or daily. Borrowing USDT lets you buy more of a coin than your balance allows. Borrowing a coin and selling it lets you go short. In futures, margin works as collateral for a contract rather than an actual loan, but the idea of trading a larger position on collateral is the same.

Your collateral must stay above a minimum level, known as the maintenance margin. If losses push your margin level below it, the exchange may issue a warning, often called a margin call, and then liquidate your position to repay the loan.

Exchanges offer different margin modes. Isolated margin limits risk to the collateral assigned to one position. Cross margin shares your whole balance across positions. Interest rates, borrowable coins and maximum leverage vary by exchange and change with demand, so check them before you borrow.
margin-trading.example: Suppose you have 2,000 USDT and use 3x spot margin to buy BTC at 40,000 USDT. You borrow 4,000 USDT and buy 0.15 BTC worth 6,000 USDT. If BTC rises to 44,000, the BTC is worth 6,600 USDT; after repaying 4,000 you keep 2,600, a 30% gain on your capital before interest. If BTC falls to 36,000, you keep 5,400 − 4,000 = 1,400, a 30% loss.
mistakes: Forgetting borrowing interest, which keeps accruing while a position stays open.
Assuming margin trading is the same as futures, when spot margin involves a real loan.
Using cross margin without realising that one losing position can drain the whole balance.

faq.q: What is the difference between margin trading and futures?
faq.a: Spot margin uses a real loan to buy or sell the actual coin, with interest. Futures are contracts on the price, with funding or a basis instead of borrowing interest.

faq.q: How does margin trading let you short a coin?
faq.a: You borrow the coin, sell it, and later buy it back to repay the loan. If the price fell in between, you keep the difference minus interest.

margin-trading.title: What is margin trading in crypto? How it works
margin-trading.description: Learn how crypto margin trading works, how borrowing and collateral amplify results and what triggers a margin call.

initial-margin.short: Initial margin is the amount of collateral you must post to open a leveraged position, usually equal to the position value divided by your leverage.
body: When you open a futures or margin position, the exchange sets aside part of your balance as initial margin. At 10x leverage the initial margin rate is 10% of the position value; at 20x it is 5%. That is why higher leverage needs less margin for the same position.

Initial margin is different from maintenance margin. Initial margin is what you need to open the position. Maintenance margin is the lower level you must keep to avoid liquidation. The gap between the two is your buffer against adverse price moves.

Exchanges often use risk tiers: the larger the position, the higher the initial margin rate, which lowers the maximum leverage available. Opening fees may also be reserved from your balance. With isolated margin, the initial margin is the most you can lose on that position; with cross margin, losses can draw on the rest of your balance.
initial-margin.example: Suppose you open a 0.5 BTC long at 60,000 USDT, a position worth 30,000 USDT, using 15x leverage. The initial margin is 30,000 ÷ 15 = 2,000 USDT. If you chose 5x instead, the same position would need 6,000 USDT of initial margin, but it would also sit much further from its liquidation price because the buffer above maintenance margin is larger.
mistakes: Thinking initial margin is the trade cost, when profit and loss are based on the full position value.
Confusing initial margin with maintenance margin.
Expecting maximum leverage on very large positions when risk tiers lower it.

faq.q: How is initial margin calculated?
faq.a: In simple terms, position value divided by leverage. Exchanges may adjust it with risk tiers and may also hold back the estimated opening fee.

faq.q: Can I lose more than my initial margin?
faq.a: In isolated mode, your loss on that position is normally limited to its margin. In cross mode, losses can use your other available balance.

initial-margin.title: What is initial margin in crypto futures? Explained
initial-margin.description: Learn what initial margin is, how it is calculated from leverage and how it differs from maintenance margin in crypto futures.

maintenance-margin.short: Maintenance margin is the minimum collateral you must keep in a leveraged position; if your margin falls below it, the position is liquidated.
body: After you open a position, your margin changes with unrealized profit and loss. The exchange compares it with a required minimum, the maintenance margin, which is a percentage of the position value. For major pairs at small sizes this rate is often well under 1%, but it rises for larger positions and riskier coins.

When your margin balance drops to the maintenance level, liquidation starts. Exchanges measure this with the mark price, not the last traded price, to avoid liquidations caused by brief spikes. Many platforms show a margin ratio; when it approaches 100%, you are close to liquidation.

You can move away from the maintenance level by adding margin, reducing the position, or lowering exposure. Because maintenance margin rates are tiered by position size, a large position can have a liquidation price closer to entry than you might expect. Check the risk limit or margin tier table on your exchange.
maintenance-margin.example: Suppose you hold a 20,000 USDT position with 2,000 USDT of margin (10x) and the maintenance margin rate is 0.5%. The required minimum is 20,000 × 0.5% = 100 USDT. Your unrealized loss can grow to about 1,900 USDT before liquidation, ignoring fees. For a long, that is a 9.5% price drop. A larger position with a 2% rate would require 400 USDT and leave only 1,600 USDT of room.
mistakes: Watching only the last price, when the exchange uses the mark price for maintenance checks.
Assuming the maintenance rate is the same for every position size.
Waiting until the margin ratio is near 100% before adding collateral.

faq.q: What happens if my margin falls below maintenance margin?
faq.a: The exchange's liquidation engine takes over the position and closes it, fully or in steps, and any remaining margin may be lost.

faq.q: How do I avoid hitting maintenance margin?
faq.a: Use lower leverage, size positions sensibly, set a stop-loss well before the liquidation price, and add margin early if needed.

maintenance-margin.title: What is maintenance margin? Crypto futures explained
maintenance-margin.description: Learn what maintenance margin is, how it sets your liquidation point and why the required rate rises with position size.

margin-call.short: A margin call is a warning that your collateral has fallen close to the minimum required for a leveraged position, so you need to add margin or reduce the position to avoid liquidation.
body: In traditional finance, a broker calls you to demand more collateral. On crypto exchanges, a margin call is usually an automatic app notification, email or on-screen alert when your margin ratio passes a warning level. It is not a request you must answer; if you do nothing and the price keeps moving, liquidation follows automatically.

You have three main responses. You can add collateral, which moves your liquidation price further away. You can close part of the position, which lowers the margin required. Or you can close the whole position and accept the loss. Doing nothing is also a choice, and it lets the liquidation engine decide for you.

Warning thresholds, notification channels and timing differ by exchange, and fast markets can move from warning to liquidation within seconds. Treat a margin call as evidence that your position was too large or your stop-loss too far away, rather than a reason to keep adding money to a losing trade.
margin-call.example: Suppose you hold an isolated 10x long worth 15,000 USDT with 1,500 USDT of margin, and the exchange warns you when your margin balance falls below half of the initial margin. After a 6% drop, your unrealized loss is 900 USDT and your margin balance is 600 USDT. You receive a margin call. Adding 600 USDT pushes your liquidation price roughly 4 percentage points lower; closing half the position cuts the required margin in half.
mistakes: Repeatedly adding margin to a losing position instead of rethinking the trade.
Relying on notifications arriving in time during a fast move.
Assuming a margin call gives you a fixed grace period before liquidation.

faq.q: Do crypto exchanges give margin calls?
faq.a: Most send automatic warnings when your margin ratio gets high, but the exchange will liquidate without waiting for you to act.

faq.q: Should I add margin after a margin call?
faq.a: Only if your original trade idea is still valid and the added amount fits your risk plan. Often reducing the position is the safer choice.

margin-call.title: What is a margin call in crypto? What to do next
margin-call.description: Learn what a margin call means on a crypto exchange, how it leads to liquidation and the options you have when you get one.

isolated-margin.short: Isolated margin is a margin mode where each position has its own separate collateral, so a liquidation can only take the margin assigned to that position.
body: When you open a trade in isolated mode, you choose how much margin to commit. That amount alone backs the position. If the trade goes badly and hits its liquidation price, you lose that margin, but the rest of your futures balance is untouched.

This makes risk easy to see and cap, which is why many beginners prefer it. The trade-off is that the position cannot draw on your spare balance in a sharp move, so its liquidation price is closer than it would be in cross margin with the same total funds. You can manually add margin to an isolated position to push the liquidation price further away.

Isolated margin is useful when you hold several unrelated trades and do not want one to endanger the others. Exchanges let you switch modes, but usually only when you have no open position or orders on that contract, and some unified accounts handle modes differently.
isolated-margin.example: Suppose your futures account holds 5,000 USDT. You open an isolated 10x long on a small token with 400 USDT of margin, a 4,000 USDT position. The token falls roughly 10% and the position is liquidated. You lose roughly the 400 USDT, but 4,600 USDT stays in your account. In cross mode the same position could have kept drawing on the whole 5,000 USDT as the price fell further.
mistakes: Thinking isolated margin cannot be liquidated, when it is often liquidated sooner than cross.
Adding margin repeatedly to an isolated position, which removes the cap it was meant to give.
Forgetting to check which mode is active before opening a trade.

faq.q: Is isolated or cross margin better?
faq.a: Isolated caps the loss on each position, which is easier to control. Cross gives positions more room by sharing your balance, but one bad trade can affect everything.

faq.q: Can I add margin to an isolated position?
faq.a: Yes. Adding margin moves the liquidation price further from the current price, but it also increases what you can lose on that trade.

isolated-margin.title: What is isolated margin in crypto futures?
isolated-margin.description: Learn how isolated margin works, how it caps your loss per position and how it compares with cross margin.

cross-margin.short: Cross margin is a margin mode where all your open positions share the available balance in your account as collateral, so profits and spare funds can absorb losses before liquidation.
body: In cross mode the exchange does not ring-fence collateral per trade. Your whole available balance in that account, plus unrealized profit from winning positions, supports every open position. This gives a losing trade more room, so its liquidation price sits further away than in isolated mode with the same funds.

The downside is shared risk. If one position keeps losing, it draws on the entire balance. When the account can no longer meet the total maintenance margin, positions are liquidated and you can lose far more than the margin you had in mind for that single trade.

Cross margin suits traders who hold related or hedged positions, or who actively manage their total exposure. Many exchanges now offer unified or multi-asset accounts where cross margin can also count other coins as collateral, with haircuts on their value. Rules for which assets count and how they are valued differ by exchange.
cross-margin.example: Suppose your account holds 3,000 USDT and you open a 10x long worth 5,000 USDT in cross mode, using 500 USDT as initial margin. In isolated mode, a drop of about 10% would liquidate it. In cross mode, the full 3,000 USDT backs it, so the price would need to fall roughly 59% before the 3,000 USDT is used up, ignoring fees and maintenance margin. If that happened, you would lose almost all 3,000 USDT, not just 500.
mistakes: Thinking you only risk the initial margin of a trade when the account is in cross mode.
Keeping a large idle balance in a cross margin account that should have stayed in spot or savings.
Forgetting that a new position in cross mode changes the liquidation price of the others.

faq.q: Is cross margin riskier than isolated margin?
faq.a: It delays liquidation but puts your whole balance on the line. Isolated caps the loss per position; cross can lose everything in the account.

faq.q: When does cross margin make sense?
faq.a: It is useful when you run hedged or offsetting positions and monitor total exposure. For single directional bets, many traders prefer isolated margin.

cross-margin.title: What is cross margin in crypto futures? Explained
cross-margin.description: Learn how cross margin shares your balance across positions, why it delays liquidation and why it can put your whole account at risk.

portfolio-margin.short: Portfolio margin is a margin system that sets your collateral requirement based on the combined risk of all your positions, so hedged positions need less margin than they would separately.
body: Standard margin looks at each position, or each asset, on its own. Portfolio margin runs scenarios across your whole account, for example moving prices and volatility up and down by set amounts, and asks how much the entire portfolio could lose. Your requirement is based on that worst-case result.

If you hold offsetting positions, such as spot BTC and a BTC short perpetual, or options hedged with futures, the losses in one scenario are partly cancelled by gains in another. Portfolio margin recognises that, so you need less collateral and can use capital more efficiently.

It is aimed at advanced traders. Exchanges such as Binance, OKX, Bybit and Deribit offer portfolio margin modes, often with minimum account sizes, eligibility checks or limits on which assets qualify. The lower margin can also mean higher effective leverage, so a portfolio that is not truly hedged can be liquidated quickly. Methods and requirements differ by exchange.
portfolio-margin.example: Suppose you hold 2 BTC spot and short 2 BTC on a perpetual at 60,000 USDT. Under standard rules the short might need, say, 10% margin, or 12,000 USDT, on its own. Under portfolio margin, a 15% price drop would lose 18,000 USDT on the spot side but gain about 18,000 on the short. The net scenario loss is close to zero, so the requirement might be only a small fraction of 12,000 USDT, depending on the exchange's model.
mistakes: Assuming any mix of positions is hedged, when correlations can break in a crash.
Using the freed-up margin to add unhedged risk.
Ignoring that the exchange can change scenario parameters and raise margin requirements.

faq.q: What is the difference between cross margin and portfolio margin?
faq.a: Cross margin shares one balance across positions but usually sums each position's requirement. Portfolio margin goes further and nets out offsetting risk between positions.

faq.q: Who should use portfolio margin?
faq.a: Experienced traders running hedged strategies, options books or basis trades. For simple directional trading it adds complexity without much benefit.

portfolio-margin.title: What is portfolio margin in crypto? Explained
portfolio-margin.description: Learn how portfolio margin calculates requirements across your whole account, why hedges need less margin and the risks.

liquidation.short: Liquidation is when an exchange forcibly closes your leveraged position because your margin has fallen below the maintenance margin requirement.
body: Every leveraged position has a point where your remaining margin is no longer enough to cover further losses. When the mark price reaches that point, the exchange's liquidation engine takes over the position and closes it, either all at once or in steps for larger positions. You usually lose most or all of the margin for that position, and many exchanges also charge a liquidation fee.

Liquidation exists to protect the exchange and other traders from losses larger than the collateral. If the engine closes a position at a better price than the bankruptcy price, the surplus often goes to the insurance fund. If the market moves too fast, the insurance fund covers the shortfall, and in extreme cases auto-deleveraging (ADL) reduces profitable opposing positions.

Large waves of liquidations can feed on themselves: forced selling pushes price lower, which triggers more liquidations. This is why crypto sometimes moves very fast. To avoid liquidation, use lower leverage, keep a stop-loss well before the liquidation price, and size positions so one move cannot wipe you out.
liquidation.example: Suppose you open a 20x long on BTC at 50,000 USDT with 1,000 USDT of margin, a 20,000 USDT position. A 1% drop costs you 200 USDT. With a maintenance margin rate of 0.5%, the position is liquidated after a drop of roughly 4.5%, near 47,750, when your margin has shrunk to about 100 USDT. If a stop-loss at 49,000 had triggered first, you would have lost about 400 USDT instead of almost all 1,000.
mistakes: Treating the liquidation price as your stop-loss.
Watching the last price on a chart while the exchange liquidates on the mark price.
Re-entering with higher leverage straight after being liquidated to win back the loss.

faq.q: What does it mean to get liquidated in crypto?
faq.a: Your leveraged position was closed by the exchange because losses used up your margin. The collateral for that position is mostly or fully lost.

faq.q: Can I get my money back after liquidation?
faq.a: No. Liquidation is final and the lost margin is not returned, which is why a stop-loss is important.

liquidation.title: What is liquidation in crypto? Why positions get closed
liquidation.description: Learn what crypto liquidation is, what triggers it, what happens to your margin and how to keep it from happening.

liquidation-price.short: The liquidation price is the mark price at which your leveraged position will be forcibly closed because your margin would fall to the maintenance margin level.
body: Exchanges show an estimated liquidation price for every open position. For a long, it sits below your entry; for a short, above it. The distance depends mainly on leverage: higher leverage means less room. Maintenance margin rate, fees and, in cross mode, your other balance and positions also affect it.

A simplified formula for an isolated long is entry × (1 − 1 ÷ leverage + maintenance margin rate). For a short it is entry × (1 + 1 ÷ leverage − maintenance margin rate). Real numbers differ slightly because of fees, funding and tiered maintenance rates, so rely on the figure your exchange shows.

The liquidation price is not fixed. Adding margin moves it further away. Funding payments and partial closes can move it, and in cross mode any change to your balance or other positions changes it. The trigger is the mark price, which is designed to resist brief spikes on a single exchange.
liquidation-price.example: Suppose you open an isolated 10x long on BTC at 60,000 USDT with a maintenance margin rate of 0.5%. Using the simplified formula, the liquidation price is 60,000 × (1 − 0.1 + 0.005) = 54,300 USDT, about 9.5% below entry. At 25x the same formula gives 60,000 × (1 − 0.04 + 0.005) = 57,900, only 3.5% away. A 10x short from 60,000 would be liquidated near 65,700.
mistakes: Assuming the liquidation price never changes after opening the trade.
Comparing it with the last traded price instead of the mark price.
Placing a stop-loss so close to the liquidation price that slippage could carry the fill past it.

faq.q: How do I move my liquidation price further away?
faq.a: Add margin, reduce the position size, or use lower leverage when opening. In cross mode, a larger free balance also helps.

faq.q: Why was I liquidated before the chart reached my liquidation price?
faq.a: Usually because the mark price, not the last price on the chart, touched the level, or because fees and funding shifted the liquidation price.

liquidation-price.title: What is liquidation price? How it is calculated
liquidation-price.description: Learn what a liquidation price is, how leverage and maintenance margin set it, and how to calculate it for longs and shorts.

mark-price.short: The mark price is a fair-value price an exchange uses to calculate unrealized profit and loss and to trigger liquidations, instead of the last traded price.
body: The last traded price on a single futures order book can spike for a moment because of one large order or thin liquidity. If liquidations used that price, traders could be wiped out by a wick that lasts a second. The mark price smooths this out.

Exchanges typically build the mark price from the index price, an average of spot prices across several major exchanges, plus a smoothed measure of the futures premium or basis. Some use a median of several inputs. The exact formula differs by exchange and is published in its documentation.

In practice, your unrealized PnL, margin ratio and liquidation are based on the mark price. Many platforms let you choose whether a stop-loss triggers on the mark price or the last price. The two are usually close, but in volatile moments they can differ, which explains many surprises about when a position closed.
mark-price.example: Suppose a perpetual's last price briefly drops from 2,500 to 2,380 USDT when a large market sell hits a thin order book, while spot prices on other exchanges stay near 2,495. The mark price, anchored to the index, only dips to about 2,492. A long with a liquidation price of 2,400 survives, because the mark price never reached it, even though the chart shows a wick to 2,380.
mistakes: Watching only the candlestick chart, which shows the last price, to judge liquidation risk.
Not checking whether stop-loss orders trigger on the mark price or the last price.
Assuming the mark price is the same on every exchange.

faq.q: What is the difference between mark price and last price?
faq.a: Last price is the latest trade on that order book. Mark price is a smoothed fair value based mainly on the index, used for PnL and liquidation.

faq.q: Why do exchanges use mark price for liquidation?
faq.a: To stop brief price spikes or manipulation on one order book from causing unfair liquidations.

mark-price.title: What is mark price in crypto futures? Explained
mark-price.description: Learn what mark price is, how exchanges calculate it, and why it decides your liquidation instead of the last traded price.

index-price.short: The index price is a reference price for an asset calculated from a weighted average of spot prices on several major exchanges, used to anchor futures pricing.
body: An exchange running a perpetual or delivery contract needs a fair reference for the underlying coin. Instead of relying on its own spot market alone, it pulls prices from several large spot venues and combines them, often with weights and rules that exclude outliers or exchanges that stop updating.

The index price feeds into the mark price, which drives liquidations and unrealized PnL. It is also the benchmark for the funding rate: when the perpetual trades above the index, funding tends to be positive. Delivery futures usually settle at an average of the index price over a set window before expiry.

Because each exchange chooses its own sources and weights, index prices differ slightly between exchanges. In DeFi, a similar role is played by oracles, which bring external prices on-chain. If an index relies on too few or thin sources, it can be manipulated, which is why exchanges publish their index components.
index-price.example: Suppose an exchange's ETH index uses three spot sources with equal weight: 3,010, 3,004 and 2,999 USDT. The index price is (3,010 + 3,004 + 2,999) ÷ 3 = 3,004.33 USDT. If the ETH perpetual trades at 3,019, it sits about 0.5% above the index, a premium that pushes funding higher. If one source suddenly printed 2,800, outlier rules would typically reduce its weight or exclude it.
mistakes: Assuming the index price is a single exchange's spot price.
Expecting the index to be identical on every derivatives exchange.
Ignoring the index when judging whether funding is likely to be high or low.

faq.q: What is the difference between index price and mark price?
faq.a: The index price is an average of spot prices. The mark price starts from the index and adds a smoothed futures premium; it is what liquidations use.

faq.q: Where can I see the index components?
faq.a: Most exchanges publish the source exchanges and weights for each index on their contract information or index pages.

index-price.title: What is index price in crypto futures? Explained
index-price.description: Learn what the index price is, how exchanges build it from spot markets, and how it links to mark price and funding.

last-price.short: The last traded price is the price at which the most recent trade on an order book was executed, and it is the price you usually see on charts and tickers.
body: Every time a buy and sell order match, the trade price becomes the new last price. Candlestick charts, 24-hour change figures and most price tickers are built from these trades. It tells you what actually just happened on that specific market.

The last price is not necessarily the price you will get. If you place a market buy, you pay the best ask, and a large order may fill across several levels. The bid-ask spread and order book depth decide your real fill price, which can differ from the last price, especially on thin markets.

On futures exchanges, three prices are often shown: last price, mark price and index price. The last price can spike briefly on one order book, so liquidations usually use the mark price instead. Stop orders can often be set to trigger on either one, so check your setting.
last-price.example: Suppose the last trade on a token was 0.800 USDT, but the order book now shows a best bid of 0.790 and a best ask of 0.812. If you buy 5,000 tokens with a market order, you pay at least 0.812, so your cost is at least 4,060 USDT, not the 4,000 USDT the last price suggests. If only 2,000 tokens sit at 0.812 and the rest at 0.820, your total becomes 1,624 + 2,460 = 4,084 USDT.
mistakes: Expecting a market order to fill at the last traded price.
Using the last price to judge liquidation risk on futures, where the mark price applies.
Trusting a last price on an illiquid pair where the most recent trade may be minutes or hours old.

faq.q: Is the last price the same as the current price?
faq.a: It is the most recent trade, which is what most people call the current price. What you can actually buy or sell at is shown by the best ask and best bid.

faq.q: Should my stop-loss trigger on last price or mark price?
faq.a: Last price reacts faster to real trades, while mark price ignores brief spikes. Choose based on whether you prefer speed or protection from wicks.

last-price.title: What is the last traded price? Last vs mark price
last-price.description: Learn what the last traded price means, why your fill price can differ, and how it compares with mark and index price.

open-interest.short: Open interest is the total number or value of derivatives contracts, such as futures or options, that are currently open and not yet closed or settled.
body: Every futures contract has a long side and a short side. When a new buyer and a new seller open positions, open interest rises. When both sides close, it falls. When one trader passes a position to another, it stays the same. Open interest is shown in contracts, coins or USD value.

Open interest is different from volume. Volume counts how much traded during a period; open interest counts how much is still outstanding at a moment. A market can have huge volume with flat open interest if traders open and close positions all day.

Traders combine open interest with price and funding. Rising price with rising open interest suggests new money is entering with leverage. Very high open interest relative to normal levels means a lot of leverage is in the system, which can lead to large liquidation cascades if price moves sharply. Data can be viewed per exchange or aggregated across many.
open-interest.example: Suppose BTC perpetual open interest on an exchange is 8 billion USDT. Over two days price rises from 60,000 to 64,000 and open interest climbs to 9.5 billion, while funding rises to well above its usual level. That points to new leveraged longs. If price then drops to 61,000 and open interest falls back to 8.2 billion within hours, about 1.3 billion USDT of positions closed, many through liquidation.
mistakes: Confusing open interest with trading volume.
Reading rising open interest as bullish without looking at whether longs or shorts are adding.
Comparing open interest in coins on one site with open interest in USD on another.

faq.q: Is high open interest bullish or bearish?
faq.a: Neither by itself. It shows how much leverage is in the market; combined with price direction and funding, it hints at who is crowded.

faq.q: Why does open interest drop suddenly?
faq.a: Usually because many positions closed at once, often through a wave of liquidations or traders taking profit after a big move.

open-interest.title: What is open interest in crypto? Meaning explained
open-interest.description: Learn what open interest measures in crypto futures, how it differs from volume and how traders read it with price and funding.

long-and-short.short: A long position profits when an asset's price rises, and a short position profits when its price falls.
body: Going long is the familiar idea of buying low and selling high. You can go long by buying a coin on the spot market or by opening a long futures position. Going short means you profit from a decline. In crypto this is usually done with perpetual futures, by spot margin borrowing, or with options.

The risk profiles differ. In spot, a long's maximum loss is what you paid, because price cannot fall below zero. A short has no natural ceiling on losses, because price can keep rising. With leveraged futures, both sides can be liquidated if price moves against them far enough.

Longs and shorts are always matched in futures: for every long contract there is a short. That is why funding rates exist on perpetuals, and why the long/short ratio on an exchange only compares how many accounts lean one way, not the total size.
long-and-short.example: Suppose two traders each open a 1,000 USDT position on a token priced at 2.00 USDT, so 500 tokens each. One goes long and one goes short. If the price rises to 2.30, the long gains 500 × 0.30 = 150 USDT and the short loses 150 USDT. If it falls to 1.60, the long loses 200 USDT and the short gains 200 USDT, before fees and funding.
mistakes: Assuming shorting is just the reverse of buying with the same risk; a short's loss can keep growing as price rises.
Opening a short on a thin, heavily shorted coin without considering a short squeeze.
Forgetting that funding can make holding one side expensive over time.

faq.q: What does it mean to go long in crypto?
faq.a: It means taking a position that profits if the price rises, either by buying the coin or by opening a long futures contract.

faq.q: How do you short crypto?
faq.a: Most commonly with perpetual futures, by opening a short position. You can also borrow and sell coins with spot margin, or buy put options.

long-and-short.title: Long vs short positions in crypto: meaning explained
long-and-short.description: Learn what long and short positions mean in crypto trading, how each one profits, and the very different risks they carry.

short-selling.short: Short selling is a way to profit from a falling price by selling an asset you have borrowed, or opening a short contract, and buying it back later at a lower price.
body: Classic short selling works like this: you borrow a coin, sell it immediately, and later buy the same amount back to repay the loan. If the price fell in between, you keep the difference. On crypto exchanges you can do this with spot margin, paying interest on the borrowed coin.

Most crypto traders short with perpetual futures instead. You simply open a short position; there is no explicit loan, but funding payments apply. Options, such as buying a put, are another way to bet on a decline with a limited maximum loss.

Shorting carries specific risks. A price can rise much further than it can fall, so losses on an uncovered short are open-ended until you close it or get liquidated. Crowded shorts can be caught in a short squeeze, and in some markets borrowing costs or funding can rise sharply. Regulations on short selling vary by country and product.
short-selling.example: Suppose you borrow 10 LINK on spot margin and sell them at 15 USDT, receiving 150 USDT. A week later LINK trades at 12 USDT. You buy 10 LINK back for 120 USDT and repay the loan, keeping 30 USDT minus interest and fees. If LINK had risen to 20 USDT instead, buying back would cost 200 USDT, a 50 USDT loss, and the loss would grow with every further rise.
mistakes: Underestimating that losses on a short are not capped by the amount you started with.
Ignoring borrowing interest or funding that builds up while the short stays open.
Shorting a coin only because it has gone up a lot, without a clear exit plan.

faq.q: Can you short sell crypto on spot exchanges?
faq.a: Only if the exchange offers margin borrowing. Otherwise, shorting is done through futures or options.

faq.q: What is the maximum loss when shorting?
faq.a: In theory it is unlimited, because price can keep rising. In practice, leveraged shorts are liquidated, which limits the loss to the margin at risk.

short-selling.title: What is short selling in crypto? How shorting works
short-selling.description: Learn how short selling works in crypto with margin or futures, how you profit from a fall and why losses can be open-ended.

long-short-ratio.short: The long/short ratio compares how many traders or how much position size on an exchange is long versus short on a futures market, as a gauge of sentiment.
body: Because every futures contract has a buyer and a seller, total long and short contracts are always equal. So the long/short ratio usually measures something narrower: the share of accounts holding net long positions versus net short ones, or the positions of the exchange's top traders. A ratio of 2 means twice as many accounts are long as short.

Exchanges publish different versions, such as all accounts, top-trader accounts and top-trader positions. These can tell different stories, for example many small accounts long while large accounts lean short. Read the definition on each exchange before comparing numbers.

Traders often use extreme readings as a contrarian hint: when almost everyone is long, there may be few buyers left and many potential forced sellers. That is not a timing signal. Combine it with funding, open interest and price structure rather than trading it alone.
long-short-ratio.example: Suppose an exchange reports that 70% of accounts on an ETH perpetual are net long, a long/short ratio of 70 ÷ 30 ≈ 2.33. Because total longs equal total shorts in size, the 30% of short accounts must hold larger average positions. If price drops 4% and long liquidations pile up, that crowded long side can push the fall further.
mistakes: Assuming a high ratio means more money is long than short; in contracts, they are always equal.
Comparing an account-based ratio on one exchange with a position-based ratio on another.
Trading the ratio as a direct buy or sell signal.

faq.q: Is a high long/short ratio bullish?
faq.a: It shows that many accounts lean long, which can be a crowding warning rather than a bullish sign. It should be read together with funding and open interest.

faq.q: Why do longs and shorts not balance in the ratio?
faq.a: Because most ratios count accounts, not contract size. Total long and short contracts are always equal.

long-short-ratio.title: What is the long/short ratio in crypto? Explained
long-short-ratio.description: Learn what the long/short ratio measures, why longs and shorts always match in size, and how traders read crowded positioning.

short-squeeze.short: A short squeeze is a rapid price rise that forces short sellers to buy back their positions, through stop-losses or liquidation, which pushes the price even higher.
body: When many traders are short and the price starts to rise, their losses grow. To close a short, they must buy. Stop-losses trigger, liquidation engines close leveraged shorts with market buys, and that extra buying pushes the price further, triggering more short exits.

Squeezes are more likely when open interest is high, funding is deeply negative because shorts are paying longs, and the coin has thin liquidity. A piece of good news or a large buyer can be enough to start the chain. The mirror case, a long squeeze, forces leveraged longs to sell into a falling market.

For a short seller, the lesson is position size and stops. For anyone else, a squeeze can create sharp, short-lived moves that reverse once the forced buying is done. Chasing a squeeze near its peak often means buying just as the forced buying runs out.
short-squeeze.example: Suppose a token trades at 1.00 USDT with 50 million USDT of open interest, mostly shorts, and funding at -0.1% per 8 hours. Positive news pushes price to 1.08. Shorts opened at 1.00 with 10x leverage start getting liquidated near 1.09, adding market buys. Price spikes to 1.35 within an hour, then slides back to 1.15 once liquidations stop and open interest has dropped to 30 million USDT.
mistakes: Opening a large leveraged short on a heavily shorted, thin coin.
Buying at the peak of a squeeze, assuming the move reflects lasting demand.
Ignoring deeply negative funding, which signals how crowded the short side is.

faq.q: What causes a short squeeze in crypto?
faq.a: A rise in price when many leveraged shorts are open. Their stop-losses and liquidations turn into market buys, which feed the rise.

faq.q: How can you spot a possible short squeeze?
faq.a: Look for high open interest, negative funding and thin liquidity together. These signs show crowding, not timing.

short-squeeze.title: What is a short squeeze in crypto? How it happens
short-squeeze.description: Learn what a short squeeze is, how liquidations of leveraged shorts fuel it and the warning signs traders watch.

unrealized-pnl.short: Unrealized PnL is the profit or loss on a position that is still open, calculated from your entry price and the current price, and it only becomes real when you close the position.
body: PnL stands for profit and loss. While a position is open, its value changes with every price move, and the exchange shows this as unrealized PnL. Once you close the position, the result is locked in as realized PnL and added to or taken from your balance.

On futures exchanges, unrealized PnL is usually calculated with the mark price, not the last traded price. Exchanges often also show ROE or ROI, which is unrealized PnL divided by your margin. With leverage, ROE can look dramatic: a 2% price move at 25x shows as a 50% gain or loss on margin.

Unrealized PnL matters for risk. A growing unrealized loss reduces your margin balance and brings you closer to liquidation. In cross margin mode, unrealized profit on one position can support others, but it can disappear quickly if the market turns. Some exchanges limit how much unrealized profit you can withdraw or use as margin.
unrealized-pnl.example: Suppose you open a long of 3 SOL perpetual contracts, each worth 1 SOL, at 150 USDT. The mark price rises to 162. Your unrealized PnL is 3 × 12 = 36 USDT. If you used 90 USDT of margin (5x), the exchange shows an ROE of 36 ÷ 90 = 40%. If the price falls back to 150 before you close, that 36 USDT disappears and your realized PnL is zero minus fees.
mistakes: Counting unrealized profit as money already earned.
Judging a trade by ROE percentage without looking at the actual amount at risk.
Forgetting that fees and funding reduce the realized result compared with the displayed unrealized PnL.

faq.q: What is the difference between realized and unrealized PnL?
faq.a: Unrealized PnL is the current paper result of an open position. Realized PnL is the final result after you close it, including fees.

faq.q: Why is my unrealized PnL different from what the chart suggests?
faq.a: Exchanges usually calculate it with the mark price, while the chart shows the last traded price. Fees may also be estimated in.

unrealized-pnl.title: What is unrealized PnL? Meaning in crypto trading
unrealized-pnl.description: Learn what unrealized PnL means, how it is calculated with mark price and how it differs from realized profit and ROE.

auto-deleveraging.short: Auto-deleveraging (ADL) is a last-resort mechanism where an exchange automatically reduces profitable opposing positions to cover a liquidation that the market and insurance fund cannot absorb.
body: Normally, when a position is liquidated, the exchange closes it in the market, and the insurance fund covers any shortfall. In extreme moves, there may be no buyers or sellers at a reasonable price and the insurance fund for that contract may not be enough. ADL then steps in.

The exchange picks traders on the opposite side of the bankrupt position and closes part or all of their positions at the bankruptcy price. Traders are ranked by profit and leverage, so those with large unrealized profit and high leverage are first in line. Many exchanges show an ADL indicator, often as lights or a queue ranking, next to each position.

ADL is rare on major pairs, but it can happen in crashes or on small, illiquid contracts. If it hits you, you are not liquidated; your profitable position is closed early, often at a decent price, but you lose the rest of the move. Rules, ranking formulas and how often ADL occurs differ by exchange.
auto-deleveraging.example: Suppose a small-cap perpetual drops 40% in minutes. A large long position worth 2 million USDT is liquidated, but the order book cannot absorb it and the insurance fund for that contract holds only 300,000 USDT. You hold a short with high unrealized profit and 20x leverage, so you rank first in the ADL queue. The exchange closes 50,000 USDT of your short at the bankruptcy price, locking in that profit but ending your trade early.
mistakes: Thinking ADL is the same as being liquidated; it closes profitable positions, not losing ones.
Ignoring the ADL indicator on highly leveraged, very profitable positions in illiquid markets.
Assuming every exchange handles ADL with the same ranking rules.

faq.q: Why did my profitable position get closed by the exchange?
faq.a: It may have been auto-deleveraged. When a liquidation cannot be filled and the insurance fund is short, the exchange reduces top-ranked profitable positions on the other side.

faq.q: How can I lower my ADL risk?
faq.a: Use lower leverage and take partial profits on large winning positions, which lowers your rank in the ADL queue.

auto-deleveraging.title: What is auto-deleveraging (ADL) in crypto futures?
auto-deleveraging.description: Learn what auto-deleveraging is, why exchanges use it after extreme liquidations and how ADL ranking works.

insurance-fund.short: An insurance fund is a reserve an exchange keeps to cover losses when liquidated positions cannot be closed at a price good enough to repay what they owe.
body: When a position is liquidated, the exchange tries to close it before the trader's margin runs out completely. If it closes at a better price than the bankruptcy price, the leftover margin usually goes into the insurance fund. If the market gaps and the fill is worse than the bankruptcy price, the fund pays the shortfall.

Without this buffer, profitable traders on the other side might not receive their full gains. The insurance fund is the first line of defence; auto-deleveraging (ADL) only comes in when the fund is not enough. Some exchanges keep separate funds per contract, others pool them.

Large exchanges publish their insurance fund balances, which helps you judge how well a market can handle extreme moves. A small or shrinking fund on an illiquid contract means a higher chance of ADL. On-chain perp exchanges use similar mechanisms, sometimes with a vault funded by liquidity providers instead.
insurance-fund.example: Suppose a trader's long has a bankruptcy price of 28,000 USDT. In a fast drop, the liquidation engine fills the position at 27,800, a 200 USDT gap per BTC on a 5 BTC position. The shortfall of 5 × 200 = 1,000 USDT comes from the insurance fund. Earlier that day another liquidation closed at 300 USDT per BTC better than its bankruptcy price on 2 BTC, adding 600 USDT to the fund.
mistakes: Thinking the insurance fund protects your own margin from liquidation.
Assuming the fund size is the same for every contract on an exchange.
Ignoring a small insurance fund when trading high leverage on illiquid contracts.

faq.q: Does the insurance fund pay me if I get liquidated?
faq.a: No. It covers losses beyond the liquidated trader's margin so the exchange and counterparties are paid. Your liquidated margin is not refunded.

faq.q: Where does the insurance fund money come from?
faq.a: Mainly from leftover margin when liquidations close at better than the bankruptcy price, and sometimes from exchange contributions.

insurance-fund.title: What is an insurance fund in crypto futures?
insurance-fund.description: Learn how a crypto exchange insurance fund works, where its money comes from and how it links to liquidation and ADL.

reduce-only-order.short: A reduce-only order is a futures order setting that can only shrink or close an existing position and will never open a new one or increase it.
body: Normally a sell order on a futures market can either close a long or open a new short. If you place a 2 BTC sell to close a 1 BTC long, the extra 1 BTC opens a short you never intended. Ticking reduce-only prevents that: the exchange only executes the part that reduces your current position.

Reduce-only is mainly used for take-profit and stop-loss orders, and for limit orders placed in advance to scale out of a trade. If your position is closed by another order first, any remaining reduce-only orders are cancelled or rejected instead of opening something new.

Many exchanges set take-profit and stop-loss orders attached to a position as reduce-only by default, but standalone limit or conditional orders may not be. In hedge mode, where you can hold a long and a short on the same contract, closing orders work slightly differently. Check how your exchange labels and handles it.
reduce-only-order.example: Suppose you are long 0.6 BTC and place two take-profit limit sells of 0.4 BTC each, at 68,000 and 70,000 USDT, both reduce-only. The first fills and your position drops to 0.2 BTC. When price reaches 70,000, the second order only sells 0.2 BTC and closes the position. Without reduce-only, it would sell 0.4 BTC and leave you with an unwanted 0.2 BTC short.
mistakes: Placing take-profit orders larger than the position without reduce-only, and ending up short.
Assuming every stop or limit order is reduce-only by default.
Forgetting that reduce-only orders cannot be used to open a position later.

faq.q: What does reduce-only mean on Binance or Bybit?
faq.a: It means the order can only reduce or close your current position. Many exchanges, including Binance and Bybit, offer it as a checkbox on futures orders.

faq.q: Why was my reduce-only order rejected?
faq.a: Usually because there was no open position in that direction, or the position was already smaller than the order.

reduce-only-order.title: What is a reduce-only order in crypto futures?
reduce-only-order.description: Learn what a reduce-only order does, why it stops take-profit orders from opening new positions and when to use it.

hedging.short: Hedging is opening a position that offsets the risk of another position, so that a loss on one is partly or fully balanced by a gain on the other.
body: The classic crypto hedge is holding a coin and shorting the same coin with futures. If the price falls, the spot holding loses value and the short gains. You keep ownership of your coins, for example for staking, tax timing or long-term plans, while reducing exposure to a drop.

A hedge can be full or partial. Shorting the same amount you hold makes you roughly market-neutral; shorting half cuts your exposure in half. Options are another tool: buying a put option limits losses below a set price in exchange for paying a premium up front.

Hedging is not free. Futures hedges have fees and funding, which can be a cost or an income. Options cost a premium. A hedge also caps your upside, and an imperfect hedge, such as shorting BTC to protect a small altcoin, can fail when the two do not move together. Margin on the hedge must be managed too, or it can be liquidated during a rally while your spot gains.
hedging.example: Suppose you hold 10 ETH at 3,000 USDT, worth 30,000 USDT. You short 10 ETH on a perpetual at 3,000 using 3,000 USDT of margin. ETH falls to 2,400: your spot loses 6,000 USDT and the short gains 6,000 USDT, so your total stays near 30,000 before fees and funding. If ETH rises to 3,600 instead, spot gains 6,000 and the short loses 6,000, so you miss the upside.
mistakes: Hedging with high leverage so the short gets liquidated in a rally while the spot gains are not available as margin.
Forgetting funding costs on a long-running perpetual hedge.
Hedging an altcoin with a BTC short and assuming the two will always move together.

faq.q: How do you hedge crypto holdings?
faq.a: The most common ways are shorting the same coin with futures or buying put options. Each reduces downside but has costs and caps or changes your upside.

faq.q: Is hedging the same as closing the position?
faq.a: The economic exposure is similar, but you keep the coins. That can matter for staking, tax timing or simply wanting to keep the asset.

hedging.title: What is hedging in crypto? How to protect a position
hedging.description: Learn how hedging works in crypto with futures or options, what a full or partial hedge does, and its costs.

futures-basis.short: The futures basis is the difference between a futures contract's price and the spot price of the same asset, often expressed as an annualised percentage.
body: Basis = futures price − spot price. When futures trade above spot, the basis is positive, a state called contango. When they trade below, it is negative, called backwardation. In crypto, dated futures have usually traded at a premium, reflecting demand for leveraged long exposure and the cost of capital.

To compare contracts with different expiry dates, traders annualise the basis: divide the percentage premium by the days to expiry and multiply by 365. A 2% premium on a 30-day contract is far higher annualised than 2% on a 180-day one.

The basis shrinks toward zero as a delivery contract approaches expiry, because it settles at the index price. That is the idea behind the cash-and-carry or basis trade: buy spot, sell the future, and earn the premium. Perpetual futures have no expiry, so their premium is handled by the funding rate instead. A very high basis also signals heavy leveraged demand.
futures-basis.example: Suppose BTC spot is 60,000 USDT and the contract expiring in 60 days trades at 60,900. The basis is 900 USDT, or 1.5% of spot. Annualised, that is 1.5% × 365 ÷ 60 ≈ 9.1% a year. A trader who buys 1 BTC spot and sells 1 BTC of that future locks in roughly 900 USDT at expiry, minus fees, whatever happens to the price.
mistakes: Comparing raw basis between contracts with different expiries instead of annualising it.
Calling a basis trade risk-free while ignoring exchange risk and margin needs on the short future.
Confusing the basis of dated futures with the funding rate of perpetuals.

faq.q: What is contango in crypto futures?
faq.a: Contango means futures trade above spot, a positive basis. It is the usual state in crypto when demand for leveraged longs is healthy.

faq.q: What does a negative basis mean?
faq.a: Futures trade below spot, called backwardation. It often appears in fearful markets or when demand to short is strong.

futures-basis.title: What is futures basis in crypto? Contango explained
futures-basis.description: Learn what futures basis is, how to annualise it, what contango and backwardation mean and how basis trades work.

funding-rate-arbitrage.short: Funding rate arbitrage is a market-neutral strategy that collects funding payments by holding opposite positions, usually spot long and perpetual short, so price moves largely cancel out.
body: When funding is positive, longs pay shorts. If you buy a coin on spot and open a short perpetual of the same size, price moves offset each other and you receive funding each interval. When funding is negative, the reverse setup, short spot via margin and long perp, can collect it, though that is harder to do.
A variation uses two exchanges: short the perp where funding is high and long the perp where it is low or negative. The goal is the same: be neutral on price and earn the difference in funding.

The strategy has real costs and risks. Trading fees on four legs (open and close, spot and perp) can eat days of funding. Funding rates change every interval and can flip negative. The short perp needs margin and can be liquidated in a sharp rally if it is under-collateralised, even though the spot side gained. Exchange risk and withdrawal limits also apply. Settlement intervals differ by exchange and pair.
funding-rate-arbitrage.example: Suppose you buy 10,000 USDT of BTC on spot and short 10,000 USDT of a BTC perpetual with 2,500 USDT of margin. Funding is +0.01% every 8 hours, paying you 1 USDT per interval, or 3 USDT a day. Opening and closing all legs at 0.1% each costs about 40 USDT, so you need around two weeks at that rate just to cover fees. Over 90 days you would collect about 270 USDT, or roughly 230 USDT net, on 12,500 USDT of capital.
mistakes: Ignoring trading fees, which can wipe out weeks of funding income.
Using too little margin on the short so a rally liquidates it while the spot side is stuck on another account.
Assuming a high funding rate will stay high.

faq.q: Is funding rate arbitrage risk-free?
faq.a: No. Funding can turn negative, fees add up, the short can be liquidated if under-margined, and exchange risk remains.

faq.q: How much can funding rate arbitrage earn?
faq.a: It depends entirely on current funding rates, fees and capital efficiency. Returns vary widely over time and are often modest after costs.

funding-rate-arbitrage.title: What is funding rate arbitrage? How it works
funding-rate-arbitrage.description: Learn how funding rate arbitrage collects perpetual funding with a spot-long, perp-short setup, and the fees and risks involved.

options.short: Crypto options are contracts that give the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) a cryptocurrency at a set strike price on or before a set expiry date.
body: The buyer pays a premium up front. A call option gains value when the price rises above the strike; a put gains when the price falls below it. If the option expires without value, the buyer loses only the premium. The seller, also called the writer, receives the premium but takes on the obligation and can face large losses.

Option prices depend on the current price, the strike, time to expiry and implied volatility, the market's estimate of how much the price may move. Crypto volatility is high, so premiums are often expensive compared with stock options. Most crypto options are European style, exercisable only at expiry, and settle in cash.

Traders use options to hedge, for example buying puts to protect holdings, or to bet on direction with a capped loss. Deribit is a major crypto options venue, and exchanges such as OKX, Binance and Bybit also list options. Products like dual investment are built on selling options. Contract sizes and settlement rules differ by venue.
options.example: Suppose BTC trades at 65,000 USDT and you buy a call for 0.1 BTC with a strike of 70,000, expiring in a month, for a premium of 200 USDT. If BTC ends at 76,000, the call pays 0.1 × 6,000 = 600 USDT, a net gain of 400 USDT. If BTC ends below 70,000, the option expires worthless and you lose the 200 USDT. Your break-even price is 72,000.
mistakes: Selling options for the premium without understanding the size of the potential loss.
Buying options that are far from the money and short-dated, where most expire worthless.
Ignoring implied volatility, which can make an option lose value even when price moves your way.

faq.q: What is the difference between options and futures?
faq.a: Futures oblige both sides to settle and can be liquidated. An option buyer has a right, not an obligation, and can lose at most the premium.

faq.q: What happens when a crypto option expires?
faq.a: If it is in the money, it usually settles automatically in cash. If not, it expires worthless and the buyer loses the premium.

options.title: What are crypto options? Calls and puts explained
options.description: Learn how crypto options work, the difference between calls and puts, premiums, strike prices and how buyers and sellers profit.

crypto-wallet.short: A crypto wallet is software or a device that stores the private keys controlling your cryptocurrency and lets you send, receive and manage it on the blockchain.
body: Your coins are not actually inside the wallet. They are recorded on the blockchain, and the wallet holds the private keys that prove you can move them. From those keys, the wallet generates public addresses you can share to receive funds.

Wallets come in two broad types. A custodial wallet, such as an exchange account, means a company holds the keys for you. A non-custodial wallet, such as MetaMask, Phantom or a hardware wallet, means you hold the keys yourself, usually backed up by a seed phrase of 12 or 24 words. Wallets are also described as hot, connected to the internet, or cold, kept offline.

Choosing a wallet is a trade-off between convenience and control. Exchange wallets are easy and offer account recovery, but you rely on the company. Self-custody removes that dependency, but losing your seed phrase means losing your funds, and nobody can reset it for you. Always check that a wallet supports the right network before sending coins to it.
crypto-wallet.example: Suppose you keep 2,000 USDT on an exchange for trading and 0.05 BTC in a hardware wallet for long-term holding. To move 500 USDT to a DeFi app, you send it from the exchange to your non-custodial wallet on a supported network, paying a withdrawal fee of a few USDT. Your hardware wallet's 24-word seed phrase, written on paper, can restore that 0.05 BTC even if the device is lost.
mistakes: Storing a seed phrase in screenshots, cloud notes or email.
Sending coins on a network the receiving wallet does not support.
Assuming a crypto wallet can be recovered by customer support like a bank account.

faq.q: What is the safest type of crypto wallet?
faq.a: For long-term holdings, many people use a hardware wallet with a seed phrase stored offline. Safety also depends on how well you protect that backup.

faq.q: Do I need a crypto wallet if I use an exchange?
faq.a: Your exchange account already acts as a custodial wallet. A separate wallet is needed if you want to hold your own keys or use DeFi apps.

crypto-wallet.title: What is a crypto wallet? Types and how they work
crypto-wallet.description: Learn what a crypto wallet really stores, the difference between custodial and non-custodial, hot and cold wallets.

custodial-wallet.short: A custodial wallet is a crypto wallet where a third party, usually an exchange or app, holds the private keys and controls the funds on your behalf.
body: When you deposit coins to an exchange, they go into wallets the exchange controls. Your account shows a balance, but the exchange holds the keys. You can trade, withdraw or transfer, as long as the company processes your request.

The benefits are convenience and support. There is no seed phrase to lose, you can reset a forgotten password, and trading is instant. Regulated custodians must meet rules on security, segregation of client assets and identity checks, which vary by country.

The main risk is counterparty risk. If the company is hacked, freezes withdrawals, becomes insolvent or blocks your account, you may not get your funds back quickly or at all. Check how an exchange protects client assets, whether it publishes proof of reserves, and enable two-factor authentication and withdrawal address whitelisting. Many users keep only trading funds on exchanges and move long-term holdings to self-custody.
custodial-wallet.example: Suppose you hold 4,000 USDT and 1 ETH on an exchange. You lose your phone and two-factor app, so you complete an identity check and support restores access within a few days. That recovery would be impossible with a lost seed phrase. However, if the same exchange paused withdrawals during a crisis, your 4,000 USDT and 1 ETH would be stuck until it resumed, because you never held the keys.
mistakes: Keeping all long-term holdings on an exchange without considering counterparty risk.
Not enabling two-factor authentication and withdrawal whitelists on a custodial account.
Assuming funds in a custodial wallet are protected like a bank deposit in every country.

faq.q: What is the difference between custodial and non-custodial wallets?
faq.a: In a custodial wallet a company holds the private keys. In a non-custodial wallet you hold them yourself, usually via a seed phrase.

faq.q: Is a custodial wallet safe?
faq.a: It can be convenient and well secured, but you depend on the company's security and solvency. Proof of reserves and strong account security reduce, but do not remove, that risk.

custodial-wallet.title: What is a custodial wallet? Pros, cons and risks
custodial-wallet.description: Learn what a custodial wallet is, how exchanges hold your keys, and the convenience and counterparty risk it brings.

non-custodial-wallet.short: A non-custodial wallet is a crypto wallet where you alone hold the private keys or seed phrase, so no exchange or company can move, freeze or recover your funds for you.
body: With a non-custodial wallet, the wallet app or device only helps you create and use keys. The keys themselves stay with you, usually backed up as a 12- or 24-word seed phrase. Whoever has that phrase controls the coins, which is why the phrase matters more than the app.

This is the opposite of keeping coins on an exchange, where the platform holds the keys and you hold a balance in its database. Self-custody removes the risk of an exchange freezing withdrawals or failing, but it moves all the responsibility to you: there is no password reset and no support desk that can reverse a mistaken transfer.

Common examples are browser and mobile wallets such as MetaMask, Phantom or Trust Wallet, and hardware wallets such as Ledger or Trezor. Some exchanges also offer a separate self-custody wallet app alongside their main exchange account; check which mode you are using before you assume who holds the keys.
non-custodial-wallet.example: Suppose you buy 0.2 BTC on an exchange and withdraw it to a new non-custodial wallet. The wallet shows you 12 words once, and you write them on paper. A year later your phone breaks. You install the wallet on a new phone, type the same 12 words in the same order, and the 0.2 BTC reappears, because the coins live on the blockchain and the words regenerate the keys. If you had lost the paper as well, nobody could restore access.
mistakes: Saving the seed phrase as a screenshot or in cloud notes, where malware or a hacked account can read it.
Assuming the wallet company can recover funds after you lose the seed phrase.
Moving a large balance before doing a small test transfer and a test restore of the backup.

faq.q: Is a non-custodial wallet safer than an exchange?
faq.a: It removes exchange risk, such as frozen withdrawals or insolvency, but adds personal risk, such as losing your seed phrase or signing a malicious transaction. It is safer only if you manage the keys carefully.

faq.q: Is MetaMask a non-custodial wallet?
faq.a: Yes. MetaMask generates keys on your device and never holds your seed phrase, so only you can sign transactions from it.

faq.q: What happens if the wallet app shuts down?
faq.a: Your funds stay on the blockchain. You can import the same seed phrase into another compatible wallet and keep access.

non-custodial-wallet.title: What is a non-custodial wallet? Self-custody explained
non-custodial-wallet.description: Learn what a non-custodial wallet is, how self-custody works, and what you are responsible for when you hold your own keys.

hot-wallet.short: A hot wallet is a crypto wallet whose private keys are stored on a device connected to the internet, such as a phone app, browser extension or exchange system, which makes it convenient but more exposed to attacks.
body: Hot means online. A mobile wallet, a desktop app or a browser extension keeps the keys on a device that is connected to the internet, so you can send, swap and use DeFi apps in seconds. Exchanges also run hot wallets to process customer withdrawals quickly.

The trade-off is exposure. Malware, fake browser extensions, phishing sites and malicious transaction requests can all reach a device that is online. Most hot wallet losses come from the user signing something harmful or leaking the seed phrase, not from the wallet software being broken.
A common setup is to treat a hot wallet like a physical wallet in your pocket: keep a spending amount there and keep long-term savings in a cold wallet or hardware wallet.
hot-wallet.example: Say you hold 5,000 USDT in total. You keep 300 USDT in a browser wallet for trying new DeFi apps and leave the remaining 4,700 USDT on a hardware wallet. One day you connect to a fake airdrop site and approve a malicious request. The attacker drains the browser wallet, and you lose 300 USDT, about 6 percent of your holdings, instead of everything.
mistakes: Keeping long-term savings in the same browser wallet you use to test new apps and airdrops.
Installing a wallet extension from a search ad instead of from the official store listing.
Signing every pop-up without reading which contract and which amount it asks for.

faq.q: Is a hot wallet safe?
faq.a: It is reasonably safe for everyday amounts if your device is clean and you check what you sign. It is not ideal for large balances you rarely touch.

faq.q: Is an exchange account a hot wallet?
faq.a: From your point of view it is a custodial account; the exchange holds the keys and keeps part of customer funds in its own hot wallets for withdrawals and the rest in cold storage.

hot-wallet.title: What is a hot wallet? Meaning and risks in crypto
hot-wallet.description: What a hot wallet is, why it is convenient, how hot wallets get drained, and how much to keep in one.

cold-wallet.short: A cold wallet is a way of storing crypto where the private keys are generated and kept offline, away from internet-connected devices, so remote attackers cannot reach them.
body: Cold storage covers hardware wallets, air-gapped computers or phones that never go online, and paper or metal backups of keys. The coins still sit on the blockchain; what is cold is the key that signs transactions.

To spend from cold storage you create a transaction, sign it on the offline device, and then broadcast it from an online device. This extra step is the point: even if your laptop is infected, the key never touches it.

Exchanges use cold storage too, often with multisig and several people needed to approve a movement. For individuals, cold storage is best for long-term holdings. The main risks shift to physical ones: loss, fire, theft of the backup, or forgetting where it is.
cold-wallet.example: Imagine you hold 1.5 ETH that you do not plan to touch for two years. You keep 0.1 ETH in a phone wallet for gas and small swaps and send 1.4 ETH to a hardware wallet, with the 24-word backup stamped on a steel plate in a separate place from the device. If your phone is hacked, the attacker can reach 0.1 ETH but not the 1.4 ETH, because signing those coins requires the physical device and its PIN.
mistakes: Calling a wallet cold while its seed phrase is stored as a photo on an online phone.
Keeping the device and its only backup in the same drawer.
Never testing a restore from the backup before relying on it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hot and a cold wallet?
faq.a: A hot wallet keeps keys on an internet-connected device, while a cold wallet keeps them offline. Hot is convenient for daily use, cold is better for savings.

faq.q: Can a cold wallet be hacked?
faq.a: Remote attacks are much harder, but you can still lose funds by signing a malicious transaction, revealing the seed phrase, or buying a tampered device from an unofficial seller.

cold-wallet.title: What is a cold wallet? Cold storage meaning
cold-wallet.description: Learn what a cold wallet is, how offline signing protects your keys, and which risks remain with cold storage.

hardware-wallet.short: A hardware wallet is a small physical device that stores your private keys offline and signs transactions inside the device, so the keys never leave it even when it is plugged into a computer or phone.
body: Well-known examples include Ledger, Trezor and Keystone. You connect the device by USB, Bluetooth or QR code, prepare a transaction in a companion app, and then confirm it with a button press on the device itself. The screen on the device is what you trust, not the screen of your computer.

When you set it up, the device creates a seed phrase. That phrase is the real backup: if the device breaks or is lost, you can restore the same wallet on a new device. A PIN protects the device against someone who picks it up.
A hardware wallet blocks remote key theft, but it cannot protect you from approving a bad transaction. Always compare the address and amount on the device screen before you confirm.
hardware-wallet.example: Suppose you want to send 250 USDC to a friend. You paste the address into the wallet app on your laptop. The hardware wallet screen then shows the address and 250 USDC. You notice the last four characters on the device differ from the ones your friend sent you, because malware replaced the address on your clipboard. You reject the transaction on the device, and nothing leaves your wallet.
mistakes: Buying a hardware wallet second-hand or from an unofficial marketplace seller.
Typing the seed phrase into a computer or website to set up or fix the device.
Confirming a transaction without reading the address and amount on the device screen.

faq.q: Do I need a hardware wallet?
faq.a: If you hold an amount you would be upset to lose and plan to keep it for a long time, a hardware wallet is a common way to reduce online risk.

faq.q: What happens if I lose my hardware wallet?
faq.a: Your coins are not on the device; they are on the blockchain. Restore the seed phrase on a new device and move funds if you think the old device and PIN could be used by someone else.

hardware-wallet.title: What is a hardware wallet? How it protects crypto
hardware-wallet.description: What a hardware wallet does, how on-device signing works, and the mistakes that still put your coins at risk.

seed-phrase.short: A seed phrase is a list of usually 12 or 24 ordinary words that encodes the master key of a crypto wallet, so anyone who has the words can restore the wallet and spend all of its funds.
body: Most wallets follow the BIP-39 standard, which picks words from a fixed list of 2,048 English words. From the phrase, the wallet derives your private keys and addresses on many blockchains. The order of the words matters, and so does any optional extra passphrase you may have set.

The seed phrase is not a password you can change at a help desk. It is the wallet. No real exchange, wallet team or support agent will ever need it. Anyone asking for it, through a pop-up, a sync tool, a support chat or a giveaway, is trying to take your funds.
Store it offline, ideally on paper or metal, in more than one safe place. Do not photograph it, email it, or keep it in a password manager linked to an account that could be phished.
seed-phrase.example: Suppose a wallet holds 0.5 BTC and 2,000 USDT across two chains, all derived from one 12-word phrase. A scammer posing as wallet support asks you to verify your wallet by entering the words into a form. Within minutes, both the 0.5 BTC and the 2,000 USDT are moved, because the attacker can now generate the same keys. With 2,048 possible words per position, guessing a 12-word phrase is practically impossible, so leaking it is the real danger.
mistakes: Entering the seed phrase on any website, form or chat that claims to validate or sync your wallet.
Storing the words as a phone photo or in cloud notes.
Writing the words out of order or skipping the check step when the wallet asks you to confirm them.

faq.q: Is a seed phrase the same as a private key?
faq.a: No. The seed phrase is a master backup that can generate many private keys, one for each address the wallet uses.

faq.q: Can I recover my wallet without the seed phrase?
faq.a: Usually not. In a non-custodial wallet, nobody else holds a copy, so a lost phrase and a lost device mean lost funds.

faq.q: Does an exchange account have a seed phrase?
faq.a: No. A custodial exchange account is protected by your login, 2FA and the exchange itself, not by a seed phrase.

seed-phrase.title: What is a seed phrase? Recovery phrase meaning
seed-phrase.description: What a seed phrase is, why it controls your whole wallet, how to store it, and the scams that try to steal it.

private-key.short: A private key is a secret number that proves ownership of a crypto address and is used to sign transactions, so whoever holds it can spend the coins at that address.
body: In most blockchains, a private key is a 256-bit number, often shown as 64 hexadecimal characters. From it, the wallet calculates a public key, and from the public key an address. This works in one direction only: you cannot work backwards from an address to the private key.

When you send crypto, your wallet uses the private key to create a digital signature. The network checks the signature against your public key and accepts the transaction without ever seeing the key itself.

Most people never handle raw private keys because wallets derive them from a seed phrase. Exporting a single private key is sometimes needed to import an account into another wallet, but it should be treated as carefully as the seed phrase.
private-key.example: Picture a wallet with one Ethereum address holding 0.8 ETH. You export its private key to import the account into a second wallet app and paste the key into a notes app that syncs to the cloud. Months later the cloud account is compromised. The attacker finds the 64-character key, imports it, and sends the 0.8 ETH away in one transaction. Your seed phrase was never exposed, yet that address is lost.
mistakes: Thinking a private key is safe to share because it is not the seed phrase.
Pasting a private key into a website that claims to check your balance or fix a stuck transaction.
Confusing the public address, which is safe to share, with the private key, which is not.

faq.q: Can someone get my private key from my wallet address?
faq.a: No. Deriving the private key from an address is computationally infeasible with current technology.

faq.q: What is the difference between a private key and a public key?
faq.a: The private key signs and must stay secret. The public key and the address derived from it are shared so others can send you funds and verify your signatures.

private-key.title: What is a private key in crypto? Meaning explained
private-key.description: Learn what a private key is, how it signs transactions, how it relates to your address and seed phrase, and why it must stay secret.

public-key.short: A public key is the shareable half of a crypto key pair, calculated from the private key, that lets the network verify your signatures and from which your wallet address is derived.
body: Public-key cryptography uses two linked keys. The private key signs, and the public key verifies. Bitcoin and Ethereum use elliptic curve cryptography, where computing the public key from the private key is easy, but the reverse is not feasible.

Your wallet address is usually a shortened, hashed version of the public key. On Ethereum, the address is the last 20 bytes of the hash of the public key. Bitcoin uses several address formats built from the public key in different ways.

You rarely need to handle a public key directly. Some advanced tools, such as multisig setups or watch-only wallets, use an extended public key (xpub) to track every address of a wallet. An xpub cannot spend funds, but it reveals your full balance and history, so share it only with tools you trust.
public-key.example: Suppose Alice signs a transaction sending 0.05 BTC to Bob. Each node on the network receives the transaction, the signature and Alice's public key. It runs the verification math and confirms that only the owner of the matching private key could have produced that signature, and that the public key matches the address holding the 0.05 BTC. The private key itself never travels across the network.
mistakes: Believing the public key is the same thing as the wallet address in every blockchain.
Sharing an xpub with an unknown app without realising it exposes every address and balance in the wallet.
Thinking a public key can be used to move funds.

faq.q: Is it safe to share my public key?
faq.a: Yes, in terms of spending. A public key cannot move funds, though it can link your addresses and reveal your activity.

faq.q: Is a public key the same as a wallet address?
faq.a: Not exactly. The address is usually derived from the public key by hashing and encoding it, which makes it shorter and adds error checks.

public-key.title: What is a public key in crypto? Meaning explained
