public-key.description: What a public key is, how it differs from a private key and a wallet address, and what an xpub reveals.

wallet-address.short: A wallet address is a string of letters and numbers that identifies where crypto can be sent on a specific blockchain, similar to an account number you can share publicly.
body: Address formats depend on the blockchain. Bitcoin addresses often start with bc1, 1 or 3. Ethereum and other EVM chains such as BNB Smart Chain, Arbitrum and Base use addresses that start with 0x. Tron addresses start with T, and Solana addresses are long base58 strings.

An address is only valid on the network it belongs to. The same 0x address can exist on several EVM chains, which is why an exchange asks you to pick a network on top of the address. Sending to the right address on the wrong network can make funds hard or impossible to recover.
Blockchain transfers cannot be reversed. Copy addresses with the copy button or a QR code, then check the first and last several characters before you confirm.
wallet-address.example: Say you withdraw 1,000 USDT from an exchange to your own wallet. Your wallet shows an address starting with T, so you choose the TRC-20 network on the exchange and paste the address. You first send 20 USDT as a test, see it arrive in your wallet, and then send the remaining 980 USDT. The test costs one extra network fee, but it confirms the address and network before the larger amount moves.
mistakes: Copying an address from your transaction history, where a look-alike poisoned address may be waiting.
Choosing a network that the receiving wallet or exchange does not support.
Typing an address by hand instead of copying it or scanning its QR code.

faq.q: Can I reuse the same wallet address?
faq.a: Yes, an address can receive many times. Some Bitcoin wallets generate a new address for each payment to improve privacy, but older ones still work.

faq.q: Is it safe to share my wallet address?
faq.a: Yes. Others can only send to it and view its public history; they cannot spend from it.

wallet-address.title: What is a wallet address? Crypto address explained
wallet-address.description: Learn what a crypto wallet address is, how formats differ by chain, and how to check an address before sending.

blockchain-network.short: A deposit network is the blockchain you choose to move a coin or token over when you deposit to or withdraw from an exchange, and the sending and receiving sides must use the same one.
body: Many assets exist on several blockchains. USDT, for example, is issued on Tron (TRC-20), Ethereum (ERC-20), BNB Smart Chain, Solana, TON and others. These are separate ledgers. A token sent over one network does not appear on another by itself.

When you withdraw, the exchange asks you to pick a network and shows the fee and minimum amount for each. When you deposit, the exchange shows an address for the network you select. Fees, speed and the number of confirmations required differ by network and by exchange.

If you send over a network that the receiver does not support, the funds may still exist on-chain but not be credited. Some exchanges can recover them for a fee, others cannot. Always match the network on both sides before sending.
blockchain-network.example: Suppose you move 500 USDT from Exchange A to Exchange B. Exchange B lists deposits on TRC-20 and ERC-20. Exchange A shows a withdrawal fee of 1 USDT on TRC-20 and 4 USDT on ERC-20, as illustrative figures. You choose TRC-20 on both sides, paste the address starting with T, and receive 499 USDT. Had you chosen BNB Smart Chain on Exchange A, the tokens could have been sent to a network Exchange B does not credit.
mistakes: Assuming that because both addresses start with 0x, any EVM network will work.
Picking the cheapest network without checking that the receiving side supports it.
Ignoring the minimum deposit amount, which can leave a small transfer uncredited.

faq.q: What happens if I choose the wrong network?
faq.a: The transfer usually completes on-chain but the receiver does not see it. Contact the receiving platform's support with the transaction hash; recovery is not guaranteed.

faq.q: Is TRC-20 the same as ERC-20?
faq.a: No. TRC-20 is a token standard on Tron and ERC-20 is a token standard on Ethereum. They are different blockchains with different fees and addresses.

blockchain-network.title: What is a deposit network? Choosing the right chain
blockchain-network.description: Why exchanges ask you to pick a network, how TRC-20, ERC-20 and others differ, and what happens if you pick the wrong one.

memo-tag.short: A memo or destination tag is an extra code attached to a transfer that tells an exchange which customer account should receive a deposit sent to a shared address.
body: Some blockchains, including XRP, Stellar (XLM), Cosmos (ATOM), EOS and TON for many exchanges, let a platform use one deposit address for many customers. To tell deposits apart, the exchange gives each user a memo, tag or comment that must be included with the transfer.

The name varies: XRP uses destination tag, Stellar and Cosmos use memo, and some exchanges show it as tag or comment. If the deposit page shows one, it is required, even if your sending wallet labels the field optional.

A missing or wrong memo means the coins reach the exchange but cannot be matched to you automatically. Many exchanges can credit them manually after you submit a request with the transaction hash, but it can take time and may involve a fee.
memo-tag.example: Say you withdraw 300 XRP from one exchange to another. The receiving exchange shows a shared XRP address and a destination tag of 104582. On the sending side, you paste the address and enter 104582 in the tag field. The 300 XRP arrives and is credited to your account within minutes. If you had left the tag empty, the 300 XRP would sit in the exchange's shared wallet until support traced it.
mistakes: Leaving the memo empty because the sending app marks the field as optional.
Reusing a memo from another exchange or an old screenshot.
Adding a memo when sending to a personal wallet that does not use one, then assuming it means something.

faq.q: Do I need a memo when sending to my own wallet?
faq.a: Usually not. Personal wallets normally have their own address. Memos matter mainly when the receiver is an exchange or service using shared addresses.

faq.q: I forgot the memo. Are my coins lost?
faq.a: Often they can be recovered. Contact the receiving exchange with the transaction hash, amount and address; policies and fees vary.

memo-tag.title: What is a memo or destination tag in crypto?
memo-tag.description: What memo and destination tags are, which coins use them, and what to do if you send a deposit without one.

transaction-hash.short: A transaction hash, or TxID, is the unique identifier of a blockchain transaction, which you can paste into a block explorer to see its status, amount, addresses and confirmations.
body: Every transaction broadcast to a blockchain gets a hash, a fixed-length string calculated from the transaction data. On Ethereum it starts with 0x and has 64 hex characters after it. On Bitcoin and Tron it is a 64-character hex string.

Exchanges show the TxID in your withdrawal history once the transfer has been sent on-chain. You can paste it into an explorer for that network, such as Etherscan, Tronscan or a Bitcoin explorer, to see whether it is pending, confirmed or failed.

The TxID is the first thing support teams ask for when a deposit is missing. It proves whether the funds left the sender and which address and network they went to. It is public information and safe to share.
transaction-hash.example: Suppose you withdraw 0.03 BTC to a friend and the friend says nothing arrived after 20 minutes. You copy the TxID from your withdrawal history and paste it into a Bitcoin explorer. It shows the transaction in the mempool with 0 confirmations because the fee was low. An hour later, the explorer shows 3 confirmations and the receiving address matches your friend's. The coins were never lost, only waiting for a block.
mistakes: Searching a TxID in an explorer for the wrong network and concluding the transaction does not exist.
Treating an exchange's internal transfer ID as an on-chain TxID.
Assuming a missing TxID means the funds left; if the exchange has not broadcast it yet, there is no hash.

faq.q: Where do I find my transaction hash?
faq.a: In your exchange's withdrawal or deposit history, or in your wallet's activity list. Tap the transaction to see or copy the TxID.

faq.q: Is it safe to share a TxID?
faq.a: Yes. It only points to public data already on the blockchain and cannot be used to move funds.

transaction-hash.title: What is a transaction hash (TxID)? How to use one
transaction-hash.description: Learn what a TxID is, where to find it, and how to track a deposit or withdrawal in a block explorer.

block-confirmations.short: Block confirmations are the number of blocks added to a blockchain since the block that includes your transaction, and exchanges wait for a set number before crediting a deposit.
body: When your transaction is included in a block, it has 1 confirmation. Each new block on top adds another. The deeper a transaction sits, the harder it is for the chain to reorganise and drop it, so more confirmations mean more certainty.

Exchanges set their own confirmation requirements for each network, which you can usually see on the deposit page. Requirements also differ by chain: Bitcoin blocks arrive roughly every 10 minutes, while chains like Tron or Solana produce blocks in seconds. Some exchanges credit a deposit for trading after fewer confirmations but unlock withdrawal only after more.
If your deposit shows on an explorer but not on the exchange yet, compare the current confirmation count with the exchange's requirement before contacting support.
block-confirmations.example: Imagine you deposit 0.1 BTC and the exchange requires 2 confirmations to credit and 3 to unlock withdrawal (illustrative numbers). Your transaction enters a block at 14:00. Blocks follow at about 14:09 and 14:21. At 14:09 you have 2 confirmations and the 0.1 BTC appears in your balance. At 14:21 you reach 3 and can withdraw it. Since Bitcoin block times vary, the same deposit could take longer.
mistakes: Contacting support before the deposit has reached the required number of confirmations.
Expecting every network to confirm as fast as the one you used last time.
Treating a transaction with 0 confirmations as final.

faq.q: How many confirmations does Bitcoin need?
faq.a: There is no single rule. Each exchange sets its own number, and many merchants and individuals treat a few confirmations as sufficient for typical amounts.

faq.q: Why is my transaction stuck at 0 confirmations?
faq.a: It is still waiting in the mempool, often because the fee was low compared with other pending transactions.

block-confirmations.title: What are block confirmations? Why deposits wait
block-confirmations.description: What block confirmations are, why exchanges wait for them, and how to check if your deposit is still confirming.

two-factor-authentication.short: Two-factor authentication (2FA) is a login and approval method that asks for a second proof, such as a code from an authenticator app or a security key, in addition to your password.
body: A password is something you know. 2FA adds something you have, such as a phone running an authenticator app, a hardware security key, or a phone number receiving SMS codes. An attacker who steals your password still cannot log in or withdraw without the second factor.

Not all second factors are equally strong. Authenticator apps (time-based one-time passwords) and hardware security keys or passkeys are generally stronger than SMS, which can be intercepted through SIM swapping. Many exchanges let you combine several methods and require 2FA for logins, withdrawals and security changes.
Keep the backup or recovery key that an authenticator app shows during setup. Without it, a lost phone can lock you out for days while the exchange verifies your identity.
two-factor-authentication.example: Suppose an attacker buys your email and password from a leaked database and tries to withdraw 2,000 USDT from your exchange account. The exchange asks for a 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds in your authenticator app. The attacker does not have your phone, so the login fails. If you had only SMS codes and the attacker had taken over your phone number, the same attempt could have succeeded.
mistakes: Relying only on SMS codes when the exchange offers an authenticator app or security key.
Typing a 2FA code into a page you reached from an email or ad rather than the official app.
Not saving the authenticator backup key, then losing access when the phone is replaced.

faq.q: Which type of 2FA is best for crypto?
faq.a: Hardware security keys or passkeys and authenticator apps are generally safer than SMS. Using more than one method gives you a fallback.

faq.q: Can 2FA be bypassed?
faq.a: Phishing sites can capture a code in real time and use it immediately. 2FA greatly reduces risk, but you still need to check that you are on the real site.

two-factor-authentication.title: What is 2FA? Two-factor authentication in crypto
two-factor-authentication.description: What two-factor authentication is, which 2FA methods are strongest, and how 2FA protects your exchange account.

anti-phishing-code.short: An anti-phishing code is a personal word or phrase you set in your exchange account that the exchange includes in its genuine emails, so you can spot fake messages that do not contain it.
body: Phishing emails often copy an exchange's logo, layout and sender name perfectly. What a scammer does not know is the private code you chose in your security settings. Exchanges such as Binance, OKX, Bybit and Bitget offer this feature, and some show the code in other official messages too.
When an email claims to be from your exchange, look for your code first. If it is missing or wrong, treat the email as fake, do not click any links, and open the exchange app directly instead.

The code only proves an email is real; it does not make links inside a real email safe to follow blindly, and scammers can still reach you through SMS, social media or calls, which usually do not carry the code. Choose something that is not easy to guess and do not share it.
anti-phishing-code.example: Say you set the anti-phishing code BlueKettle42 on your exchange. One morning you get an email saying a withdrawal of 0.4 ETH is pending and you must cancel it within 15 minutes. The design looks right, but there is no BlueKettle42 anywhere. You ignore the link, open the exchange app and see no pending withdrawal. The email was a phishing attempt.
mistakes: Setting the code but never actually checking for it when an urgent email arrives.
Assuming a message on Telegram or SMS is real because your email has a code.
Choosing an obvious code such as your name or the exchange name.

faq.q: Where do I set an anti-phishing code?
faq.a: Usually in the security section of your exchange account settings. The exact menu name differs between exchanges.

faq.q: Does an anti-phishing code stop all scams?
faq.a: No. It helps you verify emails, but you still need 2FA, a withdrawal whitelist and careful checking of links and addresses.

anti-phishing-code.title: What is an anti-phishing code? How to use it
anti-phishing-code.description: Learn what an exchange anti-phishing code is, how it helps you spot fake emails, and what it does not protect against.

withdrawal-whitelist.short: A withdrawal whitelist is an exchange security setting that only allows withdrawals to addresses you have saved and approved in advance, blocking transfers to any new address.
body: Once the whitelist is on, every withdrawal must go to an address in your address book. Adding a new address usually requires 2FA and email confirmation, and many exchanges add a waiting period before a new address can be used. Details differ by exchange.

The value is in the delay and the extra checks. If someone gets into your account, they cannot simply send funds to their own address; they first have to add it, which triggers alerts and gives you time to react and freeze the account.
A whitelist also reduces copy-paste mistakes. When you pick a labelled saved address, you are less likely to paste a wrong or poisoned address from your history.
withdrawal-whitelist.example: Suppose you whitelist two addresses: your hardware wallet and your account on another exchange. An attacker steals your login and session and tries to withdraw 1.2 BTC to a new address. The exchange requires the address to be added first, sends you an email and SMS, and holds new addresses for 24 hours as an illustrative policy. You see the alert, lock the account, and the 1.2 BTC never leaves.
mistakes: Turning the whitelist on but adding addresses copied from transaction history without checking them.
Adding an address and labelling it vaguely, so you later pick the wrong one.
Disabling the whitelist for convenience and forgetting to turn it back on.

faq.q: Is a withdrawal whitelist worth enabling?
faq.a: For most users who withdraw to the same few addresses, yes. It adds friction only when you add a new address.

faq.q: Can I withdraw to a new address with the whitelist on?
faq.a: Yes, but you first need to add and verify it, and some exchanges make you wait before it can be used.

withdrawal-whitelist.title: What is a withdrawal whitelist? Exchange security
withdrawal-whitelist.description: What a withdrawal whitelist is, how it stops account thieves, and how to use saved addresses safely.

phishing.short: Phishing is a scam where attackers impersonate a trusted exchange, wallet or person to trick you into revealing login details or a seed phrase, or into signing a transaction that hands over your funds.
body: Crypto phishing comes through fake websites with near-identical domains, search ads, emails, SMS, social media replies, fake support accounts and direct messages offering airdrops. The goal is either to collect what you type, such as passwords, 2FA codes or seed phrases, or to get you to connect a wallet and sign a malicious approval.

Signs to check: an urgent deadline, a request for your seed phrase, a domain that is slightly different, a support agent who contacts you first, or a wallet pop-up asking to approve unlimited spending or sign a message you do not understand.

Practical defences are simple. Bookmark official sites, open the app directly rather than clicking links, set an anti-phishing code, use a withdrawal whitelist, and read every wallet request before signing.
phishing.example: Imagine you search for your wallet's website and click the first result, which is an ad. The page asks you to enter your 12-word phrase to fix a sync error. A real wallet would never ask for this. Had you entered it, a wallet holding 3,000 USDC and 0.6 ETH would be emptied within minutes. Instead, you close the tab and open the bookmarked official site, which shows no error at all.
mistakes: Trusting a link because it appeared at the top of search results or in a verified-looking account.
Replying to a support agent who messaged you first on Telegram, Discord or X.
Signing a wallet request to claim a free airdrop without reading what it approves.

faq.q: What should I do if I clicked a phishing link?
faq.a: If you only opened the page, close it. If you entered a password or code, change your password and check your account; if you entered a seed phrase or signed an approval, move remaining funds to a new wallet and revoke approvals.

faq.q: How can I tell if a crypto site is fake?
faq.a: Check the exact domain spelling, use bookmarks, and be suspicious of any page that asks for your seed phrase or creates urgency.

phishing.title: What is phishing in crypto? How to spot it
phishing.description: Learn how crypto phishing works, the warning signs of fake sites and messages, and simple habits that protect you.

address-poisoning.short: Address poisoning is a scam where an attacker sends a tiny or zero-value transfer from an address that looks like one you use, hoping you later copy that fake address from your transaction history.
body: Attackers watch the blockchain for addresses you send funds to. They generate a look-alike address that matches the first and last few characters, then send you a tiny amount or a fake token transfer from it. Now the fake address sits in your history right next to the real one.

The next time you copy an address from your history instead of the original source, you may paste the attacker's address. Because many wallets shorten addresses to the first and last characters, the two can look identical.

Protection comes from habits: copy addresses from the original source or your address book, check more than the first and last four characters, use a withdrawal whitelist on exchanges, and ignore unexpected tiny transfers rather than interacting with them.
address-poisoning.example: Say you regularly send USDT to your own address 0x7a3F...91cD. After one transfer, a 0 USDT transaction arrives from 0x7a3F...91cD, but the middle characters are different. A week later you copy the top entry from your history and send 8,000 USDT. It goes to the attacker. Checking the full address, or using a saved contact, would have shown the mismatch before you confirmed.
mistakes: Copying a recipient address from your recent transaction list.
Checking only the first and last four characters of an address.
Interacting with an unknown token that appeared in your wallet after a poisoning transfer.

faq.q: Can address poisoning steal funds without my action?
faq.a: No. The scam only works if you send to the fake address yourself. Your existing funds are not at risk from the dust transfer alone.

faq.q: Should I hide or ignore the tiny transfer?
faq.a: Ignore it and do not trade or approve the token. Some wallets let you hide spam tokens, which reduces confusion.

address-poisoning.title: What is address poisoning? How the scam works
address-poisoning.description: How address poisoning scams plant look-alike addresses in your history, and how to check addresses before sending.

pig-butchering-scam.short: A pig-butchering scam is a long-con fraud where a stranger builds trust over weeks, often as a friend or romantic interest, then steers you into a fake crypto investment platform and takes everything you deposit.
body: The name comes from the Chinese phrase sha zhu pan, describing fattening a pig before slaughter. It often starts with a wrong-number text, a dating app match or a social media message. The scammer is friendly and patient, shares lifestyle photos and mentions trading profits only casually at first.

Next you are shown an app or website that looks like a real trading platform. Small first deposits appear to grow fast, and an early small withdrawal may even work to build trust. When you deposit larger sums, the balance keeps rising on screen, but any large withdrawal is blocked by sudden taxes, fees or verification charges.

Warning signs: someone you have never met pushing a specific platform, guaranteed or unusually steady returns, a platform not available on official app stores, and pressure to pay fees before you can withdraw.
pig-butchering-scam.example: Suppose a new online friend helps you open an account on a trading site and you deposit 1,000 USDT. Within two weeks the dashboard shows 1,400 USDT, and a 100 USDT withdrawal works. You add 10,000 USDT. The balance shows 15,000 USDT, but withdrawing it requires a 20 percent tax payment of 3,000 USDT first. Paying it only leads to another fee. The 11,000 USDT you sent was never traded at all.
mistakes: Trusting a trading platform because a friend you have only met online recommends it.
Treating a small successful withdrawal as proof that the platform is legitimate.
Paying an unlock fee or tax to release a balance, which only increases the loss.

faq.q: How do I check if a trading platform is real?
faq.a: Look it up independently, check whether the regulator in your country lists it, and be wary of apps installed from links rather than official stores.

faq.q: Can I get my money back from a pig-butchering scam?
faq.a: Recovery is difficult. Report it to the police and the exchange you sent from quickly, keep all records, and ignore recovery services that ask for upfront fees, which are often a second scam.

pig-butchering-scam.title: What is a pig-butchering scam? Warning signs
pig-butchering-scam.description: How pig-butchering crypto scams build trust, how fake platforms block withdrawals, and the warning signs to check.

rug-pull.short: A rug pull is a scam where the creators of a crypto project suddenly drain its liquidity, dump their tokens or abandon it after attracting buyers, leaving the token close to worthless.
body: Rug pulls are most common with new tokens on decentralized exchanges, especially memecoins. A typical pattern: the team creates a token, adds a liquidity pool, promotes it hard, and once buyers have added value, removes the liquidity or sells a large hidden allocation. The price collapses in minutes.

Some rugs are coded in from the start, for example a contract that blocks holders from selling, lets the owner mint unlimited tokens, or charges a sell tax the owner can raise to 100 percent. Others are slow: the team stops building and sells gradually.

Things to check before buying a new token: whether liquidity is locked and for how long, who controls the contract and whether ownership is renounced, how much supply sits in a few wallets, and whether you can actually sell a small amount.
rug-pull.example: Imagine a new token launches with a pool holding 50 ETH and 1 billion tokens. Over two days buyers add another 150 ETH, pushing the pool to 200 ETH. The deployer, who kept the LP tokens unlocked, withdraws all the liquidity and receives about 200 ETH plus the remaining tokens. Holders who bought the token now find almost no ETH left in the pool, so their tokens can only be sold for a tiny fraction of what they paid.
mistakes: Buying a token because it is trending without checking who controls the liquidity.
Assuming a token is safe because it is listed on a DEX, where anyone can create a pool.
Not testing a small sell before buying more, which would reveal a honeypot contract.

faq.q: How can I tell if a token might be a rug pull?
faq.a: Look for unlocked liquidity, an owner who can mint or change taxes, a few wallets holding most of the supply, and anonymous teams with no track record. None of these checks is a guarantee.

faq.q: Is a rug pull illegal?
faq.a: Deliberately deceiving buyers can be fraud in many countries, but enforcement depends on the jurisdiction and whether the team can be identified.

rug-pull.title: What is a rug pull in crypto? How to spot one
rug-pull.description: What a crypto rug pull is, how liquidity drains and malicious contracts work, and the checks to make before buying a new token.

token-approval.short: A token approval is a permission you sign in your wallet that lets a smart contract spend a set amount of a specific token from your address, often needed before swapping or depositing in DeFi.
body: On Ethereum and other EVM chains, a contract cannot move your ERC-20 tokens unless you first call approve. The approval names the contract (the spender) and an amount, called the allowance. Many apps request an unlimited allowance so you do not have to approve again for each trade.

Approvals stay active until you change them. If a contract you approved is later hacked or was malicious from the start, it can pull your approved tokens at any time, without another signature from you. Signature-based permits, such as Permit2, can grant similar rights through a message signature that may look harmless.

Good practice: approve only the amount you need when the wallet lets you edit it, read the spender address, and regularly review and revoke old approvals with a revoke tool or the approvals page of a block explorer.
token-approval.example: Say you swap 500 USDC on a DEX and approve an unlimited USDC allowance. Months later you hold 6,000 USDC in the same wallet. If that DEX contract were exploited, the attacker could take all 6,000 USDC using your old approval. If you had set the allowance to 500, the contract could not take more than the remaining allowance, which after the swap would be zero.
mistakes: Accepting unlimited approvals by default on apps you use only once.
Never revoking approvals given to old or abandoned projects.
Signing a permit message on an unfamiliar site because it does not look like a transaction.

faq.q: Does revoking an approval cost gas?
faq.a: Yes. Revoking is an on-chain transaction, so it needs a small network fee on that chain.

faq.q: Can a token approval steal my ETH?
faq.a: An ERC-20 approval covers only that token. Native ETH is not moved by approvals, but signing other malicious transactions can still lose it.

token-approval.title: What is a token approval? Allowances explained
token-approval.description: What token approvals and allowances are, why unlimited approvals are risky, and how to review and revoke them.

multisig-wallet.short: A multisig wallet is a crypto wallet that needs signatures from several separate keys, such as 2 of 3, before any transaction can be sent, so no single lost or stolen key can move the funds.
body: A multisig is described as M-of-N: N keys exist and M of them must sign. A 2-of-3 setup can survive one lost key and still blocks a thief who steals one key. On Bitcoin, multisig is built into the script system. On Ethereum and EVM chains, it is usually a smart contract wallet, with Safe as a widely used example.
Multisigs are standard for DAO treasuries, company funds and exchange cold storage. Individuals use them for large savings, often with keys on different hardware wallets stored in different places.

The trade-off is complexity. You must back up every key and, for Bitcoin, the wallet configuration that describes the setup. Each transaction takes more steps, and on EVM chains you rely on the multisig contract being secure.
multisig-wallet.example: Suppose a small team keeps 120,000 USDC in a 2-of-3 Safe. Each of three founders holds one key on a separate hardware wallet. One founder's laptop is compromised and the attacker proposes sending everything to their address. The other two founders see the proposal, refuse to sign, and move the funds to a new Safe with a replacement key. With a single-key wallet, the 120,000 USDC would already be gone.
mistakes: Storing two of the three keys in the same place, which turns 2-of-3 into a single point of failure.
Backing up the keys but not the Bitcoin wallet configuration needed to rebuild the multisig.
Signing a multisig transaction without checking what the other signer proposed.

faq.q: Is a multisig wallet worth it for individuals?
faq.a: For large long-term holdings it can be, because it removes single points of failure. For small amounts the extra complexity is often not worth it.

faq.q: What happens if one multisig key is lost?
faq.a: In an M-of-N setup, you can still sign with the remaining keys as long as you have at least M. Replace the lost key soon by moving funds to a new setup.

multisig-wallet.title: What is a multisig wallet? M-of-N explained
multisig-wallet.description: Learn how a multisig wallet works, why 2-of-3 setups protect funds, and the backup mistakes that defeat multisig.

proof-of-reserves.short: Proof of reserves is a report in which a crypto exchange shows that the assets it holds in wallets it controls are at least equal to the balances it owes its customers.
body: Most proof-of-reserves reports have two parts. First, the exchange shows which on-chain wallets it controls and how much each holds. Second, it shows total customer liabilities, often with a Merkle tree so each user can check that their own balance was included. Some exchanges add zk-proofs to show no negative balances were hidden.
The resulting reserve ratio compares assets with liabilities for each coin. A ratio of 100 percent or more means assets cover customer balances at that moment.

Proof of reserves has limits. It is a snapshot at one time, it may not show debts owed elsewhere by the company, and the quality depends on who checks it. A report reviewed by an independent auditor or verifiable on-chain is stronger than a simple self-published chart.
proof-of-reserves.example: Suppose an exchange reports customer USDT balances of 2.0 billion and USDT held in its disclosed wallets of 2.1 billion. The reserve ratio is 2.1 divided by 2.0, or 105 percent. You then use the exchange's verification tool, enter your record ID, and confirm your 1,250 USDT balance is in the Merkle tree. That tells you your balance was counted, but not whether the company has other loans outside the report.
mistakes: Reading a reserve ratio above 100 percent as proof the exchange cannot fail.
Looking only at the total ratio and ignoring individual coins with lower coverage.
Assuming an old report reflects today's position.

faq.q: Is proof of reserves the same as an audit?
faq.a: No. A full financial audit also reviews liabilities, debts and controls. Proof of reserves focuses on customer balances and the assets that back them.

faq.q: How do I verify my balance in proof of reserves?
faq.a: Most exchanges provide a verification page where you see your record ID and check that your balance is included in the Merkle tree for that snapshot.

proof-of-reserves.title: What is proof of reserves? How exchanges prove it
proof-of-reserves.description: What proof of reserves is, how the reserve ratio and Merkle tree checks work, and what the report cannot show.

defi.short: DeFi, short for decentralized finance, is a set of financial services such as trading, lending and earning yield that run on public blockchains through smart contracts instead of through banks or exchanges.
body: In DeFi, the rules are written into smart contracts that anyone can use from a self-custody wallet. You do not open an account or hand over your coins to a company. Well-known examples include Uniswap for swapping tokens, Aave for lending and borrowing, and Lido for liquid staking.

Because the contracts are public, DeFi apps can be combined like building blocks: a token you receive from one protocol can be deposited in another. This is often called composability. It enables new products quickly, but it also means a failure in one protocol can spread to others.

The main risks are different from those of a centralized exchange: smart contract bugs, manipulated price oracles, malicious token approvals, depegs of stablecoins or staking tokens, and your own mistakes, which nobody can reverse.
defi.example: Suppose you hold 2 ETH. On a lending protocol, you deposit them as collateral, worth 6,000 USDC at an illustrative price of 3,000 USDC per ETH, and borrow 2,000 USDC. You swap 1,000 USDC on a DEX for another token and keep 1,000 USDC in your wallet. Every step happens through contracts you sign from your wallet. If ETH fell to about 1,250 USDC, depending on the protocol's settings, your collateral could be liquidated to repay the loan.
mistakes: Treating a high yield as free money without asking where the yield comes from.
Using a new protocol with a large amount before it has any track record or audit history.
Forgetting that every transaction costs gas and that failed transactions still pay fees.

faq.q: Is DeFi safe?
faq.a: DeFi removes the need to trust an exchange, but adds smart contract, oracle and user-error risk. Safety depends on the protocol's code, history and how carefully you use it.

faq.q: Do I need KYC to use DeFi?
faq.a: Most DeFi protocols do not require identity checks to interact with the contracts, though some front-end websites restrict access by country.

defi.title: What is DeFi? Decentralized finance explained
defi.description: Learn what DeFi is, how smart contracts replace banks and exchanges, and the main risks to understand before you use it.

dex.short: A decentralized exchange (DEX) is a trading platform that runs on smart contracts, letting you swap tokens directly from your own wallet without depositing funds with a company.
body: Most DEXs, such as Uniswap, PancakeSwap and Curve, use automated market makers: you trade against a liquidity pool, and a formula sets the price. Others, especially perp DEXs like Hyperliquid, run an order book on-chain or on a dedicated chain.

Compared with a centralized exchange, you keep custody of your coins, any token can be listed by anyone, and there is usually no account sign-up. In exchange, you pay network gas fees, may face higher slippage on small tokens, and have no support team if you send a wrong transaction or buy a scam token.
Before swapping, check the token contract address, the expected output, the price impact and your slippage setting. A high slippage tolerance can let bots sandwich your trade.
dex.example: Imagine you want to swap 1,000 USDC for ETH on a DEX. The interface quotes 0.330 ETH with a 0.3 percent pool fee and 0.2 percent price impact. You set slippage to 0.5 percent, so the trade fails rather than fill below about 0.328 ETH. The swap confirms and you receive 0.329 ETH plus pay a network fee of a few dollars in ETH, depending on the chain.
mistakes: Buying a token by name instead of verifying its contract address.
Setting a very high slippage tolerance to make a trade go through.
Comparing DEX and exchange prices without counting gas fees and price impact.

faq.q: What is the difference between a DEX and a CEX?
faq.a: A CEX holds your funds and matches trades on its own servers. A DEX lets you trade directly from your wallet through smart contracts.

faq.q: Do DEXs require KYC?
faq.a: Most DEX contracts do not, but some front-ends block certain countries, and the token you buy can still be a scam.

dex.title: What is a DEX? Decentralized exchange explained
dex.description: What a decentralized exchange is, how DEX swaps work, how they differ from centralized exchanges, and what to check before trading.

amm.short: An automated market maker (AMM) is a type of DEX that prices trades with a mathematical formula based on the tokens held in a liquidity pool, instead of matching buyers and sellers in an order book.
body: The best-known formula is the constant product, x times y equals k, used by Uniswap v2. A pool holds two tokens. When you buy one, you add the other, and the formula moves the price so that the product of the two balances stays the same, before fees.
Liquidity providers deposit both tokens and earn the trading fee. Bigger pools mean smaller price moves for the same trade, which is why large trades in shallow pools suffer heavy price impact.

Newer designs adjust the model. Curve uses curves suited to assets that should trade near the same price, such as stablecoins. Uniswap v3 and later let providers concentrate liquidity in a price range, which makes pools deeper near the current price but requires more active management.
amm.example: Suppose a pool holds 100 ETH and 300,000 USDC, so k is 30,000,000 and the price is 3,000 USDC per ETH. You buy ETH with 30,000 USDC, ignoring fees. The pool now has 330,000 USDC, so ETH must fall to 30,000,000 divided by 330,000, about 90.91 ETH. You receive about 9.09 ETH, an average price of roughly 3,300 USDC. That 10 percent gap is the price impact of a large trade in a small pool.
mistakes: Expecting the quoted spot price for a large trade in a small pool.
Thinking AMM liquidity providers only earn fees and never lose relative to holding.
Ignoring which AMM design a pool uses when comparing fees and depth.

faq.q: How does an AMM set prices?
faq.a: By the ratio of tokens in the pool, adjusted through a formula. Arbitrage traders keep the pool price close to prices on other markets.

faq.q: Is Uniswap an AMM?
faq.a: Yes. Uniswap is one of the largest AMM-based decentralized exchanges.

amm.title: What is an AMM? Automated market maker explained
amm.description: How automated market makers price trades with a formula, why pool size drives price impact, and how AMM designs differ.

liquidity-pool.short: A liquidity pool is a smart contract holding two or more tokens that traders swap against on a DEX, funded by liquidity providers who earn a share of the trading fees.
body: When you add liquidity, you usually deposit both tokens of a pair in the current price ratio, for example ETH and USDC. In return you get LP tokens or an NFT position that represents your share of the pool. When you withdraw, you receive your share of whatever is in the pool at that time, plus fees earned.

Your earnings come from trading fees, sometimes topped up by token rewards. Your risks include impermanent loss when prices move, smart contract bugs, and for new tokens, the chance that the token itself collapses or is a rug pull.

Pool depth matters to traders too. The more value in a pool, the smaller the price impact of each trade. That is why total liquidity is one of the first numbers to check before buying a small token on a DEX.
liquidity-pool.example: Say a pool holds 500,000 USDC and 200 ETH, at 2,500 USDC per ETH, for a total of 1,000,000 USDC. You add 5,000 USDC and 2 ETH, which equals 1 percent of the pool. Over a month, traders pay 30,000 USDC in fees to the pool. Your 1 percent share earns about 300 USDC, before any impermanent loss and gas costs.
mistakes: Looking only at the advertised APR and ignoring impermanent loss and token risk.
Providing liquidity for a token whose pool liquidity is controlled by the team.
Losing or transferring the LP tokens that represent your position.

faq.q: How do liquidity pools make money?
faq.a: They collect a fee on every swap, which is shared among liquidity providers in proportion to their share of the pool.

faq.q: Can I lose money in a liquidity pool?
faq.a: Yes. Price moves cause impermanent loss, and a smart contract bug or token collapse can cause larger losses.

liquidity-pool.title: What is a liquidity pool? How LPs earn and lose
liquidity-pool.description: What a liquidity pool is, how liquidity providers earn trading fees, and the risks of impermanent loss and rug pulls.

impermanent-loss.short: Impermanent loss is the shortfall a liquidity provider has compared with simply holding the same tokens, caused by the prices of the pooled tokens moving apart after the deposit.
body: In an AMM pool, arbitrage traders rebalance the pool as prices move. If one token rises, the pool sells some of it for the other. When you withdraw, you hold less of the token that went up and more of the one that went down than if you had just held them.

It is called impermanent because the gap shrinks if prices return to where they were when you deposited. If you withdraw while prices have moved, the loss becomes real. Trading fees and rewards can offset it, but not always.

The bigger the price divergence, the bigger the loss. In a standard 50/50 pool, a 2x price change in one token relative to the other costs about 5.7 percent versus holding. Stablecoin pairs and correlated assets usually have far less impermanent loss, while concentrated liquidity positions can suffer more.
impermanent-loss.example: Suppose you deposit 1 ETH and 2,000 USDC into a 50/50 pool when ETH is 2,000 USDC, for a total value of 4,000 USDC. ETH doubles to 4,000 USDC. Rebalancing leaves you with about 0.707 ETH and 2,828 USDC, worth about 5,657 USDC. Had you just held, you would have 1 ETH plus 2,000 USDC, worth 6,000 USDC. The difference of about 343 USDC, 5.7 percent, is impermanent loss before fees.
mistakes: Assuming impermanent loss only happens when prices fall.
Comparing pool returns with zero instead of with simply holding the two tokens.
Ignoring that concentrated liquidity ranges can magnify the loss.

faq.q: Can trading fees cover impermanent loss?
faq.a: Sometimes. If the pool earns enough fees during your deposit period, they can outweigh the loss, but in volatile markets they often do not.

faq.q: Does impermanent loss happen in stablecoin pools?
faq.a: Very little while both stablecoins stay at their peg. A depeg of one coin can cause real losses.

impermanent-loss.title: What is impermanent loss? Example and formula
impermanent-loss.description: Learn what impermanent loss is, why it happens in AMM pools, and how to calculate it with a worked example.

yield-farming.short: Yield farming is the practice of moving crypto into DeFi protocols, such as liquidity pools or lending markets, to earn trading fees, interest and extra token rewards.
body: A farmer might supply liquidity to a DEX pool, stake the LP tokens in a reward contract, and claim the project's governance token on top of fees. Some strategies stack several protocols or reinvest rewards automatically through vaults.

High advertised returns usually come from token emissions, new tokens printed to attract liquidity. If many farmers sell those rewards, the reward token's price can fall, and the headline APR shrinks with it. Fee income is more durable, but it depends on trading volume.

Risks add up with each layer: smart contract bugs in every protocol used, impermanent loss, token price drops, depegs, and gas costs that can eat small positions. Check where the yield comes from before chasing the number.
yield-farming.example: Imagine you deposit 10,000 USDC worth of liquidity into a pool advertising 40 percent APR, of which 5 percent is fees and 35 percent comes from a reward token. After three months you earn about 125 USDC in fees and reward tokens that were worth 875 USDC at the start. If the reward token falls 60 percent during that time, those rewards are worth about 350 USDC, so your real return is closer to 475 USDC, before gas and impermanent loss.
mistakes: Judging a farm by its headline APR without checking how much comes from inflationary rewards.
Farming with small amounts on a chain where gas costs eat most of the rewards.
Leaving funds in a farm after rewards end or the team abandons it.

faq.q: Is yield farming the same as staking?
faq.a: No. Staking usually means locking tokens to help secure a proof-of-stake network. Yield farming means seeking returns from DeFi apps, often including liquidity provision.

faq.q: Is yield farming still profitable?
faq.a: Returns vary widely with market conditions, reward programs and fees. Sustainable yields are usually far lower than promotional rates.

yield-farming.title: What is yield farming? How DeFi rewards work
yield-farming.description: What yield farming is, where DeFi yields come from, and why headline APRs can shrink once rewards and risks are counted.

staking.short: Staking is locking up coins of a proof-of-stake blockchain to help validate transactions and secure the network, in return for staking rewards paid in that coin.
body: In proof-of-stake networks such as Ethereum, Solana and Cardano, validators put coins at stake as a guarantee of honest behaviour. They earn rewards from new issuance and transaction fees. If a validator misbehaves or goes offline, some networks cut part of its stake, which is called slashing.

You can stake in several ways: run your own validator, delegate to a validator, use a liquid staking protocol that gives you a token like stETH, or use an exchange staking product where the platform runs the validators. Each route has different lock-up periods, fees and custody risk.
Rewards are paid in the staked coin, so your value in dollars still depends on its price. Unstaking can take days or longer depending on the network, which matters if you might need to sell quickly.
staking.example: Suppose you stake 10 SOL through a validator with an illustrative 7 percent annual reward and a 5 percent validator commission. Gross rewards for a year would be 0.7 SOL, the validator keeps 0.035 SOL, and you receive about 0.665 SOL. If SOL's price drops 30 percent during that year, your 10.665 SOL can still be worth less in dollars than the original 10 SOL was.
mistakes: Counting staking rewards in coin terms only and forgetting the coin's price can fall.
Ignoring the unbonding or unstaking period before you need the funds.
Staking through an unknown site that asks you to send coins instead of delegating from your own wallet.

faq.q: Is staking crypto safe?
faq.a: Native staking is generally lower-risk than many DeFi strategies, but you still face price risk, possible slashing and, with exchanges or protocols, platform risk.

faq.q: Can I lose my staked coins?
faq.a: You can lose some through slashing, smart contract failures or a platform failing, and their value can fall with the market.

faq.q: Are staking rewards taxed?
faq.a: In many countries they are, but rules differ on when and how. Check the tax rules where you live.

staking.title: What is staking in crypto? How rewards work
staking.description: Learn what crypto staking is, how proof-of-stake rewards and slashing work, and the different ways to stake.

liquid-staking.short: Liquid staking is a way to stake coins through a protocol that issues a tradable token, such as stETH, representing your staked position, so you earn staking rewards and can still use or sell the token.
body: Normal staking locks your coins. With liquid staking, you deposit ETH or SOL into a protocol such as Lido, Rocket Pool or Jito. It stakes on your behalf and gives you a liquid staking token. Some tokens grow in number each day, others rise in value against the underlying coin.
You can hold the token to earn rewards, trade it on a DEX, or use it as collateral in DeFi. That flexibility is why liquid staking became one of the largest DeFi categories.

The risks: a smart contract bug in the protocol, slashing of its validators, and the token trading below the value of the coin it represents, a depeg. A depeg matters mostly if you need to sell quickly or used the token as collateral for a loan.
liquid-staking.example: Say you deposit 5 ETH into a liquid staking protocol and receive 5 stETH. With an illustrative 3 percent yearly reward, your balance grows to about 5.15 stETH after a year. Halfway through, you need cash and see stETH trading at 0.99 ETH on a DEX. Selling 5.07 stETH at that rate returns about 5.02 ETH, slightly less than waiting for the protocol's withdrawal queue, which can take days.
mistakes: Assuming a liquid staking token is always worth exactly one unit of the underlying coin.
Borrowing heavily against an LST, which can be liquidated if it trades below its peg.
Not knowing whether your token rebases or grows in value, then misreading your balance.

faq.q: What is the difference between staking and liquid staking?
faq.a: Standard staking locks your coins. Liquid staking gives you a token that represents the staked coins and can be traded or used in DeFi.

faq.q: Is stETH the same as ETH?
faq.a: No. stETH is a token issued by Lido that represents staked ETH. It usually trades close to ETH but can trade at a discount.

liquid-staking.title: What is liquid staking? Meaning and risks
liquid-staking.description: How liquid staking works, what tokens like stETH represent, and the depeg and smart contract risks to understand.

restaking.short: Restaking is reusing already staked ETH, or a liquid staking token, to also secure additional services, earning extra rewards in exchange for extra slashing and smart contract risk.
body: EigenLayer popularised restaking on Ethereum. Stakers opt in to let their staked ETH secure other systems, such as data availability layers, oracles or bridges, often called actively validated services. If the operator they delegate to breaks the rules of those services, part of the stake can be slashed.

Liquid restaking protocols, such as those issuing tokens like ezETH, rsETH or weETH, wrap this process: you deposit ETH or an LST and receive a liquid restaking token that you can trade or use in DeFi.

Each layer adds a risk. You carry Ethereum staking risk, the restaking protocol's contract risk, the slashing rules of every service secured, and the risk that the liquid restaking token trades below its underlying value. Extra yield is payment for those risks.
restaking.example: Imagine you hold 4 stETH earning an illustrative 3 percent staking reward. You restake them through a liquid restaking protocol and receive a token that adds an estimated 1.5 percent in extra rewards. On 4 ETH worth of stake, that is about 0.12 ETH a year from staking plus 0.06 ETH from restaking. If an operator is slashed 2 percent for misbehaviour, you could lose about 0.08 ETH, wiping out most of the extra rewards.
mistakes: Treating restaking yield as risk-free because the underlying asset is ETH.
Ignoring that liquid restaking tokens can be harder to sell quickly than ETH or stETH.
Looping restaking tokens with borrowing without understanding liquidation thresholds.

faq.q: What is the difference between staking and restaking?
faq.a: Staking secures the Ethereum network itself. Restaking extends the same stake to secure additional services, adding new rewards and new slashing risks.

faq.q: Is EigenLayer the only restaking protocol?
faq.a: No. EigenLayer is the best known on Ethereum, but other restaking protocols exist on Ethereum and other networks.

restaking.title: What is restaking? EigenLayer and LRTs explained
restaking.description: What restaking is, how liquid restaking tokens work, and the extra slashing and contract risks that come with extra yield.

defi-lending.short: DeFi lending is borrowing and lending crypto through smart contracts, where lenders earn interest from a shared pool and borrowers must lock more collateral than they borrow.
body: On protocols such as Aave, Compound or Morpho, lenders deposit tokens into a pool and earn a variable interest rate that rises when more of the pool is borrowed. Borrowers deposit collateral, such as ETH, and can borrow other assets up to a loan-to-value limit set for that collateral.

Loans are overcollateralized because there is no credit check. If the collateral value falls and your health factor drops below 1, part of your collateral can be sold to liquidators at a discount to repay the debt. Prices come from oracles, so a sharp price move is enough to trigger liquidation.
Risks for lenders include smart contract bugs, bad debt if liquidations fail during crashes, and periods when the pool is fully borrowed and withdrawals must wait.
defi-lending.example: Suppose you deposit 2 ETH at 3,000 USDC each, worth 6,000 USDC, with a liquidation threshold of 80 percent, an illustrative setting. You borrow 3,000 USDC. Your health factor is 6,000 times 0.8 divided by 3,000, which is 1.6. If ETH falls to 1,875 USDC, your collateral is worth 3,750 USDC and the health factor drops to 1.0. Below that, liquidators can repay part of your loan and take ETH plus a bonus.
mistakes: Borrowing close to the maximum and leaving no buffer for price drops.
Not watching the health factor during volatile markets.
Assuming lending interest is fixed when most DeFi rates change every block.

faq.q: Why do DeFi loans need more collateral than the loan?
faq.a: There is no identity or credit check, so the protocol protects lenders by requiring collateral worth more than the loan and liquidating it if its value falls too far.

faq.q: Where does DeFi lending interest come from?
faq.a: From borrowers who pay interest to use the pool's tokens, sometimes topped up by reward tokens.

defi-lending.title: What is DeFi lending? How crypto loans work
defi-lending.description: How DeFi lending protocols work, why loans are overcollateralized, and how the health factor triggers liquidation.

flash-loan.short: A flash loan is an uncollateralized DeFi loan that must be borrowed and repaid, with a fee, within the same blockchain transaction, or the whole transaction is cancelled.
body: Smart contracts can bundle many steps into one transaction. A flash loan uses this: you borrow, use the funds, and repay in a single transaction. If repayment fails, the blockchain reverts everything, so the lender is never at risk of default. Aave popularised flash loans, and other protocols offer similar features.

Legitimate uses include arbitrage between DEXs, refinancing a loan from one protocol to another, and swapping collateral without first closing a position. They require writing or using a smart contract, so they are a developer and bot tool rather than something you request from an app.

Flash loans are also used in attacks. They give attackers temporary access to large capital to manipulate a thinly traded pool or a weak oracle. The weakness is usually in the targeted protocol's design, not in the flash loan itself.
flash-loan.example: Suppose a token trades at 1.00 USDC on DEX A and 1.02 USDC on DEX B. A bot flash-borrows 500,000 USDC, buys about 500,000 tokens on DEX A, sells them on DEX B for about 509,000 USDC after price impact, repays 500,000 USDC plus a 0.05 percent fee of 250 USDC, and keeps roughly 8,750 USDC before gas. If prices moved and the bot could not repay, the transaction would revert.
mistakes: Believing a flash loan lets an ordinary user borrow money for days without collateral.
Blaming flash loans for exploits that were really caused by manipulable oracles.
Paying for a flash loan bot or service advertised on social media, which is a common scam.

faq.q: Can anyone take a flash loan?
faq.a: Anyone who can deploy or call a suitable smart contract can. There is no credit check, but you need technical skill.

faq.q: Are flash loans legal?
faq.a: Flash loans are a standard DeFi feature. Using them to exploit protocols may be treated as illegal depending on the jurisdiction and the circumstances.

flash-loan.title: What is a flash loan? Meaning and uses in DeFi
flash-loan.description: What a flash loan is, how it is borrowed and repaid in one transaction, and why it appears in arbitrage and exploits.

total-value-locked.short: Total value locked (TVL) is the total market value of crypto deposited in a DeFi protocol or blockchain's smart contracts, used as a rough measure of its size and usage.
body: TVL adds up assets in pools, lending markets, staking contracts and vaults, valued at current market prices. Data sites such as DefiLlama track TVL for protocols and for entire chains.

Because it is measured in dollars, TVL rises and falls with token prices even if nobody deposits or withdraws. A protocol's TVL can drop 30 percent in a market sell-off with no change in users. TVL can also be inflated by counting the same assets twice, for example ETH staked for an LST that is then deposited elsewhere.

TVL is useful for comparing size and liquidity, but it does not measure revenue, profit or safety. A high-TVL protocol can still be exploited, and rewards can attract short-lived deposits that leave when incentives end.
total-value-locked.example: Imagine a lending protocol holds 40,000 ETH at 2,500 USDC each and 150 million USDC in stablecoins. Its TVL is 40,000 times 2,500, which is 100 million, plus 150 million, for 250 million dollars. If ETH falls to 2,000 USDC, the ETH part drops to 80 million and TVL becomes 230 million, an 8 percent fall without anyone withdrawing.
mistakes: Reading a TVL drop as users leaving when it is mostly a price fall.
Treating high TVL as proof that a protocol is secure.
Comparing TVL across sites that count staked or borrowed assets differently.

faq.q: Is a higher TVL better?
faq.a: It usually means more liquidity and usage, but it does not guarantee safety, sustainable revenue or good token performance.

faq.q: How is TVL different from market cap?
faq.a: Market cap values a token's supply. TVL values assets deposited in a protocol's contracts. They measure different things.

total-value-locked.title: What is TVL (total value locked) in DeFi?
total-value-locked.description: What total value locked means, how TVL is calculated, why it moves with prices, and its limits as a DeFi metric.

cross-chain-bridge.short: A cross-chain bridge is a protocol that moves tokens or messages between two blockchains, usually by locking or burning assets on one chain and releasing or minting matching assets on the other.
body: Blockchains cannot read each other directly. A bridge connects them. In a lock-and-mint design, you lock tokens in a contract on chain A, and the bridge mints a wrapped version on chain B. Other designs use liquidity pools on both sides, or burn the token on one chain and mint it natively on the other, as Circle's CCTP does for USDC.

Bridges hold large amounts of locked assets, and they rely on validators, multisigs or other mechanisms to confirm what happened on the other chain. That makes them a frequent target: several of the largest crypto hacks were bridge exploits.

Before bridging, check that the bridge is the official or widely used one for that route, that the token you will receive is the version accepted on the destination chain, and what fees and wait times apply. Moving funds through a centralized exchange is sometimes simpler and cheaper.
cross-chain-bridge.example: Suppose you want to move 2,000 USDC from Ethereum to Arbitrum. A bridge quotes a fee of 3 USDC plus Ethereum gas of a few dollars and an arrival time of about 15 minutes. You approve the bridge contract, send the transfer and receive 1,997 USDC on Arbitrum. Alternatively, you could deposit to an exchange on Ethereum and withdraw on Arbitrum if the exchange supports both networks.
mistakes: Using a bridge link from a social media reply instead of the official site.
Receiving a wrapped token version on the destination chain that local apps do not accept.
Bridging a large amount without first sending a small test.

faq.q: Are cross-chain bridges safe?
faq.a: They carry extra risk because they hold large locked balances and depend on their security design. Many users limit the amount they keep in bridged tokens.

faq.q: How long does bridging take?
faq.a: From a minute to several days, depending on the bridge design and the chains. Some official rollup bridges take about a week to withdraw back to Ethereum.

cross-chain-bridge.title: What is a cross-chain bridge? How bridges work
cross-chain-bridge.description: Learn how cross-chain bridges move tokens between blockchains, why they are frequent hack targets, and what to check first.

wrapped-token.short: A wrapped token is a token on one blockchain that represents another asset one-to-one, such as WBTC representing bitcoin on Ethereum, backed by the original asset held by a custodian or smart contract.
body: Bitcoin cannot run Ethereum smart contracts. To use BTC in Ethereum DeFi, a custodian or protocol holds real BTC and issues an ERC-20 token, such as WBTC or cbBTC, for each BTC held. To unwrap, the token is burned and the BTC released.

Some wrapping is simpler. WETH wraps native ETH into an ERC-20 token on Ethereum itself, through a smart contract with no custodian, so apps can treat ETH like other tokens. Bridged tokens on other chains are also a form of wrapped asset.

The value of a wrapped token depends on its backing and the ability to redeem it. If the custodian, bridge or contract fails, the wrapped token can trade below the original asset. Check who holds the reserves and whether they publish proof of them.
wrapped-token.example: Say you hold 0.5 BTC and want to use it as collateral on Ethereum. You exchange it for 0.5 WBTC, which a custodian backs with 0.5 BTC. You deposit the WBTC in a lending protocol and borrow stablecoins. Months later, you repay, withdraw your 0.5 WBTC and convert it back to native BTC. If the wrapped token had lost its backing in the meantime, it could have been worth far less than 0.5 BTC.
mistakes: Assuming a wrapped token carries no risk beyond the price of the original asset.
Sending a wrapped token to an address on the original chain, for example WBTC to a Bitcoin address.
Confusing different wrapped versions of the same asset that are not interchangeable.

faq.q: Is WBTC the same as BTC?
faq.a: WBTC tracks BTC one-to-one but is an Ethereum token backed by BTC held by a custodian. It adds custodian and smart contract risk.

faq.q: Why do I need WETH?
faq.a: Some DeFi apps require tokens in ERC-20 format. WETH converts ETH into that format one-to-one and can be unwrapped at any time.

wrapped-token.title: What is a wrapped token? WBTC and WETH explained
wrapped-token.description: What wrapped tokens like WBTC and WETH are, how wrapping and unwrapping works, and the backing risk to check.

oracle.short: A blockchain oracle is a service that brings outside data, most often asset prices, onto a blockchain so smart contracts can use it for actions like liquidations, settlements and swaps.
body: Smart contracts can only read data already on their own chain. To know the price of ETH in dollars, a lending protocol needs someone to publish that price on-chain. Oracle networks such as Chainlink and Pyth collect prices from many sources and publish them, often with several independent node operators.
Oracles decide when loans get liquidated, how perp DEXs mark positions, and how synthetic assets are priced. If an oracle reports a wrong price, even briefly, contracts act on it.

Many DeFi exploits came from weak oracle design, for example using the spot price of a single thin DEX pool, which an attacker can move with a large trade or a flash loan. Stronger setups use aggregated prices, time-weighted averages and sanity checks.
oracle.example: Suppose a lending protocol reads the price of a small token from one DEX pool holding only 200,000 dollars. An attacker uses a flash loan to buy the token in that pool, pushing its price from 1 to 4 dollars. The protocol now values the attacker's 100,000 tokens of collateral at 400,000 dollars instead of 100,000, and the attacker borrows against that inflated value. An aggregated oracle using many markets would have shown a far smaller move.
mistakes: Assuming a DeFi price is always the same as the price on major exchanges.
Ignoring which oracle a lending or perp protocol uses before depositing.
Thinking oracles are only about prices, when they can also deliver data such as random numbers or event outcomes.

faq.q: What is the oracle problem?
faq.a: Blockchains cannot verify outside data by themselves, so contracts must trust the oracle's data. The challenge is making that data hard to manipulate or fake.

faq.q: Is Chainlink an oracle?
faq.a: Yes. Chainlink is one of the most widely used decentralized oracle networks, providing price feeds and other data to many blockchains.

oracle.title: What is a blockchain oracle? Price feeds in DeFi
oracle.description: What blockchain oracles are, why DeFi relies on price feeds, and how oracle manipulation has caused exploits.

dao.short: A DAO, or decentralized autonomous organization, is a community that makes decisions and manages a shared treasury through token-holder voting and smart contracts instead of a traditional management structure.
body: Members propose changes, such as adjusting protocol fees, funding a grant or upgrading a contract. Holders of the governance token vote, and if a proposal passes, a smart contract or a multisig carries it out. Uniswap, Aave and MakerDAO, now Sky, are examples of protocols governed this way.

In practice, DAOs mix on-chain and off-chain steps. Discussion often happens on forums, early votes run on gasless tools such as Snapshot, and execution may rely on a multisig of trusted signers. How decentralized a DAO really is depends on who holds the tokens and who controls the keys.
Common problems include low voter turnout, voting power concentrated among large holders or the team, and governance attacks where someone acquires enough tokens to pass a harmful proposal.
dao.example: Imagine a DAO with 100 million governance tokens and a quorum of 4 million votes. A proposal to spend 500,000 USDC from the treasury on a security audit receives 5.2 million yes votes and 0.8 million no votes. It meets quorum and passes. After a two-day timelock, the treasury contract sends the 500,000 USDC to the auditor. If only 3 million votes had been cast, it would have failed despite a yes majority.
mistakes: Assuming a project is decentralized just because it calls itself a DAO.
Believing governance tokens give a share of profits; many give only voting rights.
Ignoring how much voting power the team and early investors hold.

faq.q: How do you join a DAO?
faq.a: Usually by holding its governance token. Some DAOs also use NFTs or membership approval.

faq.q: Is a DAO legally a company?
faq.a: It depends on the country. Some jurisdictions offer legal wrappers for DAOs, while others treat members in different ways.

dao.title: What is a DAO? Decentralized organizations explained
dao.description: Learn what a DAO is, how proposals and token voting work, and why decentralization varies from one DAO to another.

governance-token.short: A governance token is a crypto token that gives holders the right to vote on a protocol's decisions, such as fee changes, upgrades and treasury spending, in proportion to the tokens they hold or delegate.
body: Examples include UNI for Uniswap, AAVE for Aave and ARB for Arbitrum. Holders can vote directly or delegate their votes to someone else. Some protocols use vote-escrow models, where locking the token for longer gives more voting power.

Voting rights do not automatically mean a claim on revenue. Some governance tokens have no direct fee share, so their market value rests on expected future decisions, token demand and speculation. Others have staking or fee-sharing features approved by governance.

Governance tokens are often distributed through airdrops, liquidity mining and allocations to teams and investors. Check the tokenomics: how many tokens exist, when locked allocations unlock, and how concentrated voting power is.
governance-token.example: Say a protocol has 1 billion governance tokens, with 40 percent held by the team and investors and 60 percent spread among users. You hold 20,000 tokens, or 0.002 percent of the supply. On a vote where 50 million tokens participate, your 20,000 tokens are 0.04 percent of the votes cast. If the team and investors vote together with even 10 percent of the supply, 100 million tokens, they would outweigh every other participant in that vote.
mistakes: Buying a governance token expecting dividends that the token does not provide.
Ignoring upcoming unlocks of team and investor tokens.
Assuming one token always equals one vote, when delegation and locking can change voting power.

faq.q: Do governance tokens pay rewards?
faq.a: Some do, through staking or fee sharing voted in by governance, but many give only voting rights.

faq.q: Can I vote with tokens held on an exchange?
faq.a: Usually not. Most on-chain votes need the tokens in your own wallet, or delegated from it.

governance-token.title: What is a governance token? Voting rights in crypto
governance-token.description: What governance tokens are, how token voting and delegation work, and why voting rights are not the same as revenue.

apr-vs-apy.short: APR is the simple annual rate of return or interest without compounding, while APY includes the effect of reinvesting earnings, so APY is higher than APR whenever returns compound.
body: APR, annual percentage rate, multiplies a periodic rate by the number of periods in a year. APY, annual percentage yield, assumes each payout is added back and earns returns of its own. The formula is APY equals (1 plus APR divided by n) to the power of n, minus 1, where n is the number of compounding periods.

The difference grows with higher rates and more frequent compounding. At 5 percent APR, daily compounding gives about 5.13 percent APY. At 100 percent APR, daily compounding gives about 171 percent APY, a number that looks much more exciting.

Crypto platforms use both terms, sometimes inconsistently. Check which one is shown, whether compounding is automatic, whether the rate is fixed or variable, and what currency the reward is paid in. A variable rate shown as APY assumes it stays the same all year, which is rare.
apr-vs-apy.example: Suppose a product pays 12 percent APR on 1,000 USDT with daily payouts. Without reinvesting, you earn 120 USDT in a year. If each day's interest is added to your balance, APY is (1 plus 0.12 divided by 365) to the power of 365, minus 1, about 12.75 percent, so you end with about 1,127.47 USDT. The extra 7.47 USDT comes only from compounding.
mistakes: Comparing one product's APY with another's APR as if they were the same measure.
Assuming a high variable APY will hold for a full year.
Forgetting that rewards paid in a different token add price risk to the stated rate.

faq.q: Is APY better than APR?
faq.a: Neither is better; they measure different things. For the same underlying rate, APY is higher because it includes compounding.

faq.q: How do I convert APR to APY?
faq.a: Use APY equals (1 plus APR divided by n) to the power of n, minus 1, where n is how many times per year earnings compound.

apr-vs-apy.title: APR vs APY in crypto: what is the difference?
apr-vs-apy.description: Learn the difference between APR and APY, how compounding changes your yield, and how to compare crypto earn rates fairly.

mev.short: MEV, or maximal extractable value, is the profit that block producers and specialised bots can make by choosing, inserting or reordering transactions inside a block, often at the expense of ordinary users.
body: Pending transactions wait in a public mempool before they are included in a block. Bots, called searchers, watch it and pay to have their own transactions placed before or after yours. Block builders and validators pick the most profitable order.

Some MEV is neutral or helpful, such as arbitrage that keeps DEX prices in line and liquidations that keep lending protocols solvent. The harmful kind for users is the sandwich attack: a bot buys just before your swap, lets your trade push the price up, then sells right after.

You can reduce exposure by setting a tight slippage tolerance, splitting large swaps, using DEX aggregators or wallets that offer MEV protection, and sending transactions through private RPC endpoints that do not broadcast to the public mempool.
mev.example: Suppose you swap 10,000 USDC for a token on a DEX with a 3 percent slippage tolerance. A bot sees the pending trade and buys first, pushing the price up 2 percent. Your swap fills at that worse price, so you receive about 2 percent fewer tokens, roughly 200 USDC worth. The bot then sells into the higher price and keeps the difference minus gas. With a 0.5 percent slippage limit, the attack would not have been worth doing, because the bot could not push the price that far without your swap failing.
mistakes: Setting a high slippage tolerance on large swaps of thinly traded tokens.
Assuming MEV only exists on Ethereum; it appears on many chains with public transaction ordering.
Paying for MEV bot software sold on social media, a common scam.

faq.q: What is a sandwich attack?
faq.a: A bot places a buy before your swap and a sell after it, profiting from the price move your trade causes. You get a worse price.

faq.q: Does MEV affect centralized exchange trades?
faq.a: Not in the same way. Trades on a centralized exchange are matched off-chain, so public mempool MEV does not apply, though deposits and withdrawals still go on-chain.

mev.title: What is MEV in crypto? Sandwich attacks explained
mev.description: Learn what MEV is, how searchers reorder transactions, and practical ways to protect your DEX swaps from sandwich attacks.

perp-dex.short: A perp DEX is a decentralized exchange for perpetual futures, letting you trade with leverage from your own wallet while margin, positions and settlement are handled on-chain or on a dedicated chain.
body: Perp DEXs use the same building blocks as perpetual futures on centralized exchanges: margin, leverage, mark price, funding rate and liquidation. Hyperliquid runs an on-chain order book on its own chain. GMX and similar platforms let traders trade against a liquidity pool priced by oracles. dYdX runs an order book on its own chain.

The main appeal is self-custody: you deposit margin from your wallet without opening an exchange account, and positions are visible on-chain. The trade-offs include smart contract or chain risk, sometimes thinner liquidity for smaller markets, oracle dependence, and the need to manage gas and bridging.
Funding intervals, fee models, maximum leverage and liquidation rules differ from platform to platform and from centralized exchanges. Read the contract specifications of the market you trade.
perp-dex.example: Suppose you deposit 1,000 USDC to a perp DEX and open a 5x long on ETH at 2,500, a position worth 5,000 USDC. If ETH rises 4 percent to 2,600, the position gains about 200 USDC, a 20 percent return on margin, before fees and funding. If ETH falls 4 percent, you lose about 200 USDC. A fall of roughly 15 to 19 percent, depending on the maintenance margin, could liquidate the position.
mistakes: Assuming funding intervals and fees are the same as on your usual centralized exchange.
Using maximum leverage on a small market with thin liquidity.
Forgetting that bridging margin to a perp DEX's chain adds its own steps and risks.

faq.q: Is Hyperliquid a DEX?
faq.a: Hyperliquid is an on-chain perpetual exchange that runs on its own blockchain, so trades and positions are recorded on-chain and users trade from self-custody wallets.

faq.q: Do perp DEXs require KYC?
faq.a: Most do not require identity checks to use the contracts, though some block access from certain countries through their front-end.

perp-dex.title: What is a perp DEX? On-chain perpetuals explained
perp-dex.description: What a perp DEX is, how on-chain perpetual futures work, and how they differ from perpetuals on centralized exchanges.

nft.short: An NFT, or non-fungible token, is a unique token on a blockchain that records ownership of a specific item, such as a digital artwork, collectible, game item or membership pass.
body: Fungible tokens, like USDT or ETH, are interchangeable: one unit equals another. Each NFT has its own token ID, so one cannot simply replace another. On Ethereum, NFTs commonly use the ERC-721 or ERC-1155 standards. Solana, Bitcoin through Ordinals, and other chains have their own formats.

The token usually points to metadata and an image stored elsewhere, on a server, IPFS or Arweave. Owning the NFT proves you hold that token, but it does not automatically give you copyright or commercial rights to the artwork unless the project's licence says so.

NFT prices depend on demand for a collection, and liquidity can be thin. Many collections sell for far less than their mint price later. Common scams include fake mint sites, impersonated collections and signature requests that let attackers list or transfer your NFTs.
nft.example: Imagine a collection of 10,000 NFTs minted at 0.05 ETH each, raising 500 ETH. Six months later, the cheapest listing, called the floor price, is 0.02 ETH. You own one and list it slightly above the floor at 0.025 ETH. After a 2.5 percent marketplace fee and a creator royalty of 5 percent, you would receive about 0.0231 ETH, less than half of the original mint price.
mistakes: Assuming owning an NFT gives you copyright over the image.
Signing a marketplace or listing signature on an unfamiliar site.
Valuing a collection by its highest recent sale instead of its floor price and volume.

faq.q: What does owning an NFT give you?
