faq.a: Proof that your address holds a specific token, plus any rights or access the project grants. Intellectual property rights depend on the project's licence.

faq.q: Can an NFT be copied?
faq.a: The image can be copied, but the token ID on the blockchain cannot. Copies of the image are not the same token.

nft.title: What is an NFT? Non-fungible tokens explained
nft.description: Learn what an NFT is, what owning one really means, how floor prices work, and the common NFT scams to avoid.

stablecoin.short: A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency designed to keep a steady value, usually 1 US dollar, by being backed by reserves such as cash and treasury bills, by crypto collateral, or by other mechanisms.
body: Stablecoins let traders hold dollar value on-chain and move it quickly between exchanges and wallets. Most trading pairs on crypto exchanges are quoted in stablecoins such as USDT and USDC.

There are several types. Fiat-backed stablecoins, like USDT from Tether and USDC from Circle, hold reserves and let approved customers redeem them. Crypto-backed stablecoins, like DAI or USDS, are overcollateralized by crypto in smart contracts. Synthetic dollars, like Ethena's USDe, use hedged positions. Algorithmic designs without solid collateral have failed in the past, most famously TerraUSD in 2022.

Stablecoins are stable, not risk-free. Risks include reserve quality, the issuer freezing addresses, regulatory changes and depegs, when the price drifts away from 1 dollar. Rules also differ by region; in the EU, MiCA stablecoin rules have applied since 30 June 2024.
stablecoin.example: Suppose you sell 0.1 BTC at 60,000 USDT on an exchange and receive 6,000 USDT. A week later BTC falls to 54,000. Your 6,000 USDT is still worth about 6,000 dollars, while 0.1 BTC would now be worth 5,400. If the stablecoin itself dipped to 0.97 dollars during a depeg, your 6,000 USDT would be worth about 5,820 dollars until it recovered.
mistakes: Treating all stablecoins as equally safe regardless of how they are backed.
Sending a stablecoin over a network that the receiving platform does not support.
Holding a little-known stablecoin because it offers a much higher yield than the main ones.

faq.q: Are stablecoins the same as dollars?
faq.a: No. They are tokens designed to track the dollar. Their value depends on the issuer's reserves, redemption and the market.

faq.q: What is the most used stablecoin?
faq.a: USDT, issued by Tether, has long been the largest stablecoin by market capitalization, with USDC from Circle second.

faq.q: Can a stablecoin lose its peg?
faq.a: Yes. Even major stablecoins have traded below 1 dollar briefly during stress, and some smaller ones never recovered.

stablecoin.title: What is a stablecoin? Types and risks explained
stablecoin.description: What a stablecoin is, how fiat-backed, crypto-backed and synthetic stablecoins differ, and the risks behind a stable price.

usdt.short: USDT, also called Tether, is the largest US dollar stablecoin, issued by Tether, designed to stay at 1 dollar and backed by reserves the company reports in regular attestations.
body: USDT is the most common quote currency on crypto exchanges and is widely used for P2P trading and cross-border transfers. It is issued on many blockchains, including Tron (TRC-20), Ethereum (ERC-20), BNB Smart Chain, Solana, TON and others. Each network has its own address format and fees, and the receiving side must support the network you send on.

Tether says USDT is backed by reserves mostly in US treasury bills and cash equivalents, along with other assets, and publishes periodic attestation reports. Over the years, critics have questioned the level of transparency, and reserve composition has changed over time.

Tether can freeze USDT at specific addresses, often at the request of law enforcement. Availability also depends on regulation: some EU platforms restricted USDT for EU users because it is not authorised under MiCA.
usdt.example: Suppose you send 1,500 USDT from an exchange to a friend. On TRC-20 the exchange shows an illustrative fee of 1 USDT and on ERC-20 a fee of 5 USDT. Your friend's wallet supports both, so you choose TRC-20 and paste their address starting with T. They receive 1,499 USDT within a few minutes. Choosing ERC-20 would have cost 4 USDT more for the same transfer.
mistakes: Sending TRC-20 USDT to an exchange that only accepts ERC-20 deposits for that address.
Assuming one USDT can always be redeemed for one dollar by anyone; direct redemption is for verified customers of Tether.
Ignoring that the cheapest network on one exchange may be expensive or slow on another.

faq.q: Is USDT backed by real dollars?
faq.a: Tether reports reserves mainly in US treasury bills, cash equivalents and other assets, rather than only cash in bank accounts. It publishes attestations, not full audits.

faq.q: Which USDT network should I use?
faq.a: The one both sender and receiver support, ideally with low fees. TRC-20 and several other chains are often cheaper than ERC-20.

faq.q: What is the difference between USDT and USDC?
faq.a: Both track the dollar. USDT is issued by Tether and USDC by Circle, with different reserve reporting, regulation and availability across regions.

usdt.title: What is USDT (Tether)? How it works and its risks
usdt.description: Learn what USDT is, how Tether backs it, which networks it runs on, and what to check before sending it.

usdc.short: USDC is a US dollar stablecoin issued by Circle, designed to stay at 1 dollar and backed by cash and short-term US government securities, with monthly reserve attestations.
body: USDC runs on many blockchains, including Ethereum, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon and others. Circle's Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP) lets USDC move between supported chains by burning it on one chain and minting it on another, instead of creating wrapped copies.

Circle publishes monthly attestations of its reserves, which are held largely in cash and a government money market fund. Like USDT, USDC can be frozen at specific addresses. In the EU, Circle operates under MiCA authorisation, which makes USDC widely available on EU-regulated platforms.

USDC is not immune to depegs. In March 2023, it briefly traded well below 1 dollar after part of its reserves was held at Silicon Valley Bank, which failed. It returned to its peg once the deposits were secured.
usdc.example: Suppose you want to move 3,000 USDC from Ethereum to Base. Through a bridge that uses CCTP, the 3,000 USDC is burned on Ethereum and 3,000 native USDC is minted on Base, minus network fees. If you used a bridge that issues a wrapped version, you might receive a token that some Base apps treat as a different asset. During the 2023 depeg, if USDC briefly traded at 0.90 dollars, those 3,000 USDC would have been priced at about 2,700 dollars on the market.
mistakes: Assuming bridged USDC and native USDC on the same chain are always interchangeable.
Believing USDC cannot depeg because it is regulated.
Sending USDC on a network the receiving exchange does not list for USDC deposits.

faq.q: Is USDC safer than USDT?
faq.a: They have different risk profiles. USDC publishes monthly attestations and is authorised under MiCA, while USDT has larger liquidity on many exchanges. Both carry issuer and freeze risk.

faq.q: Who issues USDC?
faq.a: Circle issues USDC and manages its reserves.

usdc.title: What is USDC? Circle's dollar stablecoin explained
usdc.description: What USDC is, how Circle backs it, how native USDC moves across chains, and why even USDC briefly lost its peg.

depeg.short: A depeg is when a stablecoin or pegged token trades meaningfully away from the value it is designed to track, such as a dollar stablecoin falling below 1 USD.
body: Stablecoins like USDT and USDC aim to stay at 1 US dollar. Small moves such as 0.999 or 1.001 are normal market noise. A depeg means a larger or longer gap, usually because holders doubt the backing, redemptions are paused, or liquidity on trading venues dries up.

Causes differ by design. A fiat-backed coin can wobble if part of its reserves is stuck at a troubled bank. A crypto-backed coin can slip if its collateral crashes faster than liquidations can keep up. An algorithmic coin can collapse entirely when confidence breaks, because nothing hard backs it. Pegged tokens such as liquid staking tokens can also trade at a discount when many holders rush to exit at once.

For traders, a depeg matters in two ways: the stablecoin you count as cash may suddenly be worth less, and any position or loan priced in that coin can be repriced. Exchanges may also pause trading pairs, change margin rules or adjust collateral value during a depeg, and each one handles this differently.
depeg.example: Suppose you hold 10,000 units of a dollar stablecoin and news breaks that part of its reserves is frozen. The market price drops to 0.92 USD. On paper your balance is now worth 9,200 USD, a loss of 800 USD. If the issuer later restores full redemptions and the price returns to 1.00, the loss disappears. If it settles at 0.95 instead, the 500 USD gap becomes permanent for anyone who sold or still holds.
mistakes: Treating every stablecoin as equally safe without checking what backs it and who can redeem it.
Panic selling into a thin market during a brief depeg and locking in a loss that would have recovered.
Buying a depegged coin as a sure bargain without understanding whether the backing can actually cover redemptions.

faq.q: Can USDT or USDC depeg?
faq.a: Yes, any stablecoin can trade below its target. USDC briefly fell well below 1 USD in March 2023 when part of its reserves sat at a failed US bank, then recovered after the funds were confirmed safe.

faq.q: Does a depeg always mean the stablecoin is dead?
faq.a: No. Many depegs are short and recover once redemptions work again. A permanent depeg usually means the backing is insufficient or the design has failed.

depeg.title: What is a depeg? Stablecoin depeg meaning
depeg.description: Learn what a stablecoin depeg is, why stablecoins lose their dollar peg, and how a depeg affects your balance and open positions.

crypto-backed-stablecoin.short: A crypto-backed stablecoin is a stablecoin issued against crypto collateral locked in smart contracts, usually worth more than the coins created, so the token can stay near 1 USD.
body: Instead of keeping dollars in a bank, a crypto-backed stablecoin is minted by users who deposit assets like ETH into a smart contract. DAI, originally created by MakerDAO (now Sky), is the best-known example. Because crypto prices swing, the system demands overcollateralization: you must lock more value than you borrow.

Each vault has a minimum collateral ratio. If the collateral value falls too close to that line, the vault is liquidated: the collateral is sold or auctioned to repay the stablecoin debt, and the owner usually pays a penalty. This mechanism is what keeps the coin backed.

The upside is transparency: anyone can check collateral on-chain. The risks are sharp market crashes, oracle failures that feed wrong prices, and smart contract bugs. Some designs also hold other stablecoins or tokenized real-world assets as part of their backing, which brings in off-chain risk.
crypto-backed-stablecoin.example: Suppose ETH trades at 3,000 USD and you deposit 2 ETH, worth 6,000 USD, into a vault with a 150% minimum collateral ratio. You mint 3,000 stablecoins, giving you a ratio of 200%. If ETH drops to 2,250 USD, your collateral is worth 4,500 USD and your ratio is exactly 150%, so the vault can be liquidated. To stay safe, you could repay part of the 3,000 debt or add more ETH before the price reaches that level.
mistakes: Minting the maximum amount allowed so that a small price drop triggers liquidation.
Assuming crypto-backed means fully decentralized, without checking whether part of the reserves are centralized stablecoins or real-world assets.
Forgetting that stability fees or borrow rates accrue on the debt over time.

faq.q: Is DAI a crypto-backed stablecoin?
faq.a: Yes, DAI is minted against collateral locked in smart contracts. Over time its backing has expanded beyond ETH to include other stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets.

faq.q: Why do crypto-backed stablecoins need overcollateralization?
faq.a: Crypto prices can fall quickly. Locking more value than the stablecoins issued gives the system a buffer to liquidate collateral before the debt becomes undercollateralized.

crypto-backed-stablecoin.title: What is a crypto-backed stablecoin? How DAI-style coins work
crypto-backed-stablecoin.description: How crypto-backed stablecoins work: overcollateralized vaults, collateral ratios, liquidation, and the main risks to watch.

algorithmic-stablecoin.short: An algorithmic stablecoin is a stablecoin that tries to hold its peg mainly through code-driven supply changes and incentives rather than full reserves of cash or collateral.
body: Most stablecoins are backed by dollars, short-term bonds or crypto collateral. An algorithmic stablecoin relies instead on rules: when the price is above 1 USD, the protocol expands supply; when it is below, it tries to shrink supply, often by letting users burn the stablecoin in exchange for a second, volatile token.

This works while people trust the system and the companion token keeps its value. In a panic, the loop can reverse. Holders redeem the stablecoin for the companion token, flood the market with it, its price falls, and each redemption needs even more new tokens. This is often called a death spiral.

TerraUSD (UST) is the textbook case: in May 2022 it lost its peg and its companion token LUNA collapsed toward zero within days. Since then, many projects call themselves hybrid or partially collateralized, so read how much hard backing actually exists before you treat a coin as cash.
algorithmic-stablecoin.example: Imagine an algorithmic stablecoin trades at 0.97 USD. The protocol lets you burn 1 stablecoin for 1 USD worth of its governance token, so arbitrageurs buy at 0.97, redeem, and earn about 3% if they can sell the governance token at full value. But if 50 million stablecoins are redeemed while the governance token's market cap is only 200 million USD, the new supply equals a quarter of its value, its price drops, and the next redemptions mint even more tokens.
mistakes: Treating a high advertised yield on an algorithmic stablecoin as low risk because the coin is called stable.
Ignoring the size and liquidity of the companion token that is supposed to absorb redemptions.
Assuming a coin labelled hybrid has full backing without checking the actual reserve ratio.

faq.q: Are algorithmic stablecoins safe?
faq.a: They carry more risk than fully backed stablecoins because the peg depends on market confidence and incentives. The UST collapse in 2022 showed how quickly a design can fail under stress.

faq.q: What is the difference between algorithmic and crypto-backed stablecoins?
faq.a: A crypto-backed stablecoin holds collateral worth more than its supply. An algorithmic stablecoin relies mainly on supply rules and arbitrage incentives, with little or no hard backing.

algorithmic-stablecoin.title: What is an algorithmic stablecoin? Meaning and risks
algorithmic-stablecoin.description: What an algorithmic stablecoin is, how supply rules try to hold the peg, and why designs like UST collapsed in a death spiral.

synthetic-dollar.short: A synthetic dollar is a dollar-pegged token backed by a crypto asset plus an equal short futures position, so price moves cancel out and the combined value stays near 1 USD.
body: A synthetic dollar does not hold bank deposits. Instead, the protocol holds an asset such as ETH or BTC and opens a short perpetual futures position of the same size. If ETH rises, the spot holding gains and the short loses about the same amount; if ETH falls, the opposite happens. This is called a delta-neutral hedge. Ethena's USDe is the best-known example.

The yield usually comes from two sources: staking rewards on the collateral, if any, and funding payments. When funding rates are positive, short positions receive payments from longs, which the protocol can pass on to holders who stake the token.

The risks are different from a fiat-backed stablecoin. Funding can turn negative for long periods, so the hedge costs money. The short positions sit on centralized exchanges, which adds exchange and custody risk. In extreme markets, liquidity for unwinding hedges can be thin, which can push the token below its peg.
synthetic-dollar.example: Suppose a protocol receives 1,000,000 USD and buys ETH at 2,500 USD, getting 400 ETH. It then shorts 400 ETH in perpetual futures. If ETH falls to 2,000 USD, the spot ETH loses 200,000 USD but the short gains about 200,000 USD, so backing stays near 1,000,000 USD. If funding pays shorts 0.01% every 8 hours on a 1,000,000 USD position, that is about 100 USD per payment, or roughly 300 USD per day before costs.
mistakes: Thinking the yield is fixed when it depends heavily on funding rates that can drop or turn negative.
Treating a synthetic dollar as identical to a bank-reserve stablecoin and ignoring exchange custody risk.
Overlooking cooldown or unstaking periods before the staked version can be redeemed.

faq.q: Is USDe a stablecoin?
faq.a: USDe is usually described as a synthetic dollar. It targets 1 USD using crypto collateral hedged with short futures, not cash reserves in a bank.

faq.q: What happens to a synthetic dollar when funding rates go negative?
faq.a: Short positions then pay longs, so the hedge costs money. Protocols typically use a reserve fund to cover such periods, and yields for holders fall.

synthetic-dollar.title: What is a synthetic dollar? Delta-neutral stablecoins explained
synthetic-dollar.description: How a synthetic dollar like USDe holds 1 USD with crypto plus short futures, where its yield comes from and what can go wrong.

cbdc.short: A CBDC (central bank digital currency) is a digital form of a country's official money issued and backed directly by its central bank, not by a private company.
body: Cash is a direct claim on the central bank, while the money in your bank account is a claim on a commercial bank. A CBDC would give people or institutions a digital claim directly on the central bank. China's e-CNY pilot and the Bahamas' Sand Dollar are well-known examples, and the European Central Bank has been preparing a digital euro.

There are two main types. Retail CBDCs are meant for everyday payments by the public. Wholesale CBDCs are for settlement between banks and financial institutions. A CBDC may or may not run on a blockchain; many designs use a centralized ledger controlled by the central bank.

A CBDC is not a cryptocurrency like bitcoin, and it is not a stablecoin. Stablecoins such as USDT or USDC are issued by private companies and backed by their reserves. A CBDC is legal money issued by the state, which also raises debates about privacy, spending limits and the role of commercial banks. Designs and timelines differ widely by country.
cbdc.example: Imagine a country launches a retail CBDC with a holding limit of 3,000 units per person. You receive a salary of 4,000 units into your bank account and move 1,000 into your CBDC wallet to pay a shop. The shop receives the payment instantly in central bank money. If you tried to move another 2,500, only 2,000 would fit under the limit, and the rest would stay in your bank account.
mistakes: Confusing a CBDC with a private stablecoin that only tracks the same currency.
Assuming every CBDC runs on a public blockchain that anyone can inspect.
Believing a CBDC can be traded on crypto exchanges like other tokens.

faq.q: Is a CBDC a cryptocurrency?
faq.a: No. A CBDC is official government money in digital form. It is centrally issued and controlled, unlike decentralized cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CBDC and a stablecoin?
faq.a: A CBDC is issued by a central bank and is a direct liability of that bank. A stablecoin is issued by a private company and is only as reliable as its reserves and redemption process.

cbdc.title: What is a CBDC? Central bank digital currency explained
cbdc.description: What a CBDC is, how retail and wholesale CBDCs work, and how a central bank digital currency differs from crypto and stablecoins.

on-chain-analysis.short: On-chain analysis is the study of public blockchain data, such as transactions, wallet balances and exchange flows, to understand how a network is used and how holders behave.
body: Every transaction on a public blockchain like Bitcoin or Ethereum is recorded and visible. On-chain analysts group this raw data into metrics: active addresses, transaction counts, exchange inflows and outflows, whale holdings, coin age, fees and more. Unlike price charts, these numbers show what holders actually do with their coins.

Traders use on-chain data as context. Large deposits to exchanges can hint at selling pressure, while coins leaving exchanges for self-custody may suggest long-term holding. Long-term investors look at network usage and fee revenue to judge whether a chain is growing.

The limits are important. Addresses are pseudonymous, so labels such as exchange wallet or whale come from analytics providers and can be wrong. One person can control many addresses, and one exchange address can hold funds for millions of users. Off-chain activity, such as trading inside an exchange, does not appear at all. On-chain signals work best combined with price, derivatives and news data, not as standalone buy or sell triggers.
on-chain-analysis.example: Suppose an analytics dashboard shows that 25,000 BTC moved onto exchanges in one day, compared with a 30-day average of 10,000 BTC. That is 2.5 times the usual inflow. You check further and find that 15,000 BTC came from a single labelled address belonging to an exchange moving funds between its own wallets. The real unusual inflow is closer to 10,000 BTC, roughly normal, so the alarming headline number tells you little on its own.
mistakes: Treating one on-chain metric as a precise trading signal without checking context.
Trusting address labels blindly when internal exchange transfers can distort flow data.
Comparing metrics across chains without adjusting for different fee levels and address usage patterns.

faq.q: Does on-chain analysis predict price?
faq.a: It does not predict price on its own. It shows how coins move and how networks are used, which can add context to price and sentiment analysis.

faq.q: What are common on-chain metrics?
faq.a: Popular metrics include active addresses, exchange netflow, whale balances, transaction fees, hash rate for proof-of-work chains, and stablecoin supply on exchanges.

on-chain-analysis.title: What is on-chain analysis? Meaning and key metrics
on-chain-analysis.description: Learn what on-chain analysis is, which blockchain metrics traders watch, and the limits of reading wallet and exchange flow data.

block-explorer.short: A block explorer is a website or app that lets you search a blockchain's public records, including transactions, addresses, blocks and token transfers.
body: Each blockchain has explorers that read its data and present it in a searchable form. Etherscan is widely used for Ethereum, mempool.space and others for Bitcoin, Solscan for Solana and Tronscan for TRON. You paste a transaction hash, wallet address or block number, and the explorer shows what happened.

For everyday users, the most useful job is checking a transfer. A transaction page shows the status (pending, confirmed or failed), the sending and receiving addresses, the amount, the fee paid, the block it was included in and the number of confirmations. If an exchange says it has sent your withdrawal, the transaction hash lets you verify it yourself.

Explorers only show data for their own chain. If you sent USDT on TRON, an Ethereum explorer will not find it. Many explorers also show token contracts, holder lists and labels for known addresses; treat labels as helpful hints, not guarantees, and make sure you are using the genuine explorer site, since lookalike sites exist.
block-explorer.example: Suppose you withdraw 500 USDT from an exchange to your wallet on the TRON network and it has not arrived after 20 minutes. You copy the transaction hash from your withdrawal history and paste it into a TRON explorer. The page shows status confirmed, 500 USDT sent to an address ending in 9kQ3, with 40 confirmations. Your wallet address ends in 9kQ3, so the funds have arrived on-chain and your wallet app probably just needs to refresh or add the token.
mistakes: Searching a transaction on the wrong chain's explorer and concluding it does not exist.
Relying on a screenshot from someone else instead of checking the transaction hash yourself.
Using a lookalike explorer site from a search ad or a message instead of a known one.

faq.q: How do I check if my crypto transfer went through?
faq.a: Copy the transaction hash from your wallet or exchange, open an explorer for that specific chain, and search it. The page shows whether it is pending, confirmed or failed.

faq.q: Is it safe to search my address on a block explorer?
faq.a: Searching does not give anyone access to your funds; blockchain data is already public. Never enter your seed phrase or private key on an explorer or any site that asks for it.

block-explorer.title: What is a block explorer? How to check a transaction
block-explorer.description: What a block explorer is and how to use one to check a crypto transfer, transaction hash, confirmations, fees and wallet balances.

mempool.short: The mempool is the waiting area where valid but unconfirmed transactions sit on network nodes until a miner or validator includes them in a block.
body: When you send a transaction, it is broadcast to nodes, which check it and store it in their mempool. Each node keeps its own version, so there is no single global mempool, but they are usually similar. Miners or validators then pick transactions from the pool to build the next block.

Block space is limited, so transactions usually compete on fees. On Bitcoin, miners tend to prioritize transactions with a higher fee per virtual byte. On Ethereum, users set a priority tip on top of the base fee. When the mempool is crowded, low-fee transactions can wait for hours, and some may eventually drop out of nodes' pools.

The mempool is also where MEV happens on chains with a public mempool: bots watch pending trades and try to front-run or sandwich them. Some wallets offer private transaction routes to avoid this. If your transaction is stuck, options include waiting, using replace-by-fee or a speed-up feature to pay more, or cancelling with a replacement transaction where your wallet supports it.
mempool.example: Suppose the Bitcoin mempool is busy and transactions paying 20 sat/vB are being confirmed, while yours paid 5 sat/vB. Your transaction is 140 vB, so you paid 700 satoshis. To bump it using replace-by-fee to 22 sat/vB, the new fee would be 140 x 22 = 3,080 satoshis, an extra 2,380 satoshis, and it would likely confirm within the next few blocks if demand stays the same.
mistakes: Sending a transaction with the lowest possible fee during congestion and expecting it to confirm quickly.
Resending the same payment again while the first one is still pending, risking paying twice.
Placing large DEX swaps through the public mempool with wide slippage, which invites sandwich attacks.

faq.q: Why is my transaction stuck in the mempool?
faq.a: Usually the fee is too low compared with other pending transactions. You can wait, or speed it up with a higher fee if your wallet supports replace-by-fee or a similar function.

faq.q: Can a transaction disappear from the mempool?
faq.a: Yes. Nodes can drop very low-fee transactions after a period or when the pool is full. The funds stay in your wallet if the transaction was never confirmed.

mempool.title: What is the mempool? Pending crypto transactions explained
mempool.description: What the mempool is, why crypto transactions get stuck pending, how fees decide priority and how to speed up a transaction.

hash-rate.short: Hash rate is the total computing power that miners use to secure a proof-of-work blockchain, measured in hashes per second.
body: In proof-of-work networks like Bitcoin, miners repeatedly run a hashing function to find a valid block. Each attempt is one hash. The network hash rate estimates how many attempts all miners make per second, usually shown in exahashes per second (EH/s), where one exahash is a quintillion hashes.

A higher hash rate makes the network harder to attack, because someone would need to control a large share of the total power to rewrite recent blocks. Bitcoin adjusts its mining difficulty roughly every 2,016 blocks so that blocks keep arriving about every 10 minutes no matter how much hash rate joins or leaves.

Hash rate is an estimate derived from how fast blocks are found, so daily readings are noisy; analysts often use 7-day or 30-day averages. Changes reflect miner economics: new machines, energy prices, regulation and events such as halvings, which cut miner rewards and can push less efficient miners offline. Hash rate is a security and health metric, not a direct price signal.
hash-rate.example: Suppose the Bitcoin network runs at 600 EH/s and a mining company operates machines totalling 12 EH/s. Its share is 12 / 600 = 2% of the network. With about 144 blocks per day and a reward of 3.125 BTC per block, total daily issuance is 450 BTC. A 2% share would earn about 9 BTC per day on average from block subsidies, before fees and costs, though actual results vary with luck.
mistakes: Treating a single day's hash rate spike or drop as a real trend when estimates are noisy.
Assuming a rising hash rate means the price must rise.
Confusing hash rate with difficulty, which is adjusted periodically to respond to hash rate.

faq.q: What does a high hash rate mean for Bitcoin?
faq.a: It means a lot of mining power is securing the network, making attacks more expensive. It also means more competition among miners for the same block rewards.

faq.q: Do proof-of-stake coins have a hash rate?
faq.a: No. Proof-of-stake chains such as Ethereum after September 2022 secure the network with staked coins and validators, not mining power.

hash-rate.title: What is hash rate? Bitcoin mining power explained
hash-rate.description: What hash rate means, how it is measured in EH/s, why it matters for Bitcoin security and how it links to mining difficulty.

exchange-netflow.short: Exchange inflows and outflows measure how much of a coin moves onto and off centralized exchanges, and netflow is inflows minus outflows over a period.
body: Analytics firms label wallets that belong to exchanges and track deposits and withdrawals. Inflow is the amount sent to exchange wallets, outflow is the amount sent out, and netflow is the difference. A positive netflow means more coins arrived than left; a negative one means more left than arrived.

The usual reading is that coins sent to an exchange may be sold soon, while coins withdrawn to self-custody are more likely to be held. Stablecoin inflows are often read the other way: fresh USDT or USDC on exchanges can mean buying power waiting to be used.

These are tendencies, not rules. Deposits can be used as margin for futures, moved for arbitrage, or simply shuffled between an exchange's own wallets. Labels can be incomplete, especially for newer exchanges. A single large flow from one entity can dominate the data. It works best when you look at multi-day trends and compare them with price, funding rates and open interest.
exchange-netflow.example: Suppose over one week, 42,000 ETH flowed into exchanges and 57,000 ETH flowed out. Netflow is 42,000 minus 57,000, which equals negative 15,000 ETH. If ETH trades around 3,000 USD, that is roughly 45 million USD of net withdrawals. On its own this suggests holders moved coins to storage, but you would still check whether a single exchange reshuffled wallets before drawing conclusions.
mistakes: Reading every large inflow as an immediate sell signal.
Ignoring internal exchange transfers that inflate inflow or outflow numbers.
Comparing netflow across data providers that use different wallet labels.

faq.q: Is negative exchange netflow bullish?
faq.a: It means more coins left exchanges than arrived, which is often read as holders moving to self-custody. It is one data point, not a price guarantee.

faq.q: What does a stablecoin inflow to exchanges mean?
faq.a: It often suggests money is arriving that could be used to buy crypto or post margin. It can also simply be traders moving funds between venues.

exchange-netflow.title: What is exchange netflow? Inflows and outflows explained
exchange-netflow.description: Learn what exchange inflows, outflows and netflow mean, how analysts read them, and why wallet labels can distort the signal.

active-addresses.short: Active addresses are the number of unique blockchain addresses that sent or received a transaction during a given period, often counted per day.
body: Active addresses are a simple way to gauge how much a network is being used. If more unique addresses transact each day, more activity is happening on-chain. Analysts track daily, weekly and monthly counts and compare them over time, not just across a single day.

The metric has clear limits. One person or company can control thousands of addresses, while an exchange can serve millions of users through a few addresses. Bots, airdrop farmers and spam transactions can inflate the count, especially on chains with very low fees. Some chains, like Bitcoin, encourage using a new address per transaction, which also changes the numbers.

Because of these quirks, active addresses work best as a trend within one chain. Comparing a low-fee chain with Bitcoin by raw address count is misleading. Pair the metric with fees paid, transaction value and the number of new addresses to get a clearer picture of real demand.
active-addresses.example: Suppose a network averaged 400,000 daily active addresses last month and 520,000 this month. That is an increase of 120,000, or 30%. But you also notice that 90,000 of the new addresses each received exactly 0.01 tokens from the same source, a pattern typical of an airdrop farming campaign. Removing them leaves 430,000, which is only 7.5% above last month.
mistakes: Treating active addresses as the number of real users.
Comparing raw counts between chains with very different fee levels.
Ignoring spam or airdrop farming that can inflate address activity.

faq.q: Do more active addresses mean higher prices?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Rising usage can reflect growing demand, but it can also come from spam, bots or incentive campaigns, so it is not a direct price signal.

faq.q: What counts as an active address?
faq.a: Usually any address that appears as a sender or receiver in a successful transaction during the period. Exact rules vary between data providers.

active-addresses.title: What are active addresses? On-chain usage metric explained
active-addresses.description: What active addresses measure, how analysts use them to gauge network activity, and why bots and airdrops can inflate the numbers.

fear-and-greed-index.short: The Fear and Greed Index is a sentiment gauge that combines market data such as volatility, momentum and social activity into a single score from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed).
body: Crypto versions of the index, such as the widely followed one from Alternative.me, blend several inputs: recent volatility, trading volume and momentum, social media activity, bitcoin dominance and search trends. Each provider weights them differently, so two indexes can show different scores on the same day.

The score is usually grouped into bands: extreme fear, fear, neutral, greed and extreme greed. Many traders read it contrarian-style: extreme fear can appear near capitulation lows, and extreme greed can appear when the market is overheated and crowded with leveraged longs.

Treat it as a mood thermometer, not a timing tool. Markets can stay in extreme greed for weeks during strong uptrends, and fear can deepen for a long time in bear markets. It is most useful when combined with things you can measure directly, such as funding rates, open interest and your own position size.
fear-and-greed-index.example: Suppose the index reads 85, extreme greed, while funding rates on major perpetual contracts have stayed positive for two weeks. You hold 1 BTC and planned to add another 0.5 BTC with 5x leverage. Instead of adding at peak sentiment, you keep the 1 BTC and plan to buy the extra 0.5 BTC without leverage, in five spot orders of 0.1 BTC at lower levels. If the market keeps rising, you still hold your original 1 BTC; if it pulls back 15%, you avoid a leveraged position that would have lost about 75% of its margin.
mistakes: Buying or selling the moment the index hits an extreme, as if it were a precise signal.
Assuming all fear and greed indexes use the same formula.
Ignoring that the index is mostly built for bitcoin and may not reflect a specific altcoin.

faq.q: Is extreme fear a good time to buy crypto?
faq.a: Some traders use extreme fear as a contrarian hint, but prices can keep falling while fear persists. It describes mood, not where the bottom is.

faq.q: How often is the Fear and Greed Index updated?
faq.a: Most crypto versions update once a day. Check the provider's page for its exact schedule and inputs.

fear-and-greed-index.title: What is the Fear and Greed Index in crypto?
fear-and-greed-index.description: What the crypto Fear and Greed Index measures, how its 0-100 score is built and how traders use sentiment without overtrusting it.

node.short: A node is a computer running a blockchain's software that stores, checks and relays transactions and blocks, helping keep the network decentralized and honest.
body: A blockchain has no central server. Instead, thousands of nodes each keep a copy of the ledger and follow the same rules. When a new transaction or block arrives, every node independently checks that it is valid before passing it on. Invalid data is rejected, no matter who sent it.

There are several types. A full node downloads and verifies the entire chain. An archive node also keeps every historical state, which apps and explorers need. A light node keeps only small parts and relies on full nodes for the rest. Mining nodes on proof-of-work chains and validator nodes on proof-of-stake chains also propose or attest to new blocks.

Running your own Bitcoin or Ethereum node lets you verify your transactions without trusting a third party and adds to network resilience. It needs storage, bandwidth and some maintenance. Most wallets connect to public nodes run by providers, which is convenient but means you trust their data and they can see your queries.
node.example: Suppose you run a Bitcoin full node at home. A block arrives claiming a miner reward of 6.25 BTC, but under current rules after the April 2024 halving the subsidy is 3.125 BTC plus fees. If fees in that block total 0.2 BTC, the maximum allowed reward is 3.325 BTC. Your node sees the 6.25 BTC claim exceeds that limit by 2.925 BTC, rejects the block and does not relay it, even if the miner is large.
mistakes: Thinking a node and a validator are always the same; many nodes only verify and relay.
Assuming a wallet app runs its own node when it actually relies on a provider.
Expecting to earn rewards just by running a regular full node.

faq.q: Do you get paid for running a Bitcoin node?
faq.a: No, a regular Bitcoin full node earns nothing directly. People run nodes to verify transactions themselves and support the network. Miners earn rewards, but that is a separate role.

faq.q: What is the difference between a node and a validator?
faq.a: A node stores and checks blockchain data. A validator is a node on a proof-of-stake chain that has staked coins and takes part in proposing and attesting blocks.

node.title: What is a node in blockchain? Full nodes explained
node.description: What a blockchain node is, how full, light and archive nodes differ, and why running your own node lets you verify transactions.

kyc.short: KYC (know your customer) is the identity check that regulated exchanges and financial firms run before letting you deposit, trade or withdraw, usually with an ID document and a selfie.
body: KYC is part of anti-money laundering rules. A typical crypto exchange asks for your name, date of birth and country, a photo of a passport or national ID, and a live selfie or video check. Higher levels may require proof of address or proof of where your funds come from.

Exchanges often tie features to verification levels. Without completed KYC you may only be able to view the app, or you may face low withdrawal limits. Fiat deposits, futures, P2P trading and higher limits usually require full verification. Exactly what is required depends on the exchange and on rules in your country.

KYC data is sensitive, so think about who receives it. Only complete verification on the exchange's official app or website, never through links sent by messages or third parties. Exchanges usually use specialist identity providers, and reputable ones explain this in their privacy policy. If an account was verified with someone else's documents, it can be frozen.
kyc.example: Suppose an exchange lets unverified users withdraw nothing, basic-verified users withdraw up to 2 BTC per day, and advanced-verified users up to 100 BTC per day. You complete basic KYC with your ID and a selfie and want to move 3 BTC to a hardware wallet. You could send 2 BTC today and 1 BTC tomorrow, or complete the advanced level with proof of address to move all 3 BTC at once. These limits are illustrative; each exchange sets its own.
mistakes: Uploading ID documents through a link sent in a chat or email instead of the official app.
Letting a friend or broker verify an account for you, which breaks exchange terms and can freeze funds.
Depositing a large amount before checking whether your verification level allows you to withdraw it.

faq.q: Why do crypto exchanges require KYC?
faq.a: Regulated exchanges must verify users under anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing rules. KYC also helps exchanges recover accounts and comply with sanctions.

faq.q: How long does KYC take on an exchange?
faq.a: Basic checks often finish within minutes, while manual reviews or advanced levels can take hours or days. It depends on the exchange and how clear your documents are.

kyc.title: What is KYC in crypto? Know your customer explained
kyc.description: What KYC means on crypto exchanges, which documents are usually required, how verification levels work and how to submit ID safely.

aml.short: AML (anti-money laundering) is the set of laws and internal controls that financial firms, including crypto exchanges, use to detect and prevent illegal funds from entering the system.
body: AML covers more than identity checks. It includes customer due diligence, ongoing transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, record keeping and reporting suspicious activity to authorities. KYC is the first step; AML is the whole programme around it. It often appears together with CFT, countering the financing of terrorism.

In crypto, exchanges use blockchain analytics to score incoming deposits. Funds linked to hacks, sanctioned addresses, darknet markets or certain mixers may be flagged. A flagged deposit can lead to questions about the source of funds, a temporary hold, or in serious cases a frozen account while the exchange investigates.

For ordinary users, AML mostly shows up as checks you can prepare for: being asked where your money came from, why you are sending large amounts, or who you are trading with on P2P. The international standards come from the FATF, and each country turns them into its own rules, so procedures vary by exchange and region.
aml.example: Suppose you receive 8,000 USDT from a P2P buyer and deposit it to a centralized exchange. The exchange's analytics tool shows that 2,000 USDT of it passed recently through an address linked to a reported scam. That is 25% of the deposit. The exchange places a hold on the 8,000 USDT and asks for your P2P order history and chat records. Providing clear records helps the review, but the outcome depends on the exchange's policy.
mistakes: Accepting P2P payments from third parties whose names do not match the buyer's account.
Ignoring a source-of-funds request, which often leads to longer holds.
Routing funds through mixers or unknown wallets to look private, which can trigger AML flags.

faq.q: What is the difference between KYC and AML?
faq.a: KYC is verifying who a customer is. AML is the broader programme that includes KYC plus monitoring transactions, screening sanctions and reporting suspicious activity.

faq.q: Why was my crypto deposit frozen for AML review?
faq.a: The exchange's monitoring likely linked the funds or the transaction pattern to a risk. Respond through official support with documents showing where the funds came from.

aml.title: What is AML in crypto? Anti-money laundering explained
aml.description: What AML means for crypto exchanges, how transaction monitoring and source-of-funds checks work, and why deposits get frozen.

travel-rule.short: The travel rule is an anti-money laundering requirement that makes crypto service providers share sender and recipient information when they transfer crypto for customers.
body: The rule comes from FATF Recommendation 16, originally written for bank wire transfers and extended to virtual assets. When an exchange sends a customer's crypto to another provider, it must pass along identifying details such as the sender's name and account and the recipient's name. FATF guidance sets a threshold of USD or EUR 1,000, though countries can set lower ones.

The EU applies the travel rule from the first euro since 30 December 2024, with extra checks for transfers to self-hosted wallets above 1,000 euros. Other countries apply their own thresholds and timelines. Exchanges use messaging protocols to exchange this data with each other.

In practice, you may now see extra fields when withdrawing: the recipient's name, whether the destination is an exchange or your own wallet, and which exchange. Some transfers may be delayed or returned if the receiving provider cannot match the information. Requirements and screens differ from exchange to exchange.
travel-rule.example: Suppose you live in the EU and withdraw 1,500 USDC from one exchange to an account in your own name on another exchange. The sending exchange asks you to pick the destination exchange and confirm the recipient name. Because the receiving exchange's records show the same name, the transfer passes. If you instead sent 1,500 USDC to your own self-hosted wallet, the exchange might ask you to prove you control that wallet, for example by signing a message, because the amount is above 1,000 euros.
mistakes: Entering a different recipient name than the one on the receiving account, causing a delay or return.
Choosing exchange as the destination type when sending to a self-hosted wallet, or the reverse.
Assuming the rule only applies to large transfers when your country may apply it from the first unit.

faq.q: Does the travel rule apply to transfers to my own wallet?
faq.a: It depends on the jurisdiction. In the EU, transfers to self-hosted wallets above 1,000 euros can require proof that you own or control the wallet.

faq.q: Why did my withdrawal ask for the recipient's name?
faq.a: Your exchange is collecting travel rule data to pass to the receiving provider. Fill it in exactly as it appears on the receiving account.

travel-rule.title: What is the crypto travel rule? FATF rule explained
travel-rule.description: What the crypto travel rule is, how FATF Recommendation 16 and EU rules work, and why withdrawals now ask for recipient details.

vasp.short: A VASP (virtual asset service provider) is a business that exchanges, transfers, holds or manages crypto for customers and must follow anti-money laundering rules where it operates.
body: The term comes from the FATF and covers exchanges, custodial wallets, brokers, some payment services and firms that run token offerings. Many countries require VASPs to register or obtain a licence before serving local customers. In the EU, the MiCA regulation uses the term CASP, crypto-asset service provider, for licensed firms.

Being a registered or licensed VASP means the firm is subject to rules such as KYC, AML monitoring, the travel rule and, in some places, capital and custody requirements. It does not mean a regulator guarantees your funds. Registration in one country does not allow a firm to serve customers everywhere.

For users, checking VASP status is a practical safety step. Look up the firm on your national regulator's public register, check the exact legal entity name, and compare it with the entity in the exchange's terms of service. Global exchanges often run separate entities for different regions, each with its own permissions.
vasp.example: Suppose an exchange advertises that it is licensed. You open its terms of service and find that your account is with an entity registered in Country A. You check the regulator register of your own country, Country B, and find no listing. A second, smaller exchange shows up on Country B's register under the same entity name as its terms. Of the 2 exchanges, only 1 is authorised to serve you locally under Country B's rules.
mistakes: Trusting a licence logo on a website without checking the regulator's own register.
Assuming a licence in one country covers users in every country.
Believing registration means the regulator insures or guarantees customer funds.

faq.q: Is a crypto exchange a VASP?
faq.a: Yes, centralized exchanges that hold or exchange crypto for customers are VASPs under FATF definitions, and many countries require them to register or be licensed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a VASP and a CASP?
faq.a: VASP is the FATF's global term. CASP is the term used in the EU's MiCA regulation for licensed crypto-asset service providers.

vasp.title: What is a VASP? Virtual asset service provider meaning
vasp.description: What a VASP is, which crypto businesses count as one, how VASP registration and licensing work and how to check an exchange.

mica.short: MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets) is the European Union regulation that sets common rules for crypto-asset issuers, stablecoins and crypto service providers across all EU member states.
body: MiCA creates one rulebook for the EU instead of 27 national regimes. Its stablecoin rules for e-money tokens and asset-referenced tokens applied from 30 June 2024. Its rules for crypto-asset service providers, called CASPs, applied from 30 December 2024, with national transition periods that can run up to 1 July 2026.

A CASP licensed in one EU country can passport its services to the others. Licensed firms must meet requirements on governance, capital, custody and safekeeping of client assets, conflicts of interest and clear disclosures. Token issuers must publish a white paper with prescribed information.

For users, the visible effects include exchanges restricting or delisting stablecoins that are not MiCA-compliant for EU customers, more detailed onboarding, and clearer complaint procedures. MiCA does not cover everything: most fully decentralized services and NFTs fall largely outside it, and tax remains national. Check whether the specific entity serving you holds a MiCA licence.
mica.example: Suppose you live in Spain and use an exchange whose EU entity received a MiCA licence in another member state. Through passporting, it can serve you. You hold 3,000 units of a stablecoin that has no authorised issuer under MiCA. The exchange announces that EU users can no longer buy that coin but can still sell or withdraw it for a period. You could convert the 3,000 units into a MiCA-compliant stablecoin, paying perhaps a 0.1% fee, which would be 3 units.
mistakes: Assuming every exchange operating in the EU is already MiCA licensed while transition periods run.
Thinking MiCA sets crypto tax rules, which remain the job of each country.
Treating a MiCA licence as a guarantee that you cannot lose money trading.

faq.q: When did MiCA come into force?
faq.a: Stablecoin rules applied from 30 June 2024 and service provider rules from 30 December 2024. Some countries allow transition periods up to 1 July 2026 for existing providers.

faq.q: Why are some stablecoins restricted in the EU?
faq.a: Under MiCA, stablecoins offered to the public need an authorised issuer. Exchanges therefore limit trading of non-compliant stablecoins for EU customers.

mica.title: What is MiCA? EU crypto regulation explained
mica.description: What MiCA is, when the EU crypto rules took effect, how CASP licences and passporting work, and why some stablecoins are restricted.

no-kyc-exchange.short: A no-KYC exchange is a platform that lets you trade crypto without verifying your identity, either fully or up to certain withdrawal limits.
body: There are a few types. Decentralized exchanges let you trade from your own wallet with no account at all. Some centralized exchanges allow unverified accounts with low withdrawal limits and limited features. Instant swap services and some P2P marketplaces also operate with little or no identity check.

People choose them for privacy, for speed, or because they lack documents. The trade-offs are real. Unregulated centralized platforms offer fewer protections if something goes wrong, can change their policy and suddenly request KYC before a withdrawal, and may restrict users from certain countries in their terms even if they do not check.

If you use one, keep amounts within published limits, read the terms on restricted regions, and withdraw to your own wallet rather than storing funds there. On DEXs, you control the keys, but you also carry the smart contract and scam risks yourself. Using a no-KYC service does not change your tax obligations, which depend on your country.
no-kyc-exchange.example: Suppose a centralized exchange allows unverified accounts to withdraw up to the equivalent of 1 BTC per day. You deposit 1.5 BTC and trade it. When you try to withdraw everything, you can only move 1 BTC on day one and 0.5 BTC on day two. If the exchange's risk team flags your account in between, it can ask for KYC before releasing the remaining 0.5 BTC, which is a common clause in terms of service.
mistakes: Depositing more than the unverified withdrawal limit allows you to take out.
Ignoring terms that let the platform request identity documents before releasing funds.
Assuming no KYC means no tax reporting obligations.

faq.q: Are no-KYC exchanges legal?
faq.a: It depends on where the platform and the user are. Many jurisdictions require exchanges to run KYC, while decentralized protocols are treated differently. Check the rules in your country.

faq.q: Can a no-KYC exchange ask for ID later?
faq.a: Yes. Many terms allow the exchange to request verification at any time, for example when a withdrawal is large or flagged by monitoring.

no-kyc-exchange.title: What is a no-KYC exchange? Risks and limits
no-kyc-exchange.description: What a no-KYC exchange is, how DEXs and unverified accounts work, what limits apply and the trade-offs of skipping identity checks.

spot-bitcoin-etf.short: A spot bitcoin ETF is an exchange-traded fund that holds actual bitcoin and lets investors gain exposure to its price through a regular brokerage account.
body: The fund buys and stores bitcoin with a custodian, then issues shares that trade on a stock exchange. Each share represents a slice of the bitcoin the fund holds, minus fees. US spot bitcoin ETFs started trading in January 2024, and several other markets have similar products.

A spot ETF differs from a futures ETF, which holds bitcoin futures contracts and can drift from the spot price because of rolling costs. With a spot ETF, the fund's net asset value tracks the bitcoin it actually holds. Authorised participants create and redeem shares to keep the market price close to that value.

Compared with buying bitcoin on an exchange, an ETF trades only during stock market hours, charges an annual management fee, and you cannot withdraw the bitcoin to your own wallet. In return, it fits into brokerage and retirement accounts and avoids handling private keys. Fees, tax treatment and availability depend on the fund and on your country.
spot-bitcoin-etf.example: Suppose a spot bitcoin ETF holds 0.0005 BTC per share and charges a 0.25% annual fee. If bitcoin trades at 80,000 USD, each share's net asset value is about 40 USD. You buy 100 shares for about 4,000 USD. Over a year, the fee reduces holdings by 0.25%, which is about 10 USD on 4,000 USD if the bitcoin price stays flat. If bitcoin rises 10% to 88,000 USD, your shares would be worth about 4,400 USD before that fee.
mistakes: Expecting to withdraw actual bitcoin from an ETF to a personal wallet.
Ignoring the annual management fee when comparing with holding bitcoin directly.
Confusing spot ETFs with futures ETFs, which can track bitcoin less closely.

faq.q: Is a spot bitcoin ETF the same as owning bitcoin?
faq.a: You get price exposure, but you own fund shares, not bitcoin. You cannot send ETF shares on the blockchain, and the fund's custodian holds the actual coins.

faq.q: When did spot bitcoin ETFs start in the US?
faq.a: US spot bitcoin ETFs began trading in January 2024 after regulatory approval.

spot-bitcoin-etf.title: What is a spot bitcoin ETF? How it works
spot-bitcoin-etf.description: What a spot bitcoin ETF is, how it holds real BTC, how it differs from futures ETFs and from buying bitcoin on an exchange.

fiat-on-ramp.short: A fiat on-ramp is any service that turns government money like dollars or euros into crypto, such as a bank transfer to an exchange, a card purchase or a P2P trade.
body: Common on-ramps include bank deposits to a centralized exchange, buying with a debit or credit card, P2P marketplaces where you pay another user directly, and third-party payment providers built into wallets. The reverse direction, crypto back to fiat, is called an off-ramp.

Each route has different costs and speed. Bank transfers are often cheap but can take time. Cards are instant but usually carry higher fees, and some banks block crypto purchases. P2P can offer local payment methods but needs care with counterparties. Payment providers inside wallets are convenient but often add a spread on top of the shown fee.

Almost every regulated on-ramp requires KYC. Before choosing one, compare the full cost: the deposit fee, the trading fee and the exchange rate used. Many people buy a stablecoin such as USDT or USDC first and then trade that for other coins. Available methods depend heavily on your country and bank.
fiat-on-ramp.example: Suppose you want to turn 1,000 EUR into USDC. Route A is a bank transfer to an exchange with no deposit fee, then a market trade with a 0.1% fee, giving about 999 EUR worth of USDC. Route B is a card purchase with a 2% fee plus a 1% spread built into the rate, leaving about 970 EUR worth. Route A is 29 EUR cheaper but may take a day; route B is instant.
mistakes: Comparing only the advertised fee and missing the spread hidden in the exchange rate.
Using a card cash advance option by accident and paying extra bank charges.
Paying a P2P seller outside the platform's escrow process.

faq.q: What is the cheapest way to buy crypto with fiat?
faq.a: Bank transfers to an exchange are often cheaper than cards, but it depends on your bank, country and exchange. Compare the final amount you receive, not just the listed fee.

faq.q: What is the difference between an on-ramp and an off-ramp?
faq.a: An on-ramp converts fiat money into crypto. An off-ramp converts crypto back into fiat, usually to your bank account.

fiat-on-ramp.title: What is a fiat on-ramp? Ways to buy crypto with cash
fiat-on-ramp.description: What a fiat on-ramp is, how bank transfers, cards and P2P compare, and how to see the real cost of turning cash into crypto.

geo-restrictions.short: Geo-restrictions are the rules that stop an exchange or crypto service from offering some or all of its products to users in certain countries or regions.
body: Exchanges restrict regions for legal reasons: local licensing requirements, bans on certain products such as derivatives, sanctions, or simply not having permission in that market. The list of restricted regions is usually in the terms of service, and it can differ by product. A country may have access to spot trading but not futures, copy trading or earn products.

Restrictions are enforced through KYC checks on nationality and residence, IP address detection and app store availability. Rules also change. When an exchange exits a country, it typically announces a deadline to close positions and withdraw funds.

Using a VPN or false address to bypass geo-restrictions breaks most exchanges' terms. If detected, the account can be limited to withdrawal only or closed, and recovering funds may require full documentation. It is safer to choose a service that is allowed in your country of residence.
geo-restrictions.example: Suppose you move from Country A to Country B, where a particular exchange cannot offer derivatives. You have an open futures position with 2,000 USDT margin. After you update your address, the exchange gives you 30 days to close futures positions. You close the position at a 150 USDT profit, leaving 2,150 USDT, and keep using spot trading, which is still allowed in Country B.
mistakes: Opening an account with a VPN in a restricted region and depositing funds anyway.
Failing to update your residence after moving, which can cause problems at a later KYC review.
Assuming access to spot trading means every product of that exchange is allowed for you.

faq.q: Why can't I access an exchange in my country?
faq.a: The exchange may lack a licence there, local law may restrict certain products, or sanctions may apply. Its terms of service list the restricted regions.

faq.q: Is it safe to use a VPN for a crypto exchange?
faq.a: Using a VPN to bypass geo-restrictions usually breaks the exchange's terms and can lead to frozen or closed accounts. Choose a service allowed where you live.

geo-restrictions.title: What are geo-restrictions on crypto exchanges?
geo-restrictions.description: Why crypto exchanges restrict some countries, how geo-restrictions are enforced, and what happens if you bypass them with a VPN.

copy-trading.short: Copy trading is an exchange feature that automatically mirrors another trader's positions in your own account, in proportion to the amount you allocate.
body: On copy trading platforms, experienced traders, often called lead traders, publish their performance. You pick one, allocate funds, and the system opens and closes trades in your account when they do. OKX, Bybit and Bitget all offer copy trading, for both spot and futures, though the details differ.

Most lead traders earn a share of their followers' profits, commonly a profit-sharing percentage on net gains. You keep control over settings such as the amount per trade, a maximum position size, leverage limits and a stop loss for the whole copy portfolio. Check whether the copy follows the lead's leverage or uses your own setting.

The main risks are that past results do not guarantee future ones, futures copy trading can be liquidated just like manual trading, and your entry price can differ slightly from the lead's because of slippage. Look beyond headline return: check maximum drawdown, how long the track record is, the number of followers and how much capital the lead trader risks themselves.
copy-trading.example: Suppose you allocate 1,000 USDT to copy a futures trader with a 10% profit share. The lead uses 5x leverage and puts 20% of their balance into each trade, so your account opens a 200 USDT margin position worth 1,000 USDT. If the price moves 4% in the lead's favour, your position gains 40 USDT and you pay 4 USDT profit share. If it moves 4% against, you lose 40 USDT with no profit share. A 20% move against at 5x would wipe out that 200 USDT margin.
mistakes: Picking a lead trader based only on a 30-day return that came from one lucky high-leverage trade.
Copying without setting a total stop loss for the copy portfolio.
Allocating money you need soon, without accounting for drawdowns that even good traders experience.

faq.q: Is copy trading profitable?
faq.a: It can be, but results depend entirely on the trader you copy and the market. Many followers lose money when they choose leads by short-term returns alone.

faq.q: Can I lose more than I put into copy trading?
faq.a: On most exchanges, losses are limited to the funds allocated to the copy, but futures copies can lose that full amount through liquidation.

copy-trading.title: What is copy trading in crypto? How it works
copy-trading.description: How crypto copy trading works, how lead traders are paid, which settings protect you and what risks come with copying futures.

grid-trading-bot.short: A grid trading bot is an automated tool that places a ladder of buy and sell limit orders within a price range, profiting from repeated moves up and down.
body: You choose an upper price, a lower price and the number of grids. The bot splits the range into levels and places buy orders below the current price and sell orders above it. Each time the price drops to a level, it buys; each time it rises to the next level, it sells that slice for a small profit.

Grid bots work best in sideways, volatile markets. In a strong trend, they struggle: if the price climbs above the range, the bot has sold everything and sits in stablecoins; if it falls below, it holds coins bought at higher prices and shows an unrealised loss. Futures grid bots add leverage and liquidation risk.

Most major exchanges offer spot and futures grids with suggested settings, often based on recent volatility. Before starting, check the fee per trade, because grids trade often and small profits per grid can be eaten by fees. More grids means more trades with smaller profits each.
grid-trading-bot.example: Suppose ETH trades at 3,000 USDT and you set a spot grid from 2,700 to 3,300 with 6 grids, so the levels are 100 USDT apart. Each grid trades 0.1 ETH. If the price dips to 2,900 and returns to 3,000, the bot buys 0.1 ETH at 2,900 and sells at 3,000, making 10 USDT before fees. With a 0.1% fee per side, fees are about 0.29 plus 0.30, leaving roughly 9.41 USDT. Twenty such round trips in a month would earn about 188 USDT.
mistakes: Setting a narrow range in a trending market so the price quickly leaves the grid.
Using too many grids so each profit is smaller than the trading fees.
Running a leveraged futures grid without checking the liquidation price.

faq.q: Do grid trading bots make money?
faq.a: They can profit in ranging markets with enough volatility. In strong trends, especially downtrends, a grid can show losses or sit idle outside its range.

faq.q: What is the difference between spot grid and futures grid?
faq.a: A spot grid buys and sells real coins with no leverage. A futures grid trades contracts, can go long or short and can use leverage, which adds liquidation risk.

grid-trading-bot.title: What is a grid trading bot? How grid bots work
grid-trading-bot.description: How a grid trading bot places buy and sell orders in a price range, when grids work best and how fees and trends affect results.

launchpool.short: A Launchpool is an exchange program where you lock tokens you already hold, such as the exchange token or a stablecoin, for a set period to earn a new token before or around its listing.
body: Binance Launchpool popularised the format, and other exchanges run similar programs under different names. Each campaign lists eligible staking assets, a total reward pool and a duration. Rewards are usually calculated hourly based on your share of the total staked amount and credited to your account.

Your staked tokens stay yours and can usually be withdrawn at any time, though you stop earning once they leave the pool. The real cost is price risk on what you stake: if you buy an exchange token just to join, a drop in its price can outweigh the rewards.

Rewards are often small for each participant because many users stake. Most programs require KYC and are not available in every country. Per-user caps, eligibility rules and reward schedules vary, so read each campaign's rules before staking.
launchpool.example: Suppose a campaign distributes 3,000,000 new tokens over 10 days, so 300,000 per day. You stake 2,000 USDT in a pool that holds 400,000,000 USDT in total. Your share is 2,000 divided by 400,000,000, which is 0.0005%. That earns you 1.5 tokens per day, or 15 tokens over 10 days. If the token lists at 0.40 USDT, your reward is worth about 6 USDT.
mistakes: Buying a volatile exchange token only to join a Launchpool without considering its price risk.
Expecting the advertised total rewards to translate into large personal earnings.
Missing that rewards stop accruing as soon as you unstake.

faq.q: Is Launchpool free money?
faq.a: There is no direct fee, but the assets you stake carry price risk and rewards depend on your share of the pool. Many users earn modest amounts.

faq.q: What is the difference between Launchpool and Launchpad?
faq.a: In a Launchpool you stake tokens to earn a new token for free. In a Launchpad you commit funds to buy a new token in a sale.

launchpool.title: What is a Launchpool? Earning new tokens by staking
launchpool.description: What a Launchpool is, how staking for new tokens works, how rewards are calculated and how it differs from a Launchpad sale.

launchpad.short: A launchpad is a platform, often run by an exchange, where users can buy a new project's tokens in a sale before or as the tokens list for trading.
body: Exchange launchpads, a form of IEO or initial exchange offering, select projects and sell a fixed amount of tokens at a set price. Many require you to hold or commit the exchange's own token or a stablecoin during a snapshot or subscription period. If the sale is oversubscribed, each participant receives a share and the unused funds are returned.
On-chain launchpads exist too, where you connect a wallet and buy tokens through a smart contract. These can have fewer checks on projects, so research matters more.

Key points to check: the sale price and the fully diluted valuation, how much of the supply is sold, the vesting schedule for team and investor tokens, and when tokens unlock for buyers. Launchpad tokens can fall below the sale price after listing, especially when large unlocks follow. Participation usually needs KYC and is blocked in some countries.
launchpad.example: Suppose a launchpad sells 10,000,000 tokens at 0.05 USDT, raising 500,000 USDT, but users commit 25,000,000 USDT. The sale is 50 times oversubscribed. You commit 5,000 USDT, so your allocation is 5,000 divided by 50, which is 100 USDT, buying 2,000 tokens. The other 4,900 USDT is returned. If the token lists at 0.08 USDT, your 2,000 tokens are worth 160 USDT; at 0.03 USDT, they are worth 60 USDT.
mistakes: Assuming every launchpad token will trade above its sale price.
Ignoring the vesting and unlock schedule that can add selling pressure after listing.
Joining an unknown on-chain launchpad promoted through private messages.

faq.q: What is an IEO in crypto?
faq.a: An IEO, or initial exchange offering, is a token sale run by an exchange on behalf of a project. The exchange handles the sale and usually lists the token afterwards.

faq.q: Why did I receive only part of my launchpad commitment?
faq.a: Most sales are oversubscribed, so allocations are cut pro rata. The unused amount is returned to your account after the sale.

launchpad.title: What is a crypto launchpad? Token sales and IEOs
launchpad.description: How crypto launchpads and IEOs work, how oversubscribed allocations are calculated and what to check before joining a token sale.

crypto-earn.short: Crypto Earn refers to exchange savings products that pay you a yield for depositing crypto, either flexible with withdrawal anytime or locked for a fixed term.
body: Most large exchanges group these under a name like Earn or Simple Earn. Flexible products let you redeem quickly, usually with a lower and changing rate. Fixed or locked products pay a set rate for a set term, such as 30 or 90 days, and you cannot withdraw early, or you lose part of the interest.

The yield comes from somewhere: staking rewards on proof-of-stake coins, lending to margin traders or institutions, liquidity provision or promotional budgets. Higher advertised rates often mean higher risk, a small cap per user, or a short promotional period.

Your coins sit with the exchange, so this is custodial. If the platform has problems, earn balances can be frozen. Check whether rates are shown as APR or APY, whether rewards are paid in the same coin, and the rules on redemption time. Products and availability differ by exchange and country.
crypto-earn.example: Suppose you deposit 5,000 USDC into a flexible product paying 4% APR, with interest credited daily. Daily interest is 5,000 times 0.04 divided by 365, about 0.55 USDC. Over 30 days you earn about 16.4 USDC if the rate stays the same. A 90-day locked product at 6% APR on the same amount would earn about 74 USDC, but your 5,000 USDC would be unavailable for those 90 days.
mistakes: Assuming advertised rates are fixed when flexible rates change frequently.
Locking funds you might need, and losing interest by redeeming early.
Forgetting that earn balances are held by the exchange, not in your own wallet.

faq.q: Is Crypto Earn safe?
faq.a: It carries the risk of the exchange itself plus the risk of how the yield is generated. It is not a bank deposit and is usually not covered by deposit insurance.

faq.q: What is the difference between flexible and locked savings?
faq.a: Flexible savings let you withdraw at any time at a variable rate. Locked savings pay a set rate for a fixed term but restrict early withdrawal.

crypto-earn.title: What is Crypto Earn? Exchange savings explained
crypto-earn.description: What Crypto Earn savings products are, how flexible and locked terms differ, where the yield comes from and the custody risks.

dual-investment.short: Dual investment is a structured exchange product where you earn a fixed yield but may be paid back in a different coin depending on whether the price ends above or below a target price on settlement.
body: You choose a coin such as BTC, a target price and a settlement date. In a buy low product, you deposit stablecoins; if the price at settlement is at or below the target, you receive BTC bought at the target price, otherwise you get your stablecoins back. In a sell high product, you deposit BTC; if the price ends at or above the target, you receive stablecoins, otherwise your BTC. You earn the yield in either case.

Under the hood, it works much like selling an option. The high yield is your compensation for giving up the upside or accepting the downside. If BTC crashes far below your buy low target, you still receive BTC at the target price, which is then worth less.

Funds are locked until settlement, usually with no early exit. The settlement price is typically an index average at a set time, so it can differ from the last trade you see. Terms, coins and yields vary by exchange.
dual-investment.example: Suppose BTC trades at 62,000 USDT and you deposit 6,000 USDT in a 7-day buy low product with a 60,000 target and 20% annualised yield. Interest for 7 days is 6,000 times 0.20 times 7 divided by 365, about 23 USDT. If BTC settles at 61,000, you receive 6,023 USDT. If it settles at 55,000, you receive 6,023 divided by 60,000, about 0.1004 BTC, worth about 5,522 USDT at that moment.
mistakes: Treating the high annualised yield as risk-free interest.
Choosing a buy low target on a coin you do not actually want to own.
Forgetting that a sell high product caps your gain if the price rallies far above the target.

faq.q: Can you lose money with dual investment?
faq.a: Yes, in value terms. You always get the yield, but you may be paid in a coin that is worth less than what you deposited, or miss gains above your target.

faq.q: Is dual investment the same as options trading?
faq.a: It is built on similar mechanics to selling an option, packaged as a simple product. You do not manage the option yourself.

dual-investment.title: What is dual investment in crypto? How it works
dual-investment.description: How crypto dual investment works, what buy low and sell high mean, how settlement decides your payout and where the risk lies.

p2p-trading.short: P2P (C2C) trading is buying or selling crypto directly with another user, paying in local money through bank transfer or payment apps while the platform holds the crypto in escrow.
body: On an exchange's P2P marketplace, merchants post ads with a price, limits and accepted payment methods. When you place an order to buy, the seller's crypto is locked in escrow. You pay the seller directly by the agreed method, mark the order as paid, and the seller releases the crypto. Sellers follow the same steps in reverse.

P2P is popular where bank deposits to exchanges are limited, and stablecoins like USDT are the most traded asset. Prices can be above or below the market rate, so compare ads. Many platforms charge no fee to takers, while merchants may pay one.

Most problems come from payment disputes. Only release crypto after the money is actually in your account, not when a screenshot arrives. Never move the conversation or payment off the platform. Check that the payer's name matches the buyer's verified name; third-party payments can be linked to fraud and lead to frozen bank accounts. Rules and protections vary by exchange and country.
p2p-trading.example: Suppose a merchant sells USDT at 1.02 local currency units and the market rate is 1.00. You buy 500 USDT and pay 510 units by bank transfer within the 15-minute window. The 10-unit difference, 2%, is the merchant's margin. If you had chosen an ad at 1.005, you would have paid 502.5 units, saving 7.5. After you mark the order as paid, the merchant releases 500 USDT from escrow to your funding account.
mistakes: Releasing crypto as a seller after seeing a payment screenshot instead of checking your bank balance.
Agreeing to pay or chat outside the platform, which removes escrow protection.
Accepting payment from a bank account in a different name than the buyer's.

faq.q: Is P2P crypto trading safe?
faq.a: Escrow protects the crypto side, but payment fraud is common. Stay on the platform, check payments yourself and trade with verified, experienced merchants.

faq.q: What does C2C mean in crypto?
faq.a: C2C means customer-to-customer and is another name used for P2P trading on some exchanges.

p2p-trading.title: What is P2P crypto trading? How C2C works
p2p-trading.description: How P2P (C2C) crypto trading works, how escrow protects orders, how merchant pricing works and how to avoid payment scams.

instant-convert.short: Convert is an exchange feature that swaps one coin for another at a quoted price in one click, without using the order book directly.
body: When you use Convert, the exchange shows a quote such as 1 ETH for 3,000 USDT, valid for a few seconds. If you accept, the swap executes at exactly that rate. You do not choose between maker or taker orders or worry about partial fills.
