Many exchanges advertise Convert as zero fee, but the cost is often built into the quoted rate as a spread. Compare the quote with the current order book price to see the difference. For small amounts, the convenience may be worth it. For larger trades, a limit order on the spot market is often cheaper.

Convert also helps with pairs that have no direct market, because the exchange routes through other pairs for you. Some exchanges let you convert small leftover balances, often called dust, into a single coin. Limits, supported coins and spreads differ by exchange.
instant-convert.example: Suppose the spot order book shows ETH at 3,000 USDT and the Convert screen quotes 2,985 USDT for 1 ETH with zero fee. The spread is 15 USDT, or 0.5%. Selling 2 ETH by Convert gives you 5,970 USDT. Selling on the spot market with a 0.1% taker fee gives about 6,000 minus 6, which is 5,994 USDT, assuming no slippage. The spot trade earns 24 USDT more.
mistakes: Assuming zero fee means zero cost when the spread is in the quote.
Using Convert for large trades where a spot limit order would be cheaper.
Waiting too long on the quote screen and getting a refreshed, worse price.

faq.q: Is Convert cheaper than spot trading?
faq.a: Not always. Convert is convenient but often includes a spread. For larger amounts, spot trading with limit orders is usually cheaper.

faq.q: Does Convert have fees?
faq.a: Many exchanges show no separate fee, but the price you receive can be slightly worse than the market. Compare the quote with the order book.

instant-convert.title: What is Convert on a crypto exchange? Instant swap
instant-convert.description: How the Convert or instant swap feature works on exchanges, why zero fee does not mean zero cost and when spot trading is cheaper.

unified-trading-account.short: A unified trading account (UTA) is an exchange account mode that lets you trade spot, margin, futures and sometimes options from one balance, with assets shared as collateral.
body: In older account setups, you move funds between separate spot and futures wallets. A unified account removes most of those transfers. Your coins sit in one place and count as margin across products, often with each asset valued at a discount called a collateral ratio or haircut. Bybit, OKX and other exchanges offer versions of this, with different names and modes.

The benefit is capital efficiency. You can hold BTC and use it as margin for a USDT futures position without selling it. Unrealised profit in one position can support another. Some unified accounts offer portfolio margin, which calculates margin based on the overall risk of your positions.

The trade-off is shared risk. A large loss in one position can draw on all your assets, and a falling collateral coin reduces margin at the same time. Some modes can automatically borrow when a balance goes negative, which creates interest. Read your exchange's mode descriptions, and use isolated margin or a sub-account for positions you want kept separate.
unified-trading-account.example: Suppose you hold 1 BTC worth 60,000 USDT in a unified account with a 95% collateral ratio, giving 57,000 USDT of margin value. You open a USDT perpetual position needing 10,000 USDT margin. If BTC falls 20% to 48,000 USDT, your collateral value drops to 45,600 USDT. If the position also loses 5,000 USDT, your available margin shrinks further, and both effects combine against the same account.
mistakes: Forgetting that a falling collateral coin reduces margin for every open position.
Ignoring automatic borrowing that can charge interest on negative balances.
Mixing long-term holdings and high-leverage trades in one unified balance.

faq.q: What is the advantage of a unified trading account?
faq.a: You can use one balance across spot, margin and derivatives and use coins as collateral without selling them, which reduces transfers and improves capital efficiency.

faq.q: Is a unified account riskier?
faq.a: It can be, because positions and collateral share the same pool. A loss or price drop in one area affects margin for everything else.

unified-trading-account.title: What is a unified trading account (UTA)?
unified-trading-account.description: What a unified trading account is, how shared collateral and haircuts work, and the risks of combining spot and futures margin.

sub-account.short: A sub-account is a separate account created under your main exchange account, with its own balances and positions, used to separate strategies, bots or team members.
body: Most large exchanges let a verified main account create sub-accounts. Each has its own funds, orders and margin, so a liquidation in one does not touch the others. You can move funds between the main account and sub-accounts internally, usually without fees.

Common uses include keeping a long-term spot portfolio apart from futures trading, running different bots or API keys in separate accounts, giving a team member or fund manager limited access, and tracking performance per strategy. Some sub-accounts can be set to have no withdrawal rights, so the main account controls all transfers out.

Limits differ by exchange: the number of sub-accounts allowed, whether they share the main account's fee tier, and which products each type can access. Sub-accounts normally rely on the main account's KYC. Protect the main account with strong two-factor authentication, since it controls everything below it.
sub-account.example: Suppose you have 12,000 USDT. You keep 8,000 in the main account for spot holdings, move 3,000 into a futures sub-account and 1,000 into a grid bot sub-account. A bad leveraged trade wipes out the 3,000 USDT in the futures sub-account. Your main account still holds 8,000 and the bot sub-account 1,000, because the futures loss could not reach them. Without separation, a cross margin position could have drawn on all 12,000.
mistakes: Giving withdrawal permission to API keys used by bots in a sub-account.
Assuming sub-accounts need separate KYC or a separate login method.
Forgetting balances spread across sub-accounts when checking total exposure.

faq.q: Why use a sub-account on a crypto exchange?
faq.a: To separate strategies, limit risk, run bots with dedicated API keys, or let others trade without access to your main funds.

faq.q: Do sub-accounts share the same trading fee level?
faq.a: On many exchanges they share the main account's fee tier and volume, but rules differ, so check the fee page of your exchange.

sub-account.title: What is a sub-account on a crypto exchange?
sub-account.description: What an exchange sub-account is, how it separates risk and strategies, and how to set permissions for bots and team members safely.

demo-trading.short: Demo trading is practising on an exchange with virtual funds in a simulated account, so you can learn order types, leverage and futures mechanics without risking real money.
body: Many exchanges, including OKX, Bybit and Bitget, offer a demo mode with virtual balances such as tens of thousands of virtual USDT. Some run on a testnet with separate prices, while others mirror live market prices more closely. Orders, positions, funding and liquidation work like the real thing as far as possible.

Demo trading is useful for learning the interface, testing how margin modes work, practising stop loss and take profit placement, and checking a strategy's rules before using real funds. It is especially valuable before trying leveraged futures.

Its limits matter. Fills can be more generous than in real markets, liquidity and slippage may not match, and losing virtual money does not trigger the same emotions as real losses. Treat demo results as practice, then start small with real funds and the same rules.
demo-trading.example: Suppose you start a demo account with 10,000 virtual USDT and open a BTC long at 50,000 USDT with 10x leverage, using 1,000 USDT margin for a 10,000 USDT position. You see that a 5% drop to 47,500 would erase 500 USDT, half your margin, and your liquidation price sits a little above 45,000, depending on maintenance margin. Practising this lets you choose a stop loss at 48,500, limiting the loss to about 300 USDT.
mistakes: Assuming results from demo trading will carry over unchanged to a live account.
Using much larger leverage in demo than you would ever use with real money.
Skipping demo practice entirely before using unfamiliar futures features.

faq.q: Is demo trading the same as real trading?
faq.a: It uses similar tools, but fills, slippage and emotions differ. It is good practice, not a guarantee of real results.

faq.q: Can I withdraw demo trading profits?
faq.a: No. Demo balances are virtual and cannot be withdrawn or converted to real funds.

demo-trading.title: What is demo trading in crypto? Paper trading explained
demo-trading.description: What crypto demo trading is, how virtual futures accounts work, what you can practise safely and why demo results differ from live.

referral-code.short: A referral code is a code you enter when signing up to an exchange that links your account to a referrer and can give you a discount or rebate on trading fees.
body: Exchanges run referral and affiliate programs to attract users. When you register with a code, the referrer usually earns a share of the fees you pay, and in many programs part of that share is passed back to you as a fee discount, a rebate or a welcome reward. The exact split, duration and eligible products differ by exchange and by program.

A code must normally be entered at registration. On most exchanges it cannot be added later, so check before you create the account. Rebates may apply to spot, futures or both, may last for a limited period, and are often paid in a specific coin on a daily or weekly schedule.

Use codes only from sources you trust and register on the exchange's official website or app. A legitimate code never needs your password, seed phrase or API keys. A rebate lowers your trading cost, but it does not change the risk of the trades themselves.
referral-code.example: Suppose a futures taker fee is 0.05% and your referral code gives a 20% rebate on fees. You trade 200,000 USDT of futures volume in a month. Your fees total 200,000 times 0.0005, which is 100 USDT. A 20% rebate returns 20 USDT, so your effective fee is 80 USDT, or 0.04%. These figures are illustrative; actual rates and rebates depend on the exchange and the program.
mistakes: Creating an account first and expecting to add a referral code later.
Signing up through a lookalike site that copied a referral link.
Trading more than planned just to earn a larger rebate.

faq.q: Can I add a referral code after registering?
faq.a: On most exchanges, no. The code has to be entered during sign-up, though a few exchanges allow it within a short window afterwards.

faq.q: How does a referral fee rebate work?
faq.a: The exchange returns part of the trading fees you pay, usually as a percentage, credited to your account on a regular schedule.

referral-code.title: What is a referral code on crypto exchanges? Fee rebates
referral-code.description: How exchange referral codes work, how fee rebates are calculated, why codes must be entered at sign-up and how to use them safely.

vip-tier.short: A VIP fee tier is an exchange level that gives lower trading fees and extra benefits to users who trade high volume or hold large balances.
body: Exchanges publish a fee schedule with several levels. The base level applies to most users. Higher levels, often called VIP 1, VIP 2 and so on, cut maker and taker fees step by step. Qualification usually depends on 30-day trading volume, total asset balance or holdings of the exchange's token, and is often re-checked daily.

Spot and futures volumes may be counted separately, with separate tiers. Top levels can reach zero or even negative maker fees, which means the exchange pays you for adding liquidity. VIP status can also bring higher withdrawal limits, a dedicated account manager or better borrowing rates.

For most retail traders, the base tier applies. Some exchanges run VIP trial programs or match a VIP level you hold on another exchange. Check the fee page of your exchange for exact thresholds, since they change and differ widely.
vip-tier.example: Suppose the base futures fees are 0.02% maker and 0.05% taker, and VIP 1 is 0.016% maker and 0.04% taker for 30-day volume above 10 million USDT. You trade 12 million USDT a month, all as taker. At the base level you would pay 6,000 USDT. At VIP 1 you pay 4,800 USDT, saving 1,200 USDT. The numbers are illustrative; actual thresholds and rates differ by exchange.
mistakes: Overtrading just to reach a VIP tier, increasing risk more than the fee saving is worth.
Forgetting that tier levels are recalculated and can drop when volume falls.
Assuming spot volume counts toward futures VIP levels on every exchange.

faq.q: How do you get VIP status on a crypto exchange?
faq.a: Usually by reaching a 30-day trading volume or asset balance threshold. Some exchanges also offer trial programs or match VIP levels from other exchanges.

faq.q: What is a negative maker fee?
faq.a: It means the exchange pays you a small rebate for orders that add liquidity to the order book. It is usually only available at high VIP or market maker levels.

vip-tier.title: What is a VIP fee tier on crypto exchanges?
vip-tier.description: How exchange VIP fee tiers work, how 30-day volume and balances qualify you, and how much lower maker and taker fees can save.

withdrawal-fee.short: A withdrawal fee is the amount an exchange charges when you send crypto from your account to an external address, usually to cover the blockchain network fee.
body: When you withdraw, the exchange must broadcast a transaction and pay the network's gas or transaction fee. Most exchanges charge a fixed fee per withdrawal, set per coin and per network, and adjust it when network costs change. Some add a margin on top; some withdrawals between users of the same exchange are free.

The network you choose makes a big difference. The same stablecoin can be withdrawn on several networks, and the fee on a congested layer 1 chain is often much higher than on a layer 2 or a low-fee chain. The receiving wallet or exchange must support the same network, or funds can be lost or need a manual recovery.
There is usually also a minimum withdrawal amount. Because the fee is mostly fixed, small withdrawals lose a larger percentage. Fiat withdrawals to a bank have their own separate fees and limits.
withdrawal-fee.example: Suppose you want to withdraw 100 USDT. The exchange charges 4 USDT on an Ethereum-based network, 1 USDT on a TRON-based network and 0.2 USDT on a layer 2 network. On Ethereum you lose 4%, receiving 96 USDT. On the layer 2 you receive 99.8 USDT, losing only 0.2%. If the receiving exchange only supports the TRON network, you would pay 1 USDT and receive 99 USDT.
mistakes: Choosing a network the receiving wallet does not support.
Making many small withdrawals where the fixed fee eats a large share.
Comparing exchanges on trading fees only and ignoring withdrawal fees.

faq.q: Why are crypto withdrawal fees so high?
faq.a: They often reflect the blockchain network's fee at that time plus the exchange's own pricing. Choosing a cheaper supported network usually lowers the cost.

faq.q: Is the withdrawal fee the same on every network?
faq.a: No. Each network has its own fee, so the same coin can cost much more to withdraw on one chain than another.

withdrawal-fee.title: What is a crypto withdrawal fee? How to pay less
withdrawal-fee.description: What crypto withdrawal fees are, why they change by coin and network, and how to choose the right network to avoid overpaying.

token-listing.short: A token listing is when an exchange adds a coin to its markets, letting users deposit, trade and withdraw it on that platform.
body: Projects apply to exchanges, which review things such as the team, token distribution, smart contract security, liquidity, legal status and community demand. Large exchanges publish listing announcements with timings for deposits, the opening of trading pairs and withdrawals. Some coins first appear in innovation or seed zones that carry extra risk labels.

New listings often bring big price swings. Early trading can see sharp spikes and drops as liquidity builds, and some exchanges limit order types or price ranges in the first minutes. Tokens can also list on futures markets before or after spot, sometimes as pre-market contracts.

Watch out for fake listing announcements and fake tokens with the same name. Only trust announcements on the exchange's official channels, and check the contract address before buying a token on-chain. Listing on a major exchange does not mean the exchange endorses the project.
token-listing.example: Suppose an exchange announces that a new token opens for trading at 10:00 UTC. In the first 5 minutes the price jumps from 0.50 to 1.20 USDT, then settles around 0.70 within an hour. A buyer who used a market order at the peak with 1,200 USDT got about 1,000 tokens, now worth about 700 USDT, a loss of roughly 42%. A buyer who placed a limit order at 0.60 got 2,000 tokens for the same 1,200 USDT, worth about 1,400 USDT at 0.70.
mistakes: Placing large market orders in the first minutes of a new listing.
Trusting listing rumours or screenshots from social media instead of official announcements.
Buying a token with the same name on a DEX without checking the contract address.

faq.q: Does a token's price go up after an exchange listing?
faq.a: Not reliably. Prices often swing sharply both ways after listing, and many new tokens fall below their early trading levels.

faq.q: How do exchanges decide which tokens to list?
faq.a: Each exchange has its own review process, typically looking at the project's team, tokenomics, security, liquidity, legal factors and user demand.

token-listing.title: What is a token listing? How new coins list on exchanges
token-listing.description: What a token listing is, how exchanges review and announce new coins, and why prices swing so much in the first trading minutes.

delisting.short: Delisting is when an exchange removes a token or trading pair, ending trading and usually setting a deadline to withdraw the remaining balances.
body: Exchanges delist tokens for reasons such as low trading volume and liquidity, a project that stopped developing, security problems, regulatory concerns or failure to meet updated listing standards. Many exchanges first add a monitoring or risk tag to a token as a warning before any decision.

A delisting announcement normally gives dates: when trading pairs close, when deposits stop and the last day for withdrawals. Open orders are cancelled when trading ends. If the token has perpetual futures, those contracts are usually settled earlier. After the withdrawal deadline, some exchanges convert leftover balances into a stablecoin, others do not, so read each announcement.

Prices often fall sharply after a delisting announcement because liquidity is about to shrink. If you hold the token, decide early whether to sell or move it to a wallet or another exchange that supports it, and check that the destination supports the same network.
delisting.example: Suppose an exchange announces that token XYZ will be delisted, with trading ending in 7 days and withdrawals closing in 30 days. You hold 5,000 XYZ worth 0.10 USDT each, so 500 USDT. After the news the price drops 30% to 0.07, making your holding 350 USDT. You can sell for about 350 USDT on the exchange, or withdraw the 5,000 XYZ to your own wallet for a 50 XYZ fee, leaving 4,950 XYZ to trade elsewhere.
mistakes: Ignoring the withdrawal deadline and losing access to the remaining balance.
Holding perpetual positions in a token being delisted without noting the earlier settlement date.
Withdrawing to a network or wallet that does not support the token.

faq.q: What happens to my tokens when they are delisted?
faq.a: You can usually withdraw them until a set deadline. After that, depending on the exchange, they may be converted to a stablecoin or become inaccessible.

faq.q: Why do exchanges delist tokens?
faq.a: Common reasons include low liquidity, project inactivity, security incidents, regulatory issues or failing the exchange's ongoing review standards.

delisting.title: What is delisting in crypto? What to do with your tokens
delisting.description: What a crypto delisting is, why exchanges remove tokens, what the trading and withdrawal deadlines mean and how to protect balances.

tokenized-stocks.short: Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens designed to track the price of a company's shares, usually backed one to one by real shares held by a custodian.
body: A provider buys real shares, holds them with a regulated custodian and issues tokens that represent them. The tokens can trade on exchanges or move on-chain, sometimes 24 hours a day, even when stock markets are closed. Some products pass on dividends as extra tokens or cash.

Holders usually do not get the same rights as shareholders. You typically cannot vote at company meetings, and your claim is against the issuer and its custodian, not the company itself. Availability depends heavily on the user's country; many products are not offered to US persons or in some other regions.

Prices can drift from the underlying share when stock markets are closed, because tokens may trade while the reference price is frozen, and liquidity is thinner. Compare this with stock perpetuals, which give price exposure through derivatives rather than backed tokens.
tokenized-stocks.example: Suppose a tokenized share tracks a stock that closed at 200 USD on Friday. Over the weekend the stock market is closed, but the token trades and climbs to 206 USD, a 3% premium, after positive company news. On Monday the stock opens at 203 USD. If you had bought the token at 206, you would face a 3 USD loss per token once the price realigns with the stock, even though the stock itself rose 1.5%.
mistakes: Assuming a tokenized stock gives the same voting and legal rights as owning the share.
Ignoring premiums or discounts that appear outside stock market hours.
Not checking who the issuer and custodian are and in which countries the product is allowed.

faq.q: Are tokenized stocks real shares?
faq.a: They are tokens backed by real shares held by a custodian, but you own a claim on the issuer, not the share itself. Rights such as voting usually do not pass through.

faq.q: Can I trade tokenized stocks 24/7?
faq.a: Many tokenized stocks trade around the clock on crypto platforms, but prices can move away from the stock when its market is closed.

tokenized-stocks.title: What are tokenized stocks? How stock tokens work
tokenized-stocks.description: How tokenized stocks work, what backs them, what rights holders get and why prices can drift from the real share after hours.

stock-perpetuals.short: Stock perpetuals are perpetual futures contracts that track the price of a share or stock index, letting you go long or short with leverage without owning the stock.
body: They work like crypto perpetual futures. You post margin, usually in USDT or USDC, and open a long or short position. There is no expiry date. A funding rate paid between longs and shorts keeps the contract close to the index price, which is based on the underlying stock's price.

Because stock markets close at night and on weekends, venues handle off-hours differently. Some keep trading using internal pricing, some widen limits, and some pause or switch to a different price source. Gaps when the stock reopens can move the mark price sharply and trigger liquidations.

Stock perpetuals give price exposure only. You own no shares, receive no dividends in the normal way and have no shareholder rights. Availability depends on the platform and your country. Check the contract specification page for funding interval, trading hours, leverage limits and how the index is calculated.
stock-perpetuals.example: Suppose a stock perpetual tracks a share at 100 USD and you go long 10 contracts of 1 share each with 5x leverage, posting 200 USD margin for a 1,000 USD position. On Monday the stock opens 12% lower at 88 USD after weekend news. Your position loses 120 USD, 60% of your margin. With a 20% drop, the loss would be 200 USD, your full margin, and you would be liquidated before that point.
mistakes: Holding leveraged positions over a weekend without planning for opening gaps.
Expecting dividends or shareholder rights from a perpetual contract.
Ignoring funding payments, which can add up on longer holds.

faq.q: What is the difference between stock perpetuals and tokenized stocks?
faq.a: Tokenized stocks are tokens backed by real shares. Stock perpetuals are derivatives that track the price, use margin and leverage, and do not involve owning shares.

faq.q: Do stock perpetuals trade on weekends?
faq.a: It depends on the platform. Some trade around the clock with special pricing rules, others restrict trading when the stock market is closed.

stock-perpetuals.title: What are stock perpetuals? Stock perps explained
stock-perpetuals.description: How stock perpetual futures work, how funding and off-hours pricing apply, and how they differ from owning tokenized stocks.

real-world-assets.short: Real-world assets (RWA) are traditional assets such as bonds, gold, real estate, private credit or stocks represented as tokens on a blockchain.
body: RWA tokenization takes an off-chain asset, places it under the control of a legal entity or custodian, and issues tokens that represent a claim on it. The token can then move on-chain, be used in DeFi protocols as collateral, or settle faster than traditional systems allow. Ondo Finance, BlackRock's BUIDL fund and Paxos Gold are well-known examples in this area.

The largest categories are tokenized US Treasuries, private credit, commodities such as gold, and tokenized stocks. Fiat-backed stablecoins are sometimes counted as RWAs too, since they are backed by off-chain reserves.

Unlike native crypto, an RWA token depends on off-chain trust: the issuer, the custodian, the legal structure and the reliability of the data that brings prices on-chain. Many RWA products require KYC and are limited to certain investors or countries. Before buying, check what you actually own, how redemption works and who audits the reserves.
real-world-assets.example: Suppose a fund tokenizes 50,000,000 USD of short-term government bonds and issues 50,000,000 tokens at 1 USD each. The bonds yield 4% a year, and the fund charges 0.5%, so holders earn about 3.5%. If you hold 10,000 tokens for a year, you would earn about 350 USD, either as more tokens or a rising token price, depending on the product design.
mistakes: Treating RWA tokens as risk-free because the underlying asset is traditional.
Ignoring the issuer, custodian and legal structure that the token depends on.
Assuming you can redeem directly when redemption may be limited to approved investors.

faq.q: What does RWA mean in crypto?
faq.a: RWA stands for real-world assets, meaning traditional assets like bonds, gold or real estate represented by tokens on a blockchain.

faq.q: Are RWA tokens safe?
faq.a: They carry the asset's own risk plus issuer, custody, legal and smart contract risk. Safety depends on the specific structure and the parties behind it.

real-world-assets.title: What are real-world assets (RWA) in crypto?
real-world-assets.description: What real-world assets (RWA) are in crypto, how tokenization works, the main RWA categories and the off-chain risks behind them.

tokenized-treasuries.short: Tokenized treasuries are blockchain tokens that represent shares in a fund or vehicle holding short-term government bonds such as US Treasury bills, passing their yield to holders.
body: A fund manager buys government bonds, holds them with a custodian, and issues tokens that represent fund shares. The token earns the bond yield, minus fees, either by rising in price over time or by distributing new tokens. Examples include products from Ondo Finance and BlackRock's BUIDL fund.

Their appeal is that stablecoins themselves usually do not pay interest to holders, while tokenized treasuries offer a yield linked to government rates and can still move on-chain. DAOs, crypto funds and some DeFi protocols use them for treasury management or collateral.

Many products are limited to qualified or non-US investors and require KYC and whitelisted wallets. Redemption may only be possible on business days and can take time. Yields follow central bank rates, so they change. Smart contract, custodian and legal risks apply on top of the bonds themselves.
tokenized-treasuries.example: Suppose a tokenized treasury fund holds T-bills yielding 4.5% a year and charges a 0.3% fee, giving a net yield of about 4.2%. You invest 20,000 USDC. After 6 months, your holding grows by about 20,000 times 0.042 divided by 2, which is 420 USD, to about 20,420 USD. If rates fall to 3% later, the net yield drops to about 2.7% and future earnings shrink accordingly.
mistakes: Assuming a tokenized treasury is a stablecoin you can spend anywhere.
Ignoring investor eligibility rules and buying a token you cannot redeem.
Treating today's yield as fixed when it follows interest rates.

faq.q: Are tokenized treasuries the same as stablecoins?
faq.a: No. Stablecoins aim to stay at a fixed value and usually pay no interest to holders. Tokenized treasuries pass on bond yield, and their value or token count grows over time.

faq.q: Who can buy tokenized treasuries?
faq.a: Many products are only open to verified or qualified investors in certain countries. Check the issuer's eligibility rules before buying.

tokenized-treasuries.title: What are tokenized treasuries? On-chain T-bills
tokenized-treasuries.description: How tokenized treasuries work, how they pass on government bond yields, who can buy them and how they differ from stablecoins.

tokenized-gold.short: Tokenized gold is a blockchain token backed by physical gold held in a vault, where each token represents a set amount of gold, often one fine troy ounce.
body: The issuer buys gold bars, stores them with a vault provider and issues tokens against them. Pax Gold (PAXG), issued by Paxos, and Tether Gold (XAUT) are the best-known examples, with each token representing one fine troy ounce of gold. Holders can trade the token on exchanges, move it on-chain or, under certain conditions, redeem it.

The advantage is that you can hold gold exposure in a crypto wallet, trade in small fractions and move value at any time of day. The token price follows the gold spot price closely, though small premiums or discounts can appear when crypto markets are trading and traditional gold markets are closed.

Your safety depends on the issuer's honesty, regular audits or attestations of the gold reserves, and the legal right to redeem. Physical redemption often has minimum amounts and fees, and some products allow redemption only for verified customers. Check these details for any gold token you hold.
tokenized-gold.example: Suppose gold trades at 2,400 USD per ounce and one token represents one ounce. You buy 0.25 tokens for about 600 USD. If gold rises 5% to 2,520 USD, your 0.25 tokens are worth about 630 USD. If you instead wanted to redeem for a physical bar, a minimum of, say, 400 ounces could apply, which would be about 960,000 USD at 2,400 USD per ounce.
mistakes: Assuming every gold token is equally audited and redeemable.
Expecting to redeem a small balance for physical gold when minimums apply.
Confusing a gold-backed token with a token that only tracks gold price through derivatives.

faq.q: Is PAXG backed by real gold?
faq.a: Paxos states that each PAXG is backed by one fine troy ounce of gold held in professional vaults, with regular reserve attestations.

faq.q: Can I redeem tokenized gold for physical gold?
faq.a: Some issuers allow it for verified customers, usually with minimum amounts and fees. Smaller holders typically sell the token for cash or stablecoins instead.

tokenized-gold.title: What is tokenized gold? Gold-backed tokens explained
tokenized-gold.description: How tokenized gold like PAXG and XAUT works, what backs each token, how redemption works and the issuer risks to check.
